Setup & first upload

Do this once. Afterwards every lab is: open the example, wire it, upload, open the Serial Monitor.

  1. Install MPLAB XC-DSC v4.00 or newer (the compiler) and MPLAB X (it provides ipecmd, used to program through a PICkit).
  2. Install the Arduino IDE 2.x.
  3. Install the board package with Boards Manager: File → Preferences → Additional boards manager URLs, add
    https://raw.githubusercontent.com/microchipthailand/dspic33ck-nano/main/package_dspicnano_index.json
    then Tools → Board → Boards Manager, search dsPIC33CK Nano and click Install (it also downloads the dsPIC33CK device packs).
    Alternative (for developing the core): copy the folder hardware from arduino\ into your sketchbook folder (File → Preferences → Sketchbook location, usually Documents\Arduino), so you get Documents\Arduino\hardware\dspicnano\dspic33ck\, and restart the IDE. Do not use both at once, or the board appears twice.
  4. Tools → Board → dsPIC33CK Nano (dsPIC33CK256MC005).
    Tools → Clock → 100 MIPS (recommended; Lab 22 requires it).
    Tools → Debugger → your programmer (PICkit 5 on J4).
  5. Plug the board into USB-C (power only — USB-C has no data on this board) and the PICkit into J4 (pin 1 = MCLR, marked on the silkscreen).
  6. For any lab that prints text, plug a 3.3 V USB-serial adapter into J5:
    J5 pinSignalAdapter
    13V3leave open (the board is powered by USB-C)
    2TX = RC10→ adapter RX
    3RX = RC11← adapter TX
    4GNDadapter GND
  7. File → Examples → dsPIC33CK_Nano → Lab01_Blink → Upload. Then Tools → Serial Monitor at 115200 baud for labs that print.
3.3 V only. The dsPIC I/O pins are 3.3 V. Never connect a 5 V signal directly to a pin (Lab 21 and Lab 24 tell you where this matters). The 5V pin (J2-1) is the raw USB voltage — use it only to power modules.
Status: every lab compiles with arduino-cli + XC-DSC at both clock settings (Lab 22 only at 100 MIPS, on purpose) and every J2/J3 pin number quoted here was checked automatically against the PCB netlist. The board has not yet been tested on real hardware, so the “expected output” boxes show what the code is written to print.

Why LED_ON instead of HIGH? The LED is wired 3V3 → 1k → LED → RC13, so the pin must go LOW to light it. The board package defines LED_ON (=LOW) and LED_OFF (=HIGH) so sketches read naturally.

Why does the button read LOW when pressed? A 10k resistor pulls RC12 up to 3.3 V; the button shorts it to GND.

Timers: Timer1 runs millis(). SCCP1–4 are the PWM channels for D5–D8; tone() borrows SCCP4 (so no PWM on D8 while a tone plays). The NanoTimer library (Lab 11) turns SCCP1–3 into Timer1–Timer3. Lab 13 borrows SCCP3; Labs 14, 16 (frequency check) and 19 (RTOS tick) borrow SCCP2. Labs 15 (DAC), 16 (motor PWM), 22 (WS2812B) and 26 (CAN) need 100 MIPS. The motor-control PWM generators PG1–PG3 (Lab 16) are separate hardware on RB10–RB15.

Learning path: Basics 01–09 = one peripheral at a time with the Arduino API. Advanced 10–19 = register level: pin-change and timer interrupts, interrupt-driven UART, DMA, DAC, motor-control PWM, flash EEPROM, power/reset, a small RTOS. Lab 28 (watchdog, software reset, clock switching) was added later and belongs to this group. Application 20–27 = complete projects, modules and buses: data logger, GPS, LED strip, OLED, Modbus RS485, LIN, CAN, 10BASE-T1S. Labs 29 (line follower robot with servos and a Bluetooth remote) and 30 (PID temperature control) were added later and belong to this group.

How every lab is organised: Objectives (what you will learn) → Background (the idea behind it, then what is special on the dsPIC33CK) → You need and Wiring (parts list, breadboard picture, exact header pins) → Step by step (what to do and what you should see) → Expected output → How the code works (the sketch explained with excerpts) → Key registers (register-level labs) → Try it yourself (exercises: Easy Medium Challenge) → Troubleshooting → Check your understanding (click a question to see the answer). Blue notes say what has been tested and how: nothing in this guide has been tested on real hardware yet; many labs were checked in the MPLAB simulator, and the notes say which.

Basics Labs 01–09 · one peripheral at a time, with the Arduino API

01Blink the USER LED

Your first program: prove that the tool-chain, the programmer and the board all work by making the on-board USER LED flash.

basicspinModedigitalWritedelaydigital outputactive-low LED

Objectives

  • After this lab you can select the dsPIC33CK Nano board and clock in the Arduino IDE, and upload a sketch.
  • After this lab you can explain what setup() and loop() do and in which order they run.
  • After this lab you can make a pin an output with pinMode() and switch it with digitalWrite().
  • After this lab you can explain why the USER LED is active low and why LED_ON is LOW.
  • After this lab you can create timing patterns with delay() and know where its 1 ms tick comes from.

Background

Digital output. A microcontroller pin used as a digital output can be in only two states: HIGH (the pin is connected inside the chip to the supply, here 3.3 V) or LOW (connected to ground, 0 V). Nothing in between. Turning an LED, a relay driver or a buzzer on and off is the most basic job of a microcontroller, and it is always done this way.

Ports and pins. The dsPIC33CK groups its pins into ports A, B, C and D. A pin name like RC13 means “port C, bit 13”. Inside the chip every port has a few control registers. The two that matter here are TRISx (direction: 1 = input, 0 = output) and LATx (the level the pin drives when it is an output). Arduino hides these behind simple numbers: RC13 is Arduino pin 34, and the board package calls it LED_BUILTIN. pinMode(34, OUTPUT) clears bit 13 of TRISC; digitalWrite(34, LOW) clears bit 13 of the port C output latch.

Active-low LED. On many boards the LED goes from the pin to ground, so HIGH lights it. On the dsPIC33CK Nano it is the other way round: the LED’s anode goes to 3.3 V through a 1 kΩ resistor and its cathode goes to the pin. Current can only flow (and the LED can only light) when the pin is LOW. This is called active low. To save you from remembering it, the board package defines LED_ON = LOW and LED_OFF = HIGH.

3V3 ---[ 1k ]---|>|--- RC13 (D34, LED_BUILTIN) LED RC13 = LOW : 3.3 V across resistor + LED -> current flows -> LED ON RC13 = HIGH : 3.3 V on both sides -> no current -> LED OFF

setup() and loop(). Every Arduino sketch has these two functions. After a reset the core first prepares the chip (clock, timer, pins), then calls setup() once, then calls loop() again and again forever. A microcontroller program never “ends”: there is no operating system to return to.

Time on the dsPIC33CK. delay(ms) simply waits. The core sets up Timer1 to raise an interrupt every 1 ms; each interrupt adds 1 to a counter, which is what millis() returns. delay(200) waits until that counter has moved on by 200. The timer reload value is computed from FCY (the instruction clock), so the timing stays correct whichever clock you pick in Tools → Clock: 100 MIPS (internal FRC oscillator + PLL, FOSC 200 MHz) or 4 MIPS (8 MHz FRC alone).

You need

USB-C cable + 5 V supply (PC port or charger)1USB-C is power only, it carries no data
PICkit programmer (PICkit 4 / 5 or similar) + its USB cable1plugs into J4 (ICSP). Alternatively upload with the Serial bootloader through a 3.3 V USB-serial adapter on J5, see Setup
PC with the Arduino IDE and the dsPIC33CK Nano board package1installed as described in Setup

Wiring

Nothing to wire on a breadboard. The only connection is the programmer on the ICSP header J4. The PICkit’s pin 1 (marked with an arrow) goes to J4-1.

SignalBoard pinOther end
MCLR (reset / programming voltage)J4-1PICkit pin 1
3V3 (target voltage sense)J4-2PICkit pin 2
GNDJ4-3PICkit pin 3
PGD3 (program data)RB5 J4-4PICkit pin 4
PGC3 (program clock)RB6 J4-5PICkit pin 5
not connectedJ4-6–

The LED itself is already on the board: RC13 = D34, not brought out to a header pin you need for this lab.

Step by step

  1. Plug the USB-C cable into the board. The power LED lights and stays on. If it does not, check the cable and supply before going further.
  2. Plug the PICkit into J4 (pin 1 to pin 1) and connect the PICkit to the PC. The PC should recognise the programmer; nothing changes on the board yet.
  3. In the Arduino IDE choose Tools → Board → dsPIC33CK Nano and Tools → Clock → 100 MIPS. These settings tell the compiler which chip and which clock speed the code is built for.
  4. Open File → Examples → dsPIC33CK_Nano → Lab01_Blink. A new window opens with the sketch. Read the comment at the top: it repeats the LED wiring explained above.
  5. Click Verify (the tick). The output pane at the bottom should end with the program size and no red error lines. This proves the compiler is installed correctly.
  6. Click Upload. The PICkit programs the chip through J4; this takes a few seconds. Wait for the “done” message in the output pane.
  7. Look at the USER LED. It flashes 200 ms on, 800 ms off – one short flash per second. Short on, long off is chosen so you can tell “on” from “off”: had the LED logic been inverted, you would see long on, short off.
  8. Press the RESET button. The LED stops while the button is held and starts blinking again when you release it, because the program starts again from setup().
  9. Change the two delay() values, for example to 50 and 950, and upload again. The flash becomes shorter. This proves you are really changing the program on the chip and not looking at an old one.
  10. Choose Tools → Clock → 4 MIPS and upload again. The blink rate stays the same, because delay() is calculated from FCY. The CPU is now 25 times slower, but for this program that makes no visible difference.

How the code works

#include <Arduino.h>

This brings in the board package: the pin numbers, LED_BUILTIN, LED_ON / LED_OFF, and all the Arduino functions. The IDE adds it for you anyway, but writing it makes the sketch clearer.

void setup()
{
    pinMode(LED_BUILTIN, OUTPUT);
}

setup() runs once after reset. LED_BUILTIN is pin 34 = RC13. pinMode(..., OUTPUT) clears bit 13 of TRISC, so the pin now drives a level instead of only listening. After reset every pin is an input, so this line is required before the LED can be controlled.

void loop()
{
    digitalWrite(LED_BUILTIN, LED_ON);
    delay(200);
    digitalWrite(LED_BUILTIN, LED_OFF);
    delay(800);
}

loop() is called over and over. digitalWrite(LED_BUILTIN, LED_ON) drives RC13 LOW (because LED_ON = LOW), so current flows and the LED lights. delay(200) waits 200 Timer1 ticks of 1 ms. Then the pin goes HIGH, the LED goes dark, and the program waits 800 ms. When loop() returns, the core calls it again at once, so the pattern repeats with a period of 200 + 800 = 1000 ms.

While delay() waits, the CPU does nothing else useful. That is fine here, but in Lab 02 you will see why later labs use millis() instead.

Try it yourself

  1. Easy Make the LED blink twice as fast with a 50 % on-time (on as long as off). Hint: change both numbers in the two delay() calls in loop().
  2. Easy Swap LED_ON and LED_OFF in loop(). Predict first what you will see (long on, short off), then check.
  3. Medium Make an SOS pattern: ··· ——— ··· (dot = 200 ms on, dash = 600 ms on, 200 ms off between signals, 1.5 s pause at the end). Hint: write a helper function void flash(int onMs) above loop() and call it nine times inside loop().
  4. Medium Use a for loop in loop() to blink 1 time, pause, 2 times, pause, … up to 5, then start again.
  5. Challenge Make a “heartbeat”: two quick flashes (100 ms on, 100 ms off, 100 ms on) then 700 ms off. Then change the total period to 600 ms (100 beats per minute) and calculate the new pause. Hint: all the timing lives in the delay() values in loop().

Troubleshooting

SymptomLikely causeFix
Power LED is offNo supply on USB-C, or a bad cableTry another cable and another USB port or charger.
Upload fails, “programmer not found” or “target not found”PICkit not connected, plugged in the wrong way round, or the board not poweredCheck that PICkit pin 1 is on J4-1 and that the power LED is on. Re-plug the PICkit USB cable.
Compile error about the board or a missing fileWrong board selected or the board package not installedChoose Tools → Board → dsPIC33CK Nano; repeat the installation in Setup.
LED is on most of the time with short dark gapsLOW/HIGH were written directly and swapped, forgetting the LED is active lowUse LED_ON / LED_OFF instead of HIGH / LOW.
Upload reports success but the LED does not changeThe board is held in reset, or the old program is still there because a different sketch window was uploadedRelease RESET; make sure you clicked Upload in the window you edited; press RESET once.

Check your understanding

Why does digitalWrite(LED_BUILTIN, LOW) turn the USER LED on?

The LED’s anode is tied to 3.3 V through 1 kΩ and its cathode is on RC13. Only when RC13 is at 0 V is there a voltage across the LED, so current flows. The LED is active low; LED_ON is defined as LOW for that reason.

How many times does setup() run, and how many times does loop() run?

setup() runs once after each reset. loop() runs again and again for as long as the board has power – here once per second, because one pass takes 200 + 800 ms.

You switch from 100 MIPS to 4 MIPS. Why does the blink rate not change?

delay() counts 1 ms interrupts from Timer1, and the Timer1 period is calculated from FCY for the chosen clock. So 1 ms stays 1 ms; only the CPU speed changes.

What would happen if you deleted the pinMode() line?

RC13 would stay an input (its reset state). digitalWrite() would only change the output latch, which is not connected to the pin while it is an input, so the LED would not blink.

02Button toggles the LED (debounce)

Read a digital input, remove contact bounce in software, and toggle the USER LED exactly once per press.

basicsdigitalReadmillisdebounceedge detectionpull-up

Objectives

  • After this lab you can read a push-button with pinMode(..., INPUT) and digitalRead().
  • After this lab you can explain what a pull-up resistor does and why the USER button reads LOW when pressed.
  • After this lab you can explain contact bounce and remove it with a time-based software debounce.
  • After this lab you can detect an edge (the moment of change) instead of a level, so a held button acts only once.
  • After this lab you can write a non-blocking loop that measures time with millis() instead of waiting with delay().

Background

Digital input. When a pin is an input, the chip does not drive it; it only looks at the voltage on it. A voltage close to 3.3 V reads HIGH, a voltage close to 0 V reads LOW; in the middle the result is not defined (the exact thresholds are in the data sheet). digitalRead() returns that level as HIGH or LOW.

Why a pull-up is needed. A push-button only connects or disconnects two wires. If one side goes to GND and the other to the pin, the pin is at 0 V while the button is pressed – but when it is released, the pin is connected to nothing. Such a floating input picks up noise and reads random values. A pull-up resistor from the pin to 3.3 V fixes this: when the button is open, the resistor gently pulls the pin HIGH; when the button is closed, it connects the pin straight to GND, which wins over the resistor, and the pin reads LOW. The resistor value (here 10 kΩ) limits the current while the button is held to 3.3 V / 10 kΩ = 0.33 mA.

3V3 | [10k] R6 (pull-up on the board) | +------------ RC12 (D33, BUTTON_BUILTIN) | _|_ USER button SW2 o o | GND released -> HIGH pressed -> LOW

The dsPIC33CK also has internal pull-ups that pinMode(pin, INPUT_PULLUP) switches on. The USER button already has the external 10 kΩ resistor R6, so the sketch uses plain INPUT (which switches the internal pull-up off).

Contact bounce. A button is a piece of springy metal. When it closes, it hits the contact, jumps back and hits it again, several times in a few milliseconds. The chip is fast enough to see every one of those as a separate press. If the program toggled the LED on every change, one press could toggle it 2, 3 or 5 times, and the result would look random.

button pin: HIGH ‾‾‾‾‾|_|‾|_|‾|________________|‾|_|‾‾‾‾‾ (bounces ~1-10 ms) <---- 25 ms ----> stable LOW -> accept the press

Debouncing means: only believe a new level after it has stayed the same for a while. This sketch uses 25 ms. That is longer than typical bounce, but far shorter than a human press (around 100 ms or more), so it does not feel slow.

Level versus edge. “The button is pressed” is a level; it stays true as long as you hold it. “The button has just been pressed” is an edge; it happens once. To toggle the LED once per press, the program acts on the falling edge (stable HIGH → stable LOW) only.

You need

PartQtyNotes
dsPIC33CK Nano board1USER button (SW2) and USER LED are on the board
USB-C cable + 5 V supply1power only
PICkit on J4 (or USB-serial adapter for the bootloader)1for uploading, as in Lab 01

Wiring

Nothing to wire — both parts are on the board:

SignalBoard pinOther end
USER button (SW2), 10 kΩ pull-up R6RC12 = D33 (BUTTON_BUILTIN), also on J2-10on-board button to GND
USER LED, active lowRC13 = D34 (LED_BUILTIN), also on J2-11on-board LED + 1 kΩ to 3V3

Step by step

  1. Power the board and connect the programmer as in Lab 01. The power LED is on.
  2. Open Examples → dsPIC33CK_Nano → Lab02_ButtonLED and click Upload. After the upload the USER LED is off, because setup() writes LED_OFF.
  3. Press USER once and release. The LED turns on at the moment you press (about 25 ms later, too short to notice), not when you release.
  4. Press again: the LED turns off. Repeat ten times quickly: every press toggles exactly once.
  5. Press and hold USER for several seconds. The LED changes once and then stays as it is. This shows the edge detection: holding is not a new press.
  6. Release slowly and press lightly to try to make the button “chatter”. The LED still toggles once per press, because short changes shorter than 25 ms are ignored.
  7. To see why debouncing matters, change DEBOUNCE_MS to 0 and upload. Now press many times: some presses will toggle twice (on then off again) and look ignored, or the LED changes on release. How often this happens depends on your particular button.
  8. Set DEBOUNCE_MS to 500 and upload. A press must now be held for more than 0.5 s before the LED reacts; a quick tap is ignored completely, and a quick double press counts as one, because the level never stays the same for 500 ms in between. Put the value back to 25 when you are done.

How the code works

const unsigned long DEBOUNCE_MS = 25;

int  stableState   = HIGH;          /* debounced button level */
int  lastReading   = HIGH;
unsigned long lastChange = 0;
bool ledOn = false;

Global variables keep their value between calls of loop(). stableState is the level we believe (debounced); lastReading is the raw level seen last time; lastChange is the millis() time when the raw level last changed; ledOn remembers the LED state. Both levels start as HIGH because the button is released at reset. Times use unsigned long because millis() returns that type.

void setup()
{
    pinMode(LED_BUILTIN, OUTPUT);
    digitalWrite(LED_BUILTIN, LED_OFF);
    pinMode(BUTTON_BUILTIN, INPUT);  /* external pull-up on the board */
}

The LED pin becomes an output and is switched off. The button pin becomes an input. INPUT (not INPUT_PULLUP) is enough because R6 already pulls the pin up.

    int reading = digitalRead(BUTTON_BUILTIN);

    if (reading != lastReading) {      /* contact bounced or moved */
        lastChange  = millis();
        lastReading = reading;
    }

Every pass of loop() reads the raw pin. If it differs from the last reading, something moved (a real press or a bounce), so the “quiet” timer is restarted by storing the current time. During bouncing this happens again and again, so lastChange keeps moving forward.

    if ((millis() - lastChange) > DEBOUNCE_MS && reading != stableState) {
        stableState = reading;
        if (stableState == LOW) {      /* pressed: falling edge */
            ledOn = !ledOn;
            digitalWrite(LED_BUILTIN, ledOn ? LED_ON : LED_OFF);
        }
    }

millis() - lastChange is how long the raw level has been unchanged. Only when that is more than 25 ms and the level differs from what we believed, the new level is accepted. If the newly accepted level is LOW, the button has just been pressed (falling edge): ledOn is flipped with ! and the LED is written. When the button is released, the stable level goes back to HIGH, but nothing else happens – the release is accepted silently.

The subtraction millis() - lastChange also stays correct when the millis() counter wraps around after about 49.7 days, because unsigned arithmetic wraps the same way.

Note that millis() is used instead of delay(): the loop never stops, it runs thousands of times per second and just checks the clock. This “non-blocking” pattern is what every later lab builds on, because it leaves the CPU free to do other jobs in the same loop.

Try it yourself

  1. Easy Make the LED toggle on release instead of press. Hint: change stableState == LOW to HIGH in the inner if.
  2. Easy Make the LED simply follow the button (on while held, off when released), without toggling. Hint: inside the debounce if, write the LED from stableState directly.
  3. Medium Count presses in a new global variable and, 2 s after the last press, blink the count back on the LED. Hint: increment the counter where ledOn is flipped; store the time of the last press and check it with millis() at the end of loop().
  4. Medium Long press (> 1 s) = fast blink mode, short press = toggle as before. Hint: store millis() on the falling edge, and on the rising edge (stableState == HIGH) compare the held time.
  5. Challenge Move the debounce code into a function bool buttonPressed() that returns true once per press, so loop() becomes one line: if (buttonPressed()) { ... }. Use static local variables instead of globals.

Troubleshooting

SymptomLikely causeFix
Some presses seem ignored or toggle twiceDEBOUNCE_MS too small for this buttonSet it back to 25, or try 40.
Fast double presses count as oneDEBOUNCE_MS too largeUse a value between 10 and 50 ms.
LED toggles once and then never againThe edge test was changed to a level test, or stableState is never updatedCompare with the original sketch: stableState = reading; must run every time a new level is accepted.
LED blinks on its own when nothing is pressed (after you change to another pin)The new input pin is floating – it has no pull-upUse INPUT_PULLUP or add an external 10 kΩ resistor to 3V3.
LED does nothing at allUpload failed, or the board is held in resetCheck the upload messages; release RESET; the LED should be off right after reset.

Check your understanding

Why does the USER button read LOW when it is pressed?

The 10 kΩ pull-up R6 holds the pin at 3.3 V while the button is open. Pressing it connects the pin directly to GND, which wins over the resistor, so the pin sees 0 V.

What would happen without the debounce check, toggling on every raw change to LOW?

Each bounce of the contact would be seen as a new press, so one press could toggle the LED several times. With an even number of toggles the press looks ignored.

Why does holding the button not keep toggling the LED?

The LED is toggled only when the stable level changes to LOW (the falling edge). While the button is held, reading equals stableState, so the inner code does not run again.

Why is millis() better than delay(25) here?

delay() would freeze the whole program for 25 ms each time. With millis() the loop keeps running and only compares times, so other tasks can be added to the same loop.

03Serial Monitor: print and receive commands

Talk to the PC through the UART header J5: print text to the Serial Monitor and control the LED with one-letter commands.

basicsSerial.beginSerial.printSerial.readUARTbaud ratemillis

Objectives

  • After this lab you can connect a 3.3 V USB-serial adapter to J5 with TX and RX crossed.
  • After this lab you can explain what a UART is, what a baud rate is, and why both sides must use the same one.
  • After this lab you can print text and numbers with Serial.print() / Serial.println().
  • After this lab you can receive single-character commands with Serial.available() and Serial.read().
  • After this lab you can run two jobs in one loop (commands and a 2 s heartbeat) without delay().

Background

Why a serial port? The board has no screen. The easiest way to see what a program is doing – and to send it commands – is to exchange text with the PC. Almost every microcontroller lab from here on uses this. On the dsPIC33CK Nano the USB-C socket carries power only, so the text goes through the UART header J5 and a small USB-serial adapter (CP2102, CH340, FT232 …) that appears on the PC as a COM port.

UART. A UART (Universal Asynchronous Receiver/Transmitter) sends bytes one bit at a time over a single wire, TX (transmit). A second wire, RX (receive), carries bytes the other way. “Asynchronous” means there is no clock wire: both sides agree in advance how long one bit lasts. The line rests HIGH. Each byte starts with a LOW start bit, then 8 data bits (lowest bit first), then a HIGH stop bit. This is called 8N1 (8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit).

idle start b0 b1 b2 b3 b4 b5 b6 b7 stop idle TX line ‾‾‾‾‾|_____|‾‾‾|___|___|___|___|‾‾‾|‾‾‾|___|‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾ = 'a' (0x61 = 0110 0001) |<-- 10 bits = 1 character, 86.8 µs at 115200 baud -->|

Baud rate. The baud rate is the number of bits per second. At 115200 baud one bit lasts 1/115200 s = 8.68 µs and one character (10 bits with start and stop) takes 86.8 µs, so about 11 500 characters per second fit on the line. The receiver samples each bit in its middle, so the two clocks only have to agree within a few percent. If the Serial Monitor is set to a different baud rate than the sketch, the bits are sampled at the wrong moments and you see garbage characters or nothing.

Crossed wires. One side’s TX must go to the other side’s RX, like a telephone: your mouth to their ear. GND must be shared, otherwise the two sides do not agree on what “0 V” is.

On the dsPIC33CK. Serial uses UART1. Peripheral Pin Select routes its TX to RC10 (J5-2) and RX to RC11 (J5-3). The core uses the fractional baud generator: the divider is FCY / baud, rounded. At 100 MIPS that gives 115207 baud (0.01 % off), at 4 MIPS 114286 baud (−0.8 %), both well inside what a receiver tolerates. Received bytes are stored by an interrupt in a 64-byte buffer, so none are lost while your code is busy for a moment; Serial.available() tells how many are waiting. Sending waits only until the UART can accept the next byte.

You need

PartQtyNotes
dsPIC33CK Nano board1USER LED and USER button are on the board
USB-C cable + 5 V supply1power only, no data
3.3 V USB-serial adapter (CP2102, CH340, FT232 set to 3.3 V)1its driver must be installed so it shows up as a COM port
Female-female jumper wires3TX, RX, GND
PICkit on J4 (or the Serial bootloader over the same adapter)1for uploading, see Setup

Wiring

SignalBoard pinAdapter pin
Board TX (MCU transmit)RC10 J5-2RX
Board RX (MCU receive)RC11 J5-3TX
GroundGND J5-4GND
3V3J5-1leave unconnected (the board is powered from USB-C)
Use an adapter with 3.3 V logic levels. Do not connect the adapter’s 5 V or 3.3 V supply pin to J5-1 while the board is powered from USB-C – two supplies would fight each other.

Step by step

  1. Wire the adapter: J5-2 (TX) → adapter RX, J5-3 (RX) ← adapter TX, J5-4 → GND. Plug the adapter into the PC and power the board from USB-C. A new COM port appears in Tools → Port (on Windows also in Device Manager).
  2. Open Examples → dsPIC33CK_Nano → Lab03_SerialHello and upload it. The USER LED stays off (setup() writes LED_OFF).
  3. Tools → Port → choose the adapter’s COM port, then open Tools → Serial Monitor. Set the speed box to 115200 baud and the line ending to Newline. You should see tick 0, tick 1, … appear, one every 2 seconds.
  4. Press RESET (SW1) to see the greeting. The two greeting lines appear first, then the ticks start again from 0, because counter starts at 0 after every reset. The first tick comes 2 s after reset.
  5. Type 1 in the input line and press Enter. The Monitor shows LED ON and the USER LED lights.
  6. Type 0 and Enter: LED OFF, and the LED goes dark. The ticks keep coming at the same rate in between: both jobs share one loop.
  7. Type ? and Enter: the board prints how many milliseconds have passed since reset and the state of the USER button. Hold USER and send ? again: the second line now says pressed.
  8. Type 10 and Enter. You see LED ON immediately followed by LED OFF: the board receives the characters one by one, '1' then '0', and handles each. The Newline character at the end is ignored because no command matches it.
  9. Change the Monitor speed to 9600 baud. The text becomes garbage or disappears. Set it back to 115200 and the text is readable again. This shows that both sides must use the same baud rate.

Expected output

Lab 03 - dsPIC33CK Nano says hello!
Send 1 (LED on), 0 (LED off) or ? (status)
tick 0
LED ON
uptime ms = 3521
button    = released
tick 1

The first line is empty (from Serial.println() with no text). LED ON appears after sending 1, the two status lines after sending ?. Your uptime ms value depends on when you send the command.

How the code works

unsigned long counter = 0;

void setup()
{
    pinMode(LED_BUILTIN, OUTPUT);
    digitalWrite(LED_BUILTIN, LED_OFF);
    Serial.begin(115200);
    Serial.println();
    Serial.println("Lab 03 - dsPIC33CK Nano says hello!");
    Serial.println("Send 1 (LED on), 0 (LED off) or ? (status)");
}

Serial.begin(115200) sets up UART1: pins RC10/RC11 through Peripheral Pin Select, the baud rate divider, the receive interrupt. It must come before any other Serial call. Serial.println() sends the text followed by a carriage return and line feed (\r\n), so the next output starts on a new line. The first println() without text just ends any half line that may already be on the screen.

    if (Serial.available() > 0) {
        int c = Serial.read();
        if (c == '1') {
            digitalWrite(LED_BUILTIN, LED_ON);
            Serial.println("LED ON");
        } else if (c == '0') {
            digitalWrite(LED_BUILTIN, LED_OFF);
            Serial.println("LED OFF");
        } else if (c == '?') {
            ...
        }
    }

Serial.available() returns how many received bytes are waiting in the 64-byte buffer. If there is at least one, Serial.read() takes the oldest one out. Each pass of loop() handles at most one character; if more are waiting, the next passes take them. Characters are compared with character constants like '1' (the ASCII code 49), not the number 1. Any other character – including the Newline sent by the Monitor – matches no branch and is silently dropped.

            Serial.print("uptime ms = ");
            Serial.println(millis());
            Serial.print("button    = ");
            Serial.println(digitalRead(BUTTON_BUILTIN) == LOW ? "pressed" : "released");

Serial.print() sends text without a line end, so the number from millis() lands on the same line. print and println turn numbers into decimal text for you. The ? : operator picks one of two strings: the USER button reads LOW when pressed (Lab 02).

    static unsigned long last = 0;
    if (millis() - last >= 2000) {     /* heartbeat every 2 s */
        last = millis();
        Serial.print("tick ");
        Serial.println(counter++);
    }

This is the non-blocking timer from Lab 02. static means last keeps its value between calls of loop() but is only visible inside it. Every time 2000 ms have passed since the last tick, one line is printed and counter is printed and then increased (counter++ uses the old value first). Because there is no delay(), the command check at the top runs thousands of times between two ticks, so commands are answered at once.

Try it yourself

  1. Easy Change the heartbeat to every 500 ms and print millis() on the same line as the tick number. Hint: the 2000 in the heartbeat if, plus one more Serial.print().
  2. Easy Add a command t that toggles the LED. Hint: add another else if (c == 't') branch; you need a variable that remembers the LED state.
  3. Medium Print a help text when an unknown character is received, but not for '\n' and '\r'. Hint: a final else if / else after the '?' branch.
  4. Medium Add commands + and - that make the heartbeat faster and slower, and print the new interval. Hint: replace the constant 2000 with a global variable.
  5. Challenge Accept a whole number, for example b250 + Enter, meaning “blink the LED every 250 ms”. Hint: collect digits into a number until '\n' arrives, then act; the blinking needs its own millis() timer like the heartbeat.

Troubleshooting

SymptomLikely causeFix
Nothing at all in the Serial MonitorTX and RX not crossed, or wrong COM port selectedSwap the two signal wires first; check Tools → Port is the adapter’s port.
Random garbage charactersBaud rate in the Monitor is not 115200Set the speed box to 115200.
Ticks arrive but commands do nothingAdapter TX is not connected to J5-3, or GND is missingCheck the adapter TX → J5-3 wire and the GND wire.
No COM port appearsAdapter driver not installed, or a charge-only USB cable on the adapterInstall the CP210x / CH340 / FTDI driver; try another cable.
Greeting lines are missingThe Monitor was opened after the board had already printed themPress RESET with the Monitor open.
“Port busy” when uploading with the bootloaderThe Serial Monitor holds the COM portClose the Serial Monitor before uploading, reopen it afterwards.

Check your understanding

How long does one character take at 115200 baud, and why 10 bits?

One start bit + 8 data bits + one stop bit = 10 bits. 10 / 115200 s ≈ 86.8 µs per character.

Why must board TX go to adapter RX?

TX is the output that sends, RX is the input that listens. Connecting TX to TX would put two outputs together and nobody would listen.

You type ? while the program is printing a tick. Is the command lost?

No. The receive interrupt stores the byte in the 64-byte buffer as soon as it arrives. The next pass of loop() finds it with Serial.available().

What is the difference between Serial.print(x) and Serial.println(x)?

println adds a carriage return and line feed after the value, so the next output starts on a new line; print does not.

TX and RX always cross: board TX goes to adapter RX. If you see nothing, swap the two wires first.

04Read a potentiometer with the ADC

Convert a voltage into a number with the analog-to-digital converter, turn the number back into volts, and show the level on the LED.

basicsanalogReadADCSerial Plotterpotentiometerresolution

Objectives

  • After this lab you can wire a potentiometer as a voltage divider to an analog input.
  • After this lab you can explain what an ADC does, and what resolution and reference voltage mean.
  • After this lab you can read a voltage with analogRead() and convert the result to volts.
  • After this lab you can explain why analogRead() returns 0–1023 although the dsPIC33CK ADC is 12-bit.
  • After this lab you can make a decision from an analog value (a threshold) and plot values with the Serial Plotter.

Background

Analog versus digital. In Lab 02 a pin could only be HIGH or LOW. Many sensors (light, temperature, position, a knob) give a voltage that can be anything between 0 and 3.3 V. To work with such a value the chip needs an ADC (analog-to-digital converter): a circuit that measures the voltage on a pin and returns it as a whole number.

The potentiometer. A potentiometer (“pot”) is a resistor track with a sliding contact, the wiper. With one end on 3.3 V and the other on GND, the wiper picks off any voltage in between: a voltage divider whose ratio you set by turning the knob.

3V3 (J3-1) ---+ | [ ] 10k track [ ]<------- wiper ----> RA0 = A0 (J2-15) [ ] | GND (J3-2) ---+ knob fully one way: 0 V, other way: 3.3 V

Resolution. An ADC divides its input range into a fixed number of steps. An n-bit ADC has 2n steps: 10-bit = 1024 steps (0–1023), 12-bit = 4096 steps (0–4095). The more bits, the smaller the voltage change it can notice.

Reference voltage. The ADC compares the input with a reference voltage: 0 V gives 0, the reference gives the highest number. On this board the reference is the analog supply AVDD = 3.3 V. So the size of one step is 3.3 V / 4096 ≈ 0.8 mV for the raw 12-bit result, or 3.3 V / 1024 ≈ 3.2 mV for the 0–1023 value. To turn a reading back into volts: volts = raw × 3.3 / 1023. A reading can never show more than the reference, and the result is only as accurate as the 3.3 V supply itself.

Wiper voltage12-bit resultanalogRead() (example values)
0 V00
1.65 V (middle)about 2048about 512
3.3 V40951023

On the dsPIC33CK. The chip has a 12-bit ADC (0–4095). Each analog pin is one channel: A0 is pin RA0, channel AN0. analogRead() switches the pin to analog mode, starts one conversion on that channel by software, waits until it is ready and reads the result. The core then shifts the result right by 2 (divides by 4), so analogRead() returns the familiar Arduino range 0–1023 and sketches written for other Arduino boards work unchanged. Lab 14 reads the full 12-bit value.

The analog inputs must never see more than 3.3 V. Connect the pot ends to 3V3 (J3-1), never to +5V (J2-1).

You need

PartQtyNotes
dsPIC33CK Nano board1USER LED shows “above half”
USB-C cable + 5 V supply1power only
3.3 V USB-serial adapter on J51wired as in Lab 03, for the Serial Monitor / Plotter
10 kΩ potentiometer (linear)1any value from 1 kΩ to 50 kΩ works
Breadboard + jumper wires33V3, GND, wiper
PICkit on J4 (or the Serial bootloader)1for uploading

Wiring

PotBoardNotes
end 13V3 J3-1top of the divider
wiper (middle)A0 = RA0 J2-15analog channel AN0
end 2GND J3-2bottom of the divider

The USB-serial adapter stays on J5 as in Lab 03 (adapter RX → J5-2, adapter TX → J5-3, GND → J5-4, J5-1 open).

Step by step

  1. Wire the pot as in the table. Check once more that the end goes to 3V3 (J3-1), not +5V. Power the board.
  2. Upload Lab04_AnalogRead and open the Serial Monitor at 115200 baud. Press RESET: you see the line Lab 04 - pot on RA0 (A0), then five lines per second (one every 200 ms).
  3. Turn the knob fully to one end. raw goes to 0 and volts to 0.000 (or the other way round to 1023 / 3.300, depending on which end is on 3V3). Small changes in the last digit are normal: that is electrical noise of about one step.
  4. Turn the knob slowly across its range: raw goes 0 … 1023 and volts 0.000 … 3.300. Check with the formula: raw 511 → 511 × 3.3 / 1023 = 1.648 V.
  5. Past the middle (raw > 512) the USER LED lights; below it the LED is off. The LED is decided by the program from the number, not by the voltage directly.
  6. If you have a multimeter, measure between J2-15 and GND and compare with volts. The two should be close; the difference shows how far the 3.3 V supply is from exactly 3.300 V.
  7. Close the Serial Monitor and open Tools → Serial Plotter (115200 baud). Turn the knob and watch the graph follow it.
  8. Disconnect the wiper wire from J2-15 and watch the numbers. They drift or jump randomly: an analog input with nothing connected is floating, like the digital input without a pull-up in Lab 02. Reconnect it.

Expected output

Lab 04 - pot on RA0 (A0)
raw=0  volts=0.000
raw=511  volts=1.648
raw=1023  volts=3.300

Shown: the start line, then one line each with the knob at one end, in the middle and at the other end. While you turn the knob, many more lines with values in between are printed.

How the code works

void setup()
{
    pinMode(LED_BUILTIN, OUTPUT);
    Serial.begin(115200);
    Serial.println("Lab 04 - pot on RA0 (A0)");
}

The LED pin becomes an output, the serial port is started as in Lab 03, and a start line is printed. There is no pinMode() for A0: analogRead() puts the pin into analog input mode itself. The ADC is switched on and configured the first time analogRead() is called.

    int raw = analogRead(A0);
    double volts = raw * 3.3 / 1023.0;

analogRead(A0) converts the voltage on RA0 and returns 0–1023 (the 12-bit result shifted right by 2). The conversion to volts must be done in floating point: writing 3.3 and 1023.0 makes C calculate with decimals. With only integers, raw * 3 / 1023 would give just 0, 1, 2 or 3.

    Serial.print("raw=");
    Serial.print(raw);
    Serial.print("  volts=");
    Serial.println(volts, 3);

The four calls build one line. The second argument of Serial.println(volts, 3) is the number of digits after the decimal point.

    /* LED lights when the pot is above half scale */
    digitalWrite(LED_BUILTIN, raw > 512 ? LED_ON : LED_OFF);
    delay(200);

A simple threshold: if the reading is more than 512 (half of 1023, about 1.65 V), the LED is switched on, otherwise off. delay(200) limits the output to five lines per second, so the Monitor stays readable.

Try it yourself

  1. Easy Print the value in millivolts as a whole number. Hint: after the volts line, compute long mv = (long)raw * 3300 / 1023; and print it.
  2. Easy Light the LED only in the top quarter of the range. Hint: change the 512 in the digitalWrite() line.
  3. Medium Add hysteresis: LED on above 600, off below 400, unchanged in between, so it does not flicker at the threshold. Hint: replace the ? : line with two ifs and a variable that remembers the LED state.
  4. Medium Reduce noise by averaging 16 readings before printing. Hint: a for loop that adds analogRead(A0) into a long, then divide by 16.
  5. Challenge Make the LED blink with a period set by the pot (50 ms to 1 s) while still printing every 200 ms. Hint: remove delay(200) and use two millis() timers as in Lab 03; map() (Lab 05) converts 0–1023 into a period.

Troubleshooting

SymptomLikely causeFix
Value jumps around randomlyWiper not connected to J2-15 (floating input)Check the wiper wire; the wiper is the middle leg of the pot.
Always 0 or always 1023Wiper on the wrong leg, or an end of the pot not connectedMeasure the wiper with a multimeter while turning; it must change.
Reaches 1023 at about two thirds of the knob and stays therePot connected to +5V instead of 3V3Disconnect at once and move the wire to J3-1 (3V3).
volts always shows 0, 1, 2 or 3The formula was changed to integer arithmeticKeep 3.3 and 1023.0 as decimal numbers.
Serial Plotter shows no linesThe Plotter cannot split raw=… into values in your IDE versionTry printing raw: and volts: instead of raw= and volts=, or just the bare numbers separated by a space.
Nothing in the MonitorSerial wiringSee the Lab 03 troubleshooting table.

Check your understanding

The ADC is 12-bit. How many steps is that, and what voltage is one step of the raw result?

212 = 4096 steps (0–4095). One step is 3.3 V / 4096 ≈ 0.8 mV.

Why does analogRead() return at most 1023?

The core shifts the 12-bit result right by 2 (divides by 4) so the range matches standard Arduino boards with a 10-bit ADC.

analogRead() returns 300. About what voltage is on the pin?

300 × 3.3 / 1023 ≈ 0.968 V.

What is the reference voltage, and what happens if the supply is really 3.25 V?

The reference is AVDD, the 3.3 V supply. If it is really 3.25 V, full scale (1023) means 3.25 V, and the formula with 3.3 shows values about 1.5 % too high.

Lab 14 reads the full 12-bit value straight from the ADC result register.

05PWM: fade an LED

Fake an analog output by switching a pin on and off very fast with a variable duty cycle: an LED “breathes”, or follows a potentiometer while USER is held.

basicsanalogWritePWMmapduty cycleSCCP

Objectives

  • After this lab you can explain PWM, duty cycle and PWM frequency, and why a fast PWM signal looks like a steady brightness.
  • After this lab you can wire an external LED with a series resistor and calculate its current.
  • After this lab you can set a duty cycle with analogWrite(pin, 0..255) on the PWM pins D5–D8.
  • After this lab you can rescale a value from one range to another with map().
  • After this lab you can combine an input (button, pot) and an output (PWM) to make two operating modes.

Background

The problem. A digital pin can only be 0 V or 3.3 V. But often you want “half bright” or “a bit faster”. The dsPIC33CK has no true analog output on these pins, so it uses a trick: PWM (pulse-width modulation).

PWM. The pin is switched HIGH and LOW again and again at a fixed rate, the PWM frequency. What changes is how long it stays HIGH in each cycle. The duty cycle is the share of time the pin is HIGH: 0 % = always LOW, 50 % = HIGH half the time, 100 % = always HIGH. The average voltage is duty × 3.3 V, for example 25 % → about 0.8 V on average.

|<-- one period, about 2 ms (~490 Hz) -->| duty 25%: _|‾|___|‾|___|‾|___ ~490 Hz, too fast to see -> looks dim duty 75%: _|‾‾‾|_|‾‾‾|_|‾‾‾|_ -> looks bright

Why the LED looks dimmed. At about 490 switchings per second the LED really is fully on or fully off, but the eye cannot follow so fast and sees the average light. The same idea controls motor speed, heater power and (with a filter) can make an analog voltage. The eye is much more sensitive to changes at low brightness than at high brightness, so a linear fade seems to change quickly near off and slowly near full.

analogWrite() values. In Arduino, analogWrite(pin, value) takes 0–255: 0 = 0 %, 128 ≈ 50 %, 255 = 100 %. On this board 0 and 255 switch the PWM off and simply drive the pin LOW or HIGH. Despite its name, analogWrite() has nothing to do with the ADC of Lab 04.

On the dsPIC33CK. PWM is produced by the SCCP modules (single capture/compare/PWM), one per pin: SCCP1–SCCP4 on D5 = RB0, D6 = RB1, D7 = RB2, D8 = RB3. The first analogWrite() on a pin connects the module’s output to the pin with Peripheral Pin Select (PPS) and starts the timer; later calls only change the duty-cycle register, without a glitch. At 100 MIPS the timer counts with a 1:64 prescaler and a period of 3188 counts, which gives about 490 Hz, the same as a classic Arduino. The 0–255 value is scaled to 0–3188 counts. Only D5–D8 can do PWM — the USER LED (RC13) cannot, which is why this lab uses an external LED.

The LED resistor. An LED needs a resistor in series to limit its current. With a red LED (about 2 V forward voltage) and 330 Ω: I = (3.3 V − 2 V) / 330 Ω ≈ 4 mA, bright enough and gentle on the pin.

Never connect an LED to a pin without the series resistor: the current would only be limited by the pin driver and could damage the LED or the pin.

You need

PartQtyNotes
dsPIC33CK Nano board1USER button selects the mode
USB-C cable + 5 V supply1power only
LED (any colour, 3 or 5 mm)1long leg = anode (+)
330 Ω resistor1220 Ω–1 kΩ also works
10 kΩ potentiometer1optional, the one from Lab 04
Breadboard + jumper wiresabout 5
PICkit on J4 (or the Serial bootloader)1for uploading. This sketch prints nothing, so no Serial Monitor is needed.

Wiring

PartBoardNotes
330 Ω resistor, one endD5 = RB0 J3-21PWM output (SCCP1)
330 Ω resistor, other end → LED anode (long leg)–on the breadboard
LED cathode (short leg, flat side)GND J3-2via the breadboard ground rail
pot end 1 (optional)3V3 J3-1as in Lab 04, never +5V
pot wiper (optional)A0 = RA0 J2-15as in Lab 04
pot end 2 (optional)GND J3-2same ground rail

Step by step

  1. Wire the LED and resistor. Check the LED direction: the long leg must be on the resistor side, the short leg on GND. A reversed LED simply stays dark.
  2. Optionally wire the pot as in Lab 04. Power the board.
  3. Upload Lab05_PWMFade. The LED “breathes”: it fades up from off to full in about 0.8 s and back down in another 0.8 s, over and over. That is 52 steps of 15 ms each way.
  4. Watch the low end of the fade: the brightness seems to change faster there than near full brightness. That is your eye, not the PWM (see Background).
  5. Hold USER: now the pot sets the brightness directly. The sketch only checks the button between two complete breaths, so it can take up to about 1.6 s after you press before the LED reacts. Keep holding.
  6. While holding USER, turn the pot. The brightness follows the knob within 10 ms. Knob at one end = off, at the other end = full.
  7. Release USER. The auto-fade starts again, from off.
  8. If no pot is connected and you hold USER, the brightness is random or flickers, because A0 is floating (Lab 04).
  9. If you have an oscilloscope, look at J3-21: a square wave of about 490 Hz whose HIGH part grows and shrinks with the fade. A multimeter on DC volts shows roughly the average voltage.

How the code works

const uint8_t PWM_PIN = 5;   /* RB0 */

void setup()
{
    pinMode(PWM_PIN, OUTPUT);
    pinMode(BUTTON_BUILTIN, INPUT);
}

The pin number is kept in one constant, so moving the LED to D6, D7 or D8 means changing one line. D5 becomes an output, and the USER button an input (it has its external pull-up, Lab 02).

    if (digitalRead(BUTTON_BUILTIN) == LOW) {
        /* manual: pot sets brightness */
        int duty = map(analogRead(A0), 0, 1023, 0, 255);
        analogWrite(PWM_PIN, duty);
        delay(10);
        return;
    }

If USER is pressed (LOW), the pot is read (0–1023, Lab 04) and map() rescales it to the PWM range 0–255. map(x, inLow, inHigh, outLow, outHigh) does the straight-line calculation (x - inLow) × (outHigh - outLow) / (inHigh - inLow) + outLow with integers, so here it is x × 255 / 1023, about x / 4. return leaves loop() early, so the fade code below is skipped; the core calls loop() again 10 ms later and the button is checked again.

    /* automatic: breathe up and down */
    for (int duty = 0; duty <= 255; duty += 5) {
        analogWrite(PWM_PIN, duty);
        delay(15);
    }
    for (int duty = 255; duty >= 0; duty -= 5) {
        analogWrite(PWM_PIN, duty);
        delay(15);
    }

When the button is not pressed, two for loops ramp the duty up from 0 to 255 and back down in steps of 5. Each step holds for 15 ms, so each ramp takes 52 × 15 ms = 780 ms. During these loops the button is not looked at: this is the blocking style of Lab 01, and it is the reason for the delay you noticed in step 5. At duty 0 and 255 the core switches the PWM off and drives the pin LOW or HIGH directly; in between it only updates the duty register of SCCP1.

Try it yourself

  1. Easy Make the breathing slower and smoother. Hint: change the step 5 to 1 in both for loops (note: 255 is then still reached exactly) and adjust delay(15).
  2. Easy Move the LED to D6 (RB1, J3-20). Hint: only PWM_PIN at the top changes. Then try the USER LED (pin 34): it cannot fade. On a non-PWM pin the core just writes LOW for values below 128 and HIGH from 128 up, so the active-low USER LED is on during the dim half of the fade and off during the bright half.
  3. Medium Invert the pot direction in manual mode, so the other end of the knob is bright. Hint: swap the last two arguments of map().
  4. Medium Make the fade look more even to the eye by squaring the value: analogWrite(PWM_PIN, (long)duty * duty / 255). Hint: both analogWrite() lines inside the for loops.
  5. Challenge Rewrite the fade without for and delay(): keep duty and a direction in global variables and change it by one step every 15 ms with a millis() timer (Lab 02/03). Then the button reacts immediately in both modes.

Troubleshooting

SymptomLikely causeFix
LED never lightsLED reversed, or wired to the wrong header pinTurn the LED round; check the resistor goes to J3-21 (RB0) and the cathode to GND.
LED only on or off, no fadingThe LED is on a pin without PWMUse D5–D8 (RB0–RB3) only.
Holding USER seems to do nothing at firstThe button is only checked between full breathsHold it for up to about 1.6 s; see Challenge 5 for a fix.
Manual mode flickers or random brightnessNo pot, or the wiper is not on J2-15Wire the pot as in Lab 04.
LED is very dim even at fullResistor too large (for example 10 kΩ instead of 330 Ω)Check the colour bands: 330 Ω = orange-orange-brown.

Check your understanding

What is the duty cycle for analogWrite(5, 64), and the average voltage on the pin?

64 / 255 ≈ 25 %. The average voltage is about 0.25 × 3.3 V ≈ 0.83 V.

Why do you not see the LED flicker at 490 Hz?

The eye cannot follow changes that fast; it averages the light, so the LED looks steadily dimmer or brighter depending on the duty cycle.

What does map(512, 0, 1023, 0, 255) return?

512 × 255 / 1023 = 127 (integer arithmetic drops the fraction).

Why can the USER LED not be faded with analogWrite()?

PWM comes from the SCCP modules, which this core connects only to D5–D8 (RB0–RB3). RC13 has no PWM output assigned.

06External interrupt on the button

React to a button press the instant it happens, while the main loop is busy with something else and never looks at the button.

basicsattachInterruptvolatileatomic accessdebounceISR

Objectives

  • After this lab you can explain the difference between polling a pin and letting an interrupt tell you about it.
  • After this lab you can attach a function to a pin edge with attachInterrupt(digitalPinToInterrupt(pin), fn, FALLING).
  • After this lab you can write a short, safe interrupt handler and know what must not go inside it.
  • After this lab you can explain why a shared variable must be volatile and when it needs noInterrupts() / interrupts() around it.
  • After this lab you can debounce a button by time inside a handler with millis().

Background

Polling versus interrupts. In the earlier labs the loop asked the button “are you pressed?” again and again with digitalRead(). That is polling. It works, but if the loop is busy (a long delay(), a calculation, printing) a short press can be missed. An interrupt turns this around: the hardware watches the pin, and when the chosen event happens it stops the main program for a moment, runs a small function of yours, and then returns exactly where it left off. That small function is the interrupt service routine (ISR), also called the handler.

loop(): ...blink...blink...blink...| |...blink...blink... | | button: HIGH ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~\___________/~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ ^ falling edge (HIGH -> LOW) | ISR: onButton(): pressCount++ (a few µs) then the CPU goes back into loop()

Edges. An interrupt is triggered by a change, called an edge. A falling edge is HIGH→LOW, a rising edge is LOW→HIGH, and CHANGE means both. The USER button on this board has an external 10 kΩ pull-up resistor, so the pin reads HIGH when released and LOW when pressed. Pressing the button therefore makes a falling edge, which is why the sketch uses FALLING.

volatile. The compiler likes to keep a variable in a CPU register to save time. If the loop has read pressCount once, the compiler may assume it cannot change and never read RAM again — it does not know that an ISR can change it “behind its back”. The keyword volatile tells the compiler: always read and write this variable in RAM. Every variable that an ISR and the loop share must be volatile.

Atomic access. An operation is atomic when it cannot be cut in half by an interrupt. The dsPIC33CK is a 16-bit CPU: reading a 16-bit unsigned int is one instruction, but reading a 32-bit long or unsigned long takes two. If the ISR changes the value between those two reads, the loop gets half of the old value and half of the new one (a “torn” read). The cure is to switch interrupts off for the copy: noInterrupts(), copy, interrupts(). Here pressCount is only 16 bits, so its read is already atomic; the sketch uses the pair anyway because it is a good habit, and it becomes necessary the moment you change the counter to a long. Interrupts that arrive while they are off are not lost — they wait and run right after interrupts().

On the dsPIC33CK. In this Arduino core, attachInterrupt() uses the chip’s Change Notification (CN) hardware, which can watch every pin of PORTA–PORTD (Lab 10 looks at it in detail). The USER button is RC12, so its events arrive through the PORTC CN interrupt and the core then calls your function. These handlers run at priority 2, below millis() (Timer1, priority 4) and Serial receive (priority 3), so millis() keeps counting inside your handler. digitalPinToInterrupt(p) simply returns the pin number; it exists so that sketches written for other Arduino boards compile unchanged.

PriorityWho uses it
5tone() timer (SCCP4)
4Timer1 → millis(), micros(), delay()
3Serial receive (UART1)
2attachInterrupt() handlers (Change Notification)
0your loop()

You need

PartQtyNotes
dsPIC33CK Nano board1uses the on-board USER button (RC12) and USER LED (RC13)
USB-C cable + 5 V supply1power only, no data
3.3 V USB-serial adapter1on J5, for the Serial Monitor at 115200 baud
PICkit (J4) or Serial bootloader (J5)1to upload the sketch

Wiring

Nothing to wire on a breadboard. Only the USB-serial adapter is connected:

SignalBoard pinOther end
UART TX (board sends)RC10 J5-2adapter RX
UART RX (board receives)RC11 J5-3adapter TX
GNDJ5-4adapter GND
3V3J5-1leave open
USER buttonRC12 = D33 (on board)–
USER LED (active low)RC13 = D34 (on board)–

Step by step

  1. Connect the USB-serial adapter to J5 and power the board from USB-C. The power LED lights.
  2. Open File > Examples > dsPIC33CK_Nano > Lab06_Interrupt and upload it (PICkit on J4, or the Serial bootloader on J5).
  3. Open the Serial Monitor at 115200 baud and press RESET. You read Lab 06 - press USER, the interrupt counts it. This is printed once in setup().
  4. Watch the USER LED: it blinks slowly, 0.5 s on and 0.5 s off. This “heartbeat” shows that the loop is busy with its own job. Notice that the loop never calls digitalRead() on the button.
  5. Press USER once. presses: 1 appears straight away, and the blinking does not stutter. The hardware saw the falling edge and ran onButton() for you.
  6. Press a few more times: presses: 2, 3, … Each line appears only when the count changes, because the loop compares it with the last reported value.
  7. Hold the button down for a second, then release. Only one press is counted: the interrupt is on the falling edge only, and releasing makes a rising edge.
  8. Tap the button as fast as you can. Taps that come closer than 50 ms are ignored by the debounce, so very fast tapping may count fewer presses than you made.
  9. If one press ever counts as two, you have seen contact bounce: the metal contacts spring back and make several edges. See Troubleshooting and exercise 2.

Expected output

Lab 06 - press USER, the interrupt counts it
presses: 1
presses: 2
presses: 3

How the code works

Shared variables. Two variables are used by both the ISR and the rest of the program, so both are volatile:

volatile unsigned int  pressCount = 0;
volatile unsigned long lastIsrMs  = 0;

pressCount is the number of presses. lastIsrMs remembers when the last accepted press happened, for the debounce.

The handler.

void onButton()
{
    unsigned long now = millis();
    if (now - lastIsrMs > 50) {       /* simple debounce inside the ISR */
        pressCount++;
        lastIsrMs = now;
    }
}

It takes no arguments and returns nothing — every attachInterrupt() handler looks like this. It reads the time, and if more than 50 ms have passed since the last accepted edge it counts the press. Edges closer together are treated as bounce and dropped. The subtraction now - lastIsrMs stays correct even when millis() wraps around after about 49 days. The handler is a few lines long and finishes in microseconds. It does not print and does not wait.

setup().

pinMode(LED_BUILTIN, OUTPUT);
pinMode(BUTTON_BUILTIN, INPUT);
Serial.begin(115200);
Serial.println("Lab 06 - press USER, the interrupt counts it");
attachInterrupt(digitalPinToInterrupt(BUTTON_BUILTIN), onButton, FALLING);

The button is a plain INPUT because the board already has the 10 kΩ pull-up. The last line is the important one: from now on, every HIGH→LOW edge on RC12 calls onButton(). Inside, the core makes the pin an input, sets the PORTC Change Notification module to edge mode, enables the falling edge for bit 12, and enables the PORTC CN interrupt at priority 2.

loop() – reading the counter safely.

static unsigned int reported = 0;

noInterrupts();                   /* read the shared value atomically */
unsigned int n = pressCount;
interrupts();

The loop takes a private copy n with interrupts switched off for just one instruction. After that it works only with the copy, so the value cannot change while it is being printed. reported is static, so it keeps its value from one pass of loop() to the next.

if (n != reported) {
    reported = n;
    Serial.print("presses: ");
    Serial.println(n);
}

Printing happens here, in the loop, not in the ISR. This is the usual pattern: the ISR records the event, the loop does the slow work.

digitalWrite(LED_BUILTIN, (millis() / 500) % 2 ? LED_ON : LED_OFF);

The heartbeat. millis() / 500 goes up by one every half second; % 2 turns that into 0, 1, 0, 1… The LED is active low, so the sketch uses LED_ON / LED_OFF instead of HIGH / LOW.

Try it yourself

  1. Easy Count releases instead of presses: change FALLING to RISING in the attachInterrupt() line in setup(). Now the count goes up when you let go.
  2. Easy Change the debounce time 50 in onButton() to 0 and press the button many times. Do some presses count twice? Then try 200 and tap fast. What is a good value?
  3. Medium Use CHANGE and count both edges. Print the number of presses as n / 2. Hint: change the mode in setup() and the print in loop().
  4. Medium Change pressCount to volatile unsigned long (and n, reported too). Now the noInterrupts() / interrupts() pair is really needed, because a 32-bit read takes two instructions on this 16-bit CPU.
  5. Challenge Make the loop really slow: add delay(3000); at the end of loop(). Press the button three times during one delay. All presses are still counted (the ISR runs during delay()), but they are reported together. Then write a polling version with digitalRead() and compare.

Troubleshooting

SymptomLikely causeFix
Nothing in the Serial MonitorWrong baud rate, or adapter TX/RX swappedSet 115200. Adapter RX → J5-2, adapter TX → J5-3, GND → J5-4.
LED blinks but presses are never countedWrong pin name in attachInterrupt(), or the mode does not match the buttonUse BUTTON_BUILTIN and FALLING. The USER button reads LOW when pressed.
One press counts 2 or moreContact bounce longer than the 50 ms window (for example bounce on release)Increase the time in onButton(), or add a 100 nF capacitor across the button.
Fast taps are missedThe 50 ms debounce drops edges that come too closeLower the debounce time a little; that is the trade-off.
Garbled text when you print from the ISRSerial.print() in a handler interrupts a print in the loop and mixes the twoKeep printing in loop(); let the ISR only change variables.

Check your understanding

Why does the sketch use FALLING and not RISING?

The button has a pull-up and reads LOW when pressed, so the moment of pressing is a HIGH→LOW (falling) edge. RISING would count the release.

What could go wrong if pressCount were not volatile?

The compiler could keep the value in a register and never re-read RAM in the loop, so the printed count would never change even though the ISR increments it.

pressCount is 16 bits. Why is noInterrupts() still a good idea here, and when is it essential?

A 16-bit read is one instruction on the dsPIC, so it cannot be torn. The pair costs almost nothing and keeps the code correct if the variable later becomes 32 bits (long, unsigned long, float), where the read takes two instructions and could be split by the ISR.

Why does millis() work inside onButton() on this board?

The handler runs at priority 2 and Timer1, which drives millis(), runs at priority 4. A higher priority can interrupt a lower one, so the millisecond counter keeps going.

ISR rules: short, no Serial, no delay(), share data only through volatile variables.

07Play a melody with tone()

Generate audio frequencies on a pin and play a short tune stored in two arrays.

basicstonenoTonearraystimerssquare wave

Objectives

  • After this lab you can explain how a square wave of a given frequency makes a musical note.
  • After this lab you can play a note with tone(pin, frequency, duration) and stop it with noTone(pin).
  • After this lab you can store a melody in two parallel arrays and play it with a for loop.
  • After this lab you can describe how the core uses timer SCCP4 to make the tone, and why it clashes with analogWrite() on D8.
  • After this lab you can tell a passive buzzer from an active one.

Background

Sound and frequency. Sound is air pressure moving back and forth. A buzzer or speaker makes it by moving a thin plate. If the plate moves 440 times per second you hear the note A4; the number of cycles per second is the frequency, measured in hertz (Hz). Higher frequency = higher note. One octave up doubles the frequency: C4 is 262 Hz, C5 is 523 Hz.

Square wave. A digital pin can only be HIGH (3.3 V) or LOW (0 V). If we switch it HIGH and LOW again and again, we get a square wave. The period is the time for one full cycle (HIGH plus LOW) and equals 1 / frequency. For 262 Hz the period is about 3.82 ms, so the pin must change state every 1.91 ms (one half-cycle). A square wave sounds a bit harsher than a pure tone, but the pitch is exactly right.

|<--- period = 1/f --->| 3.3 V +----------+ +----------+ +--- | | | | | 0 V --+ +-----------+ +-----------+ toggle toggle toggle toggle |<- half ->| (the timer interrupt fires at every toggle, 2 × f per second)

Passive and active buzzers. A passive piezo buzzer is just a crystal disc: it sounds at whatever frequency you feed it, so it can play melodies. An active buzzer has a small oscillator inside and beeps at its own fixed pitch as soon as it gets DC voltage. This lab needs a passive one.

How tone() works on this board. Making the square wave by hand with digitalWrite() and delayMicroseconds() would block the CPU. Instead the core uses a hardware timer. On the dsPIC33CK, tone() (in cores/arduino/wiring_tone.c) takes the timer SCCP4 and sets it up as a 16-bit timer. SCCP4 counts the CPU clock (FCY = 100 MHz at 100 MIPS) through a prescaler — a divider of 1, 4, 16 or 64 — and raises an interrupt every time the count reaches a period value. Each interrupt flips the pin (one half-cycle). The core picks the smallest prescaler whose period still fits in 16 bits:

period ticks = FCY / (prescaler × 2 × frequency) example, 100 MIPS, C4 = 262 Hz: prescaler 1 : 100 000 000 / (1 × 2 × 262) = 190 839 > 65 536, too big prescaler 4 : 100 000 000 / (4 × 2 × 262) = 47 709 fits -> used

Because the pin is flipped by an interrupt routine and not by the timer’s own output, tone() works on any digital pin. The duration is handled in the same interrupt: tone() works out how many half-cycles fit into the duration (duration × frequency / 500) and counts them down; at zero it stops the timer and leaves the pin LOW. Without a duration, the tone plays until noTone(). The tone interrupt has priority 5, the highest in the core. tone() returns at once — the sound plays “in the background”.

The catch. SCCP4 is also the PWM channel of D8 (RB3). Only one of them can use it at a time: calling tone() turns off PWM on D8, and analogWrite(8, ...) stops a tone. Only one tone can play at a time.

NoteC4D4E4F4G4A4B4C5
Hz (sketch)262294330349392440494523

You need

PartQtyNotes
dsPIC33CK Nano board1USER button and USER LED on board
USB-C cable + 5 V supply1power only, no data
Passive piezo buzzer1or an 8 Ω speaker with a 330 Ω resistor in series (about 10 mA, safe for the pin; use a transistor for more volume); NOT an active buzzer
Breadboard + 2 jumper wires1–
PICkit (J4) or USB-serial adapter (J5)1only to upload; the sketch does not use Serial

Wiring

SignalBoard pinOther end
tone outputD9 = RB4 J3-15buzzer + (or 330 Ω → speaker)
groundGND J3-2buzzer − (or speaker other terminal)

Many piezo buzzers have a longer leg or a red wire for +. A piezo does not really care about polarity, but follow the marking.

Step by step

  1. Plug the buzzer into the breadboard and wire + to J3-15 and − to J3-2 (GND).
  2. Open Lab07_Tone and upload it. As soon as the sketch starts you hear the tune C–E–G–C–G–E–C: up an arpeggio and back down. setup() plays it once.
  3. Watch the USER LED while it plays: it is on during each note and goes off at the end. The last entry of the melody is a rest (0 Hz), during which the LED is off and nothing sounds.
  4. Listen to the rhythm: most notes are short (200 ms); the high C5 and the final C4 are longer (400 ms). Between notes there is a short silence — that is the 30 % gap the code adds.
  5. Press USER. The tune plays again. The whole tune takes about 2.6 s (2000 ms of note lengths × 1.3).
  6. Hold USER down. The tune plays once and then stops: the code waits for the release before it can play again.
  7. Press RESET: the tune plays once more at start-up, because setup() runs again.
  8. If you only hear one fixed beep, or a click, read Troubleshooting: you probably have an active buzzer.

How the code works

Pin and notes.

const uint8_t BUZZER_PIN = 9;   /* RB4 */

#define NOTE_C4 262
#define NOTE_E4 330
...
#define NOTE_C5 523

Names for frequencies make the melody readable. They are plain numbers in Hz.

The melody as two arrays.

const unsigned int melody[]   = { NOTE_C4, NOTE_E4, NOTE_G4, NOTE_C5, NOTE_G4, NOTE_E4, NOTE_C4, 0 };
const unsigned int duration[] = { 200,     200,     200,     400,     200,     200,     400,     200 };
const int NOTES = sizeof(melody) / sizeof(melody[0]);

These are parallel arrays: element i of melody[] belongs to element i of duration[]. A frequency of 0 means a rest (silence). sizeof(melody) / sizeof(melody[0]) is the total size in bytes divided by the size of one element, which gives the number of notes (8). If you add notes, NOTES updates by itself — but both arrays must have the same length.

playMelody().

for (int i = 0; i < NOTES; i++) {
    digitalWrite(LED_BUILTIN, melody[i] ? LED_ON : LED_OFF);
    if (melody[i]) {
        tone(BUZZER_PIN, melody[i], duration[i]);
    }
    delay(duration[i] * 13 / 10);  /* small gap between notes */
    noTone(BUZZER_PIN);
}
digitalWrite(LED_BUILTIN, LED_OFF);

For each note the LED is switched on (or off for a rest). tone() starts the note and returns immediately; the timer stops it by itself after duration[i] ms. The delay() waits 130 % of the note length (* 13 / 10 in integer maths), so after the note ends there is 30 % silence. Without this gap two equal notes in a row would melt into one long note. noTone() makes sure the pin is quiet and LOW before the next note.

setup() and loop().

void setup()
{
    pinMode(LED_BUILTIN, OUTPUT);
    digitalWrite(LED_BUILTIN, LED_OFF);
    pinMode(BUTTON_BUILTIN, INPUT);
    playMelody();                      /* once at start-up */
}

void loop()
{
    if (digitalRead(BUTTON_BUILTIN) == LOW) {
        playMelody();
        while (digitalRead(BUTTON_BUILTIN) == LOW) { }   /* wait for release */
    }
}

There is no pinMode() for the buzzer: tone() makes the pin an output by itself. The loop polls the USER button (LOW = pressed). After playing, the empty while waits until the button is released, so holding it does not repeat the tune.

Try it yourself

  1. Easy Change the tempo: multiply every value in duration[] by 2, or change the gap factor 13 / 10 in playMelody() to 11 / 10 or 20 / 10. How does the gap change the feel?
  2. Easy Play a scale: put NOTE_C4, NOTE_D4, NOTE_E4, NOTE_F4, NOTE_G4, NOTE_A4, NOTE_B4, NOTE_C5 into melody[] and eight durations into duration[].
  3. Medium Write your own tune (for example the first line of a song you know). Add more #define NOTE_... lines; each octave up doubles the frequency (A5 = 880 Hz).
  4. Medium Make a siren: in loop(), call tone(BUZZER_PIN, f) with no duration for f from 400 to 1200 in steps of 10, with delay(5) between steps, then back down. Stop it with noTone().
  5. Challenge Remove the blocking delay() from playMelody(): keep the current note index and a start time, and in loop() use millis() to start the next note when the time is up. Then the board can read the button while the tune plays.

Troubleshooting

SymptomLikely causeFix
Only a single fixed beep, or a click per noteActive buzzer (built-in oscillator)Use a passive piezo buzzer.
Silence, but the LED blinks with the notesBuzzer on the wrong pin or not connected to GNDBuzzer + to J3-15 (RB4 = D9), − to GND.
Very quiet soundPiezos are quiet at 3.3 V, and loudest near their own resonance (often 2–4 kHz)Normal. Try higher notes, or a small transistor driver.
PWM on D8 stops workingtone() and analogWrite(8, ...) share SCCP4Do not use D8 PWM while a tone plays; use D5–D7 for PWM.
Tune plays again and again while the button is heldThe while that waits for release was removedKeep the wait-for-release loop in loop().

Check your understanding

For a 440 Hz tone, how often does the tone interrupt flip the pin?

Twice per cycle, so 880 times per second: once for the rising half and once for the falling half.

tone() is given a duration. Why does playMelody() still call delay()?

tone() returns immediately and the note plays in the background. Without the delay the loop would start the next note at once, cutting off the current one. The delay waits for the note plus a 30 % gap.

Why can you not use analogWrite(8, ...) while a melody plays?

Both tone() and the PWM on D8 (RB3) use the same timer, SCCP4. Starting one stops the other.

What does a 0 in melody[] do?

It is a rest: tone() is not called and the LED is off, so there is silence for that duration (plus the 30 % gap).

An active buzzer (the kind with a built-in oscillator) only beeps at one pitch. Use a passive one for melodies.

08I2C bus scanner

Find the address of any I2C module — the first thing to do with a new sensor.

basicsWireI2CACKpull-up7-bit address

Objectives

  • After this lab you can explain how two wires, SDA and SCL, connect many devices on one I2C bus.
  • After this lab you can explain what a 7-bit address, START, STOP, ACK and NACK are.
  • After this lab you can explain why an I2C bus needs pull-up resistors.
  • After this lab you can use Wire.begin(), Wire.beginTransmission() and Wire.endTransmission(), and read its return code.
  • After this lab you can find the address of an unknown module and print it in hexadecimal.

Background

The I2C bus. I2C (“I-squared-C”, Inter-Integrated Circuit) connects a microcontroller to sensors, displays and memories with only two signal wires plus ground. SCL is the clock and SDA carries the data, one bit per clock. The board is the master (it makes the clock and starts every transfer); the modules are slaves (also called targets). Many modules can share the same two wires.

3V3 --+--------+ (pull-ups, often on the module) | | 4k7 4k7 | | SDA ---+--------)------+-------------+-------------- SCL ------------+------)------+------)------+------- | | | | +----+------+-+ +--+------+----+ dsPIC33CK Nano | OLED 0x3C | | BME280 0x76 | ... (master) +-------------+ +--------------+

Pull-ups and open drain. No device ever drives an I2C line HIGH. A device can only pull the line LOW, or let it go (this is called open drain). A pull-up resistor from each line to 3.3 V makes the line HIGH when nobody pulls it down. This way two devices can never short-circuit each other by driving opposite levels. Typical values are 4.7 kΩ. Most breakout modules already have them; a bare chip on a breadboard needs you to add them. Without pull-ups the lines never go HIGH and nothing works.

Addresses. Every device has a 7-bit address (0x00–0x7F), usually fixed by the chip and sometimes changeable with a jumper or pin. Addresses 0x00–0x07 and 0x78–0x7F are reserved, so the scanner tries 0x08–0x77. The address is sent as the top 7 bits of the first byte; the lowest bit says the direction: 0 = master writes, 1 = master reads.

START, ACK, STOP. A transfer starts with a START condition (SDA falls while SCL is HIGH). The master then clocks out the 8-bit address byte. On the 9th clock the master releases SDA and listens: the device with that address pulls SDA LOW — this is the ACK (acknowledge). If no device has that address, SDA stays HIGH because of the pull-up: a NACK (not acknowledged). The transfer ends with a STOP (SDA rises while SCL is HIGH). A scanner just tries every address and notes which ones are ACKed.

START A6 A5 A4 A3 A2 A1 A0 R/W ACK STOP SDA ~~~~\____X__X__X__X__X__X__X__0__\___/~~~~~ ACK: device pulls SDA low SCL ~~~~~~\__/~~\_/~~\_/~~\_/~~\_/~~\_/~~\_/~~\_/~~~~ on the 9th clock pulse 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9

On the dsPIC33CK Nano. The Wire library (libraries/Wire) uses the chip’s I2C1 module on its dedicated pins: SDA = RB9 (J3-7), SCL = RB8 (J3-8). It is master-only and polled (it waits in loops, no interrupts). Wire.begin() sets the clock to 100 kHz, called standard mode, with the baud-rate register I2C1BRG = FCY / (2 × 100 000) − 1. Wire.endTransmission() returns 0 when the address was ACKed, 2 for a NACK on the address and 3 for a NACK on a data byte.

Common moduleUsual address
SSD1306 OLED display0x3C (sometimes 0x3D)
BME280 / BMP280 sensor0x76 or 0x77
MPU6050 motion sensor0x68 or 0x69
24LC EEPROM0x50–0x57

You need

PartQtyNotes
dsPIC33CK Nano board1USER button to rescan, USER LED shows the result
USB-C cable + 5 V supply1power only, no data
3.3 V USB-serial adapter1on J5, Serial Monitor at 115200
3.3 V I2C module1 or moreBME280, MPU6050, SSD1306 OLED, 24LC EEPROM…
4.7 kΩ resistors2only for a bare chip without pull-ups
Breadboard + jumper wires14 wires per module

Wiring

SignalBoard pinModule
power 3.3 V3V3 J3-1VCC (or VIN)
groundGND J3-2GND
I2C dataRB9 = D14 J3-7SDA
I2C clockRB8 = D13 J3-8SCL
pull-ups (bare chip only)4.7 kΩ from J3-7 to J3-1 and from J3-8 to J3-1–
Serial (adapter)J5-2 TX, J5-3 RX, J5-4 GNDadapter RX, TX, GND

To scan several modules at once, connect all their SDA pins together to J3-7 and all their SCL pins to J3-8.

Use 3.3 V modules only. The I/O pins of this board are not 5 V tolerant. A module powered from 5 V may pull SDA/SCL up to 5 V through its own pull-ups.

Step by step

  1. With the power off, wire the module as in the table. Check twice that VCC goes to 3V3 (J3-1), not to +5V.
  2. Connect the USB-serial adapter to J5 and power the board. The module’s own power LED (if it has one) should light.
  3. Upload Lab08_I2CScanner and open the Serial Monitor at 115200 baud. Press RESET to see the start.
  4. Read the first lines: Lab 08 - I2C scanner (SDA RB9, SCL RB8) and Scanning I2C bus (0x08..0x77).... The scan of 112 addresses takes only a fraction of a second.
  5. Each device prints device found at 0x... Compare the address with the module’s datasheet or the table above. Write it down: you will need it in Wire.beginTransmission(address) in later projects.
  6. The last line says how many devices answered, for example done, 1 device(s). The USER LED is on when at least one device was found and off when none.
  7. Unplug the SDA wire and press USER to scan again. Now done, 0 device(s). appears and the LED goes off: without SDA nobody can ACK.
  8. Plug SDA back in, add a second module on the same two wires, and press USER. Both addresses are listed. If two modules have the same address they clash; change one with its address jumper.

Expected output

Example with an SSD1306 OLED (0x3C) and a BME280 (0x76) connected:

Lab 08 - I2C scanner (SDA RB9, SCL RB8)
Scanning I2C bus (0x08..0x77)...
  device found at 0x3C
  device found at 0x76
done, 2 device(s).

The hex digits are printed in capitals (3C). Addresses below 0x10 get a leading zero (0x0A).

How the code works
