(example values – the numbers depend on the pot position and the clock.) If a hardware trigger does not work, its line shows the fallback instead: SCCP2 trigger event -> ADC -> DMA (0 CPU per sample) or timer ISR starts ADC -> DMA moves data (fallback) for channel 0, SCCP3 ISR kicks DMA (fallback) for channel 2, and UART1 TX event did not work - CPU prints for channel 3. NONE ... means nothing worked for that channel.

How the code works

The sketch has two tabs. DMA.h is a small driver for all four channels. Lab14_DMA.ino only says what each channel moves. The channel numbers are named at the top: CH_ADC 0, CH_COPY 1, CH_WAVE 2, CH_TEXT 3.

1. One driver for four channels (DMA.h).

typedef struct {
    volatile uint16_t CH, INT, SRC, DST, CNT;
} DmaRegs;

static inline DmaRegs *dmaReg(uint8_t ch)
{
    return (DmaRegs *)((volatile uint16_t *)&DMACH0 + 5 * ch);
}

The five registers of each channel sit next to each other, and channel n starts 5 words after channel n−1. dmaReg(n) lays a struct over them, so dmaReg(2)->CNT is DMACNT2. dmaBegin() powers all four channels (PMD6), switches the module on (DMAEN), selects fixed priority, and sets the RAM window the DMA may use (DMAL/DMAH).

void dmaSetup(uint8_t ch, const volatile void *src, volatile void *dst, uint16_t count,
              uint8_t trigger, uint8_t trmode, uint8_t srcStep, uint8_t dstStep,
              uint8_t size, uint8_t reload)

dmaSetup() switches the channel off, writes source, destination and count, puts the trigger number into CHSEL and builds the control word: word or byte size, transfer mode, and whether each address stays (DMA_FIXED) or moves on (DMA_INC). dmaStart(), dmaStop(), dmaKick() (software trigger), dmaLeft() (transfers left) and dmaDone() are one-line helpers.

2. Channel 0: ADC → RAM (startAdcChannel()).

    dmaSetup(CH_ADC, &ADCBUF9, adcBuf, N_BUF, DMA_TRG_ADC_AN(AN_CH),
             DMA_REPEAT_ONE_SHOT, DMA_FIXED, DMA_INC, DMA_16BIT, DMA_RELOAD);
    dmaHalfInterrupt(CH_ADC, true);        /* interrupt at half AND at full */
    dmaInterrupt(CH_ADC, 5);
    dmaStart(CH_ADC);

    pwmRetime(CLOCK_PIN, SAMPLE_HZ);       /* SCCP2 = 1 kHz sample clock on D6 */
    ADTRIG2Lbits.TRGSRC9 = 0x15;           /* SCCP2 OC/IC event */
    if (moves(CH_ADC, 30)) { adcPath = 1; return; }

Source = &ADCBUF9 (fixed, every result lands there), destination = adcBuf (moves on one word each time), count 256, trigger “ADC AN9 conversion complete” (0x31). Repeated one-shot moves one word per trigger; RELOAD starts again at adcBuf[0] after 256 words. Earlier, one analogRead(A2) lets the core power the ADC, and ADIELbits.IE9 = 1 makes AN9 produce its “done” event while its CPU interrupt stays off. pwmRetime() lets analogWrite() set up SCCP2, then rewrites its period for exactly 1 kHz. TRGSRC9 chooses what starts each conversion; moves() waits 30 ms and checks whether DMACNT0 changed. If 0x15 does not work, 0x0D is tried, and finally a tiny SCCP2 interrupt (_CCT2Interrupt) starts each conversion in software – the DMA still moves the data.

extern "C" void __attribute__((interrupt, no_auto_psv)) _DMA0Interrupt(void)
{
    uint16_t f = dmaTakeFlags(CH_ADC);
    uint8_t h = 0;
    if (f & DMAINT_HALFIF) h = 1;
    if (f & DMAINT_DONEIF) h = 2;          /* RELOAD: starts again at adcBuf[0] */
    if (h) {
        if (halfReady) overruns++;         /* CPU did not finish the last half */
        halfReady = h;
        halves++;
    }
    _DMA0IF = 0;
}

This is the only CPU work for channel 0: twice per 256 samples. loop() sees halfReady and calls processHalf(), which computes min, max, mean (in mV: mean × 3300 / 4095) and the RMS of (sample − mean), the AC noise. overruns counts any time a new half arrived before the CPU had finished the last one.

3. Channel 1: RAM → RAM (dmaCopyStart() and copyRace()).

    dmaSetup(ch, src, dst, words, DMA_TRG_CRC, DMA_CONTINUOUS,
             DMA_INC, DMA_INC, DMA_16BIT, DMA_STOP_AT_END);
    dmaStart(ch);
    dmaKick(ch);                          /* one request moves the whole block */

Continuous mode moves the whole block on one trigger, both addresses increment, and the trigger is a software request (CHREQ). The CRC event is chosen as CHSEL only because this lab never uses the CRC module, so it never fires by itself. copyRace() times 200 DMA copies, a CPU loop and memcpy(), checks the result with memcmp(), and then starts one more DMA copy and counts how many loop passes the CPU makes until DONEIF is set – work the CPU gets “for free”.

4. Channel 2: RAM → PWM duty (fillWave() and startWaveChannel()).

    wavePeriod = pwmRetime(WAVE_PIN, WAVE_PWM_HZ);
    fillWave(waveShape);
    dmaSetup(CH_WAVE, wave, &CCP3RB, N_WAVE, DMA_TRG_SCCP3,
             DMA_REPEAT_ONE_SHOT, DMA_INC, DMA_FIXED, DMA_16BIT, DMA_RELOAD);
    dmaInterrupt(CH_WAVE, 2);              /* count passes (DONE) */
    dmaStart(CH_WAVE);

SCCP3 runs as a 256 Hz PWM on D7. The source walks through wave[], the destination is always CCP3RB (the PWM falling edge, i.e. the duty), and the trigger is the SCCP3 event (0x12). fillWave() computes 512 duty values: for “breathe” it squares a raised cosine, because the eye sees brightness roughly as the square root of the light, so squaring makes the fade look even. It keeps every value between 1 and period − 1, because a duty of exactly 0 % or 100 % has no compare event to trigger the DMA. The DONE interrupt only counts waveCycles. Fallback: if the count does not move, the SCCP3 period interrupt (_CCT3Interrupt) calls dmaKick() once per period.

5. Channel 3: text → UART (dmaPrint(), dmaPrintf(), dmaSerialWait()).

    while (U1STAHbits.UTXBF) { }          /* room for the kicked first byte */
    dmaTxLen = n;
    dmaSetup(dmaTxCh, dmaTxBuf, &U1TXREG, n, DMA_TRG_UART1_TX, DMA_ONE_SHOT,
             DMA_INC, DMA_FIXED, DMA_8BIT, DMA_STOP_AT_END);
    dmaStart(dmaTxCh);
    dmaTxBusy = true;
    dmaKick(dmaTxCh);

dmaPrint() copies the text into its own 160-byte buffer (so the caller may reuse its string), then sets up an 8-bit, one-shot transfer to U1TXREG. dmaSerialBegin() sets UTXISEL = 0, so the UART event fires each time its transmit buffer becomes empty; the first byte is started by a software kick and each following byte by the UART itself. The function returns at once. dmaPrintf() formats with vsnprintf() (whole numbers only, no %f). dmaSerialWait() waits until the message is out; if the count stops moving for 3 ms it stops the channel, prints the rest with Serial.write() and switches DMA text off, so no character is ever lost.

6. loop(). It counts idle passes, processes a ready half, reads the commands w m b p s, and every 5 s prints the status line with all four channel counters. All text goes through dmaPrintf().

Try it yourself

  1. Easy Make the LED breathe twice as fast. Hint: WAVE_PWM_HZ at the top (512 steps / 512 Hz = 1 s).
  2. Easy Print a ch0 half line for every half instead of every 8th. Hint: (halves & 7) == 0 in processHalf().
  3. Medium Add a fourth LED shape, for example a fast blink or a candle flicker using random(). Hint: add a branch in fillWave() and change % 3 in the b command.
  4. Medium Make processHalf() deliberately slow (add delay(150)) and watch overruns rise – but notice that the LED keeps breathing smoothly. Explain why. Hint: which work does the CPU do, and which does the DMA do?
  5. Challenge Use the ADC data to drive channel 2: every half, copy the pot value into the table so the pot sets the LED’s maximum brightness. Hint: scale wave[i] in loop() after processHalf(); keep every value between 1 and wavePeriod - 1.

Check your understanding

Why is the ADC on channel 0 and the text on channel 3?

With fixed priority, channel 0 always wins when two channels want the bus in the same cycle. ADC samples must be stored on time; a character for the UART can wait a few cycles without anyone noticing.

Channel 0 uses “source unchanged, destination incremented”. Channel 2 uses the opposite. Why?

Every ADC result appears in the same register (ADCBUF9) and must go into the next array element. For the LED it is the other way round: each value comes from the next table element and always goes into the same register (CCP3RB).

What is the difference between one-shot and continuous mode?

One-shot moves one unit per trigger (channels 0, 2 and 3 – one sample, one duty value, one character each time). Continuous moves the whole block on a single trigger (channel 1, the memory copy).

You sample at 1000 Hz and feed in 490 Hz. What do you see, and what would prevent it?

A false wave at |1000 − 2 × 490| = 20 Hz (aliasing). An analog low-pass filter in front of the ADC that removes everything above 500 Hz would prevent it.

Trigger-path fallbacks. Register codes come from Microchip’s MCC device data, but three trigger paths have not been checked on hardware: which SCCP2 event reaches the ADC in PWM mode, whether the SCCP3 event fires once per PWM period, and the UART1 TX event. setup() therefore checks each channel and falls back if its count does not move: the ADC tries 0x15, then 0x0D, then a small SCCP2 interrupt that starts each conversion; channel 2 falls back to a small SCCP3 interrupt that kicks one transfer per period; channel 3 falls back to the CPU printing the text. The four # ch lines at the start tell you which one ran — please note them during bring-up.
Simulator: the MPLAB X v6.35 simulator cannot run this lab’s DMA transfers. Its DMA reads the source into DMABUF but never writes it out (DBUFWF stays 1), so every channel reports NONE and the CPU prints the text. Only the start-up checks, the fallbacks and the program flow were checked there.
The sketch as a whole is not hardware-tested yet.

15DAC: a true 12-bit analog output + the analog comparator

analogWrite() is only PWM. This chip has a real DAC: DC levels, waveforms, and a hardware voltage-threshold detector.

advanced12-bit DACcomparator CMP1hysteresiswaveformslinearityregisters

Objectives

  • After this lab you can explain the difference between a PWM “analog” output and a real DAC output.
  • After this lab you can convert between a DAC code and a voltage (Vout = 3.3 V × code / 4096) and set a DC level in millivolts.
  • After this lab you can generate sine, triangle and staircase waveforms from a table or a formula, and check them with the ADC.
  • After this lab you can measure DAC linearity by reading the output back with the ADC.
  • After this lab you can use the analog comparator with the DAC as its threshold, explain hysteresis, and react to crossings with an interrupt.

Background

PWM is not a real analog output. analogWrite() switches a pin fully on and off very fast; only the average is the wanted voltage, and you need a filter (or a slow load like an LED or motor) to see it. A DAC (digital-to-analog converter) instead produces a steady voltage directly. You give it a number (the code), it gives you a voltage.

Resolution. This DAC is 12-bit: codes 0 to 4095. The full range is the analog supply, 3.3 V, so one step is 3.3 V / 4096 ≈ 0.8 mV. Code 2048 gives about 1.65 V. The sketch’s dacWriteMv() turns millivolts into a code with mv × 4095 / 3300.

Waveforms. If you change the code at a regular rate, the output follows: a table of 64 sine values played 50 times a second gives a 50 Hz sine (64 × 50 = 3200 updates per second, one every 312 µs). The output is a fine staircase that approximates the curve; more points per period make it smoother.

The comparator. A comparator is a tiny analog circuit with two inputs. Its output is 1 when the (+) input is higher than the (−) input, else 0. It answers in nanoseconds, with no software involved. On the dsPIC33CK the DAC sits inside comparator module 1, so the DAC voltage can be the comparator’s threshold. In motor control it is the over-current trip that switches the PWM off before software could react.

Hysteresis. If the input sits right at the threshold, noise would make the output flip back and forth (“chatter”). Hysteresis means the comparator needs the input to move a little past the threshold (here 30 mV) before it changes its mind.

DAC1DATH (12 bit) --> DAC --+--> DACOUT1 pin RA3 Vout = 3.3 V x DATA / 4096 +--> (-) comparator CMP1 --> CMPSTAT bit + CMP1 interrupt pot on RA0 = CMP1A ------> (+) 30 mV hysteresis against chatter input ^ ______ threshold + hysteresis | _____/ \______ | _/ \___ threshold CMPSTAT ___|‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾|____ one clean edge each way

What is special on the dsPIC33CK. The DAC needs a fast clock from the PLL. With Tools → Clock = 100 MIPS the PLL output FPLLO is 200 MHz; with the 4 MIPS setting there is no PLL, so the sketch stops the build with an error message.

SignalBoardOther end

Step by step

  1. Set Tools → Clock = 100 MIPS. Put the jumper J2-18 → J2-17, upload Lab15_DAC and open the Serial Monitor at 115200. It starts at 1650 mV and prints the ADC read-back. Read: the title line and # DC 1650 mV -> read-back on A2: ... mV, close to 1650. Why: the DAC drives RA3, the jumper takes the voltage to RA2, and the ADC measures it.
  2. Send v500, v2500. Read: # DC 500 mV, read-back ... mV, and the same for 2500. Measure J2-18 with a meter. It should match within a few tens of mV.
  3. Send l: the linearity table steps the DAC through its range (codes 0, 455, 910 … 4095) and compares each code with the ADC. Read: one line per code with the expected mV, the measured mV and the error, then the worst error. Why: a perfect DAC would give a straight line; the error column shows how far it is off (plus the ADC’s own 3.2 mV steps).
  4. Send s (sine), t (triangle) or c (staircase). Read: # sine 50 Hz, 0.1..3.2 V, # triangle 50 Hz or # staircase, 16 steps. With a scope on J2-18 you see the waveform.
  5. Send p, close the Serial Monitor and open the Serial Plotter. See: the waveform, read back by the ADC every 2 ms (values 0..1023). Send any character to stop streaming. Why: at 2 ms per point a 20 ms period gives 10 points per wave, so the plot is coarse, but the shape is visible.
  6. Comparator: pot wiper on J2-15, send k2000. Read: # comparator threshold = 2000 mV. Turn the pot on J2-15 through it. Turn the pot: the LED lights above 2.0 V and an interrupt prints comparator edge at every crossing, with no ADC involved.
  7. Turn the pot very slowly through the threshold. Read: one edge per crossing, not a burst. Why: the 30 mV hysteresis stops chatter.
  8. Send k1000 and repeat: now the LED lights above 1.0 V. k also sets the DC output, so with the jumper still in place J2-18 shows 1000 mV.

Expected output

Lab 15 - DAC on DACOUT1 = RA3 (J2-18). v<mV> s t c l p k<mV>
# DC 1650 mV -> read-back on A2: 1648 mV
# DAC code -> expected mV -> ADC read-back mV (jumper J2-18 -> J2-17)
#  0      0     3     err 3
...
#  2275   1833  1829  err -4
...
# worst error ... mV (ADC is 10-bit here = 3.2 mV/step; a few tens of mV is normal)
# comparator threshold = 2000 mV. Turn the pot on J2-15 through it.
# comparator edge #1  pot ABOVE threshold
# comparator edge #2  pot below threshold     (example)

If the read-back after l stays near 0 V, the sketch also prints # read-back ~0 V: jumper missing, or DACOUT1 not driven (see header).

How the code works

1. Clock check.

#if FCY < 50000000UL
#error "Lab15 needs Tools > Clock = 100 MIPS (the DAC is clocked from the PLL)"
#endif

At 4 MIPS the build stops with this message instead of producing a program whose DAC does nothing.

2. dacBegin(): clock and module.

    PMD7bits.CMP1MD = 0;          /* power comparator/DAC module 1 */

    DACCTRL1L = 0;
    DACCTRL1Lbits.CLKSEL  = 3;    /* FPLLO */
    DACCTRL1Lbits.CLKDIV  = 0;    /* 1:1 */
    DACCTRL1Lbits.FCLKDIV = 0;

The DAC sits inside comparator module 1. PMD7.CMP1MD = 0 powers it. DACCTRL1L: CLKSEL = FPLLO (the DAC needs the PLL clock, hence 100 MIPS), DACON = master on (set at the end). DACCTRL2H/L get the MCC default values for slope mode, which this lab does not use.

3. dacBegin(): this DAC and its comparator.

    DAC1CONL = 0;
    DAC1CONLbits.INSEL  = 0;      /* comparator input A = CMP1A = RA0 */
    DAC1CONLbits.HYSSEL = 2;      /* 30 mV hysteresis: no chatter at the threshold */
    DAC1CONLbits.IRQM   = 3;      /* interrupt on rising and falling edge */
    ...
    ANSELAbits.ANSELA3 = 1; TRISAbits.TRISA3 = 1;
    ANSELAbits.ANSELA0 = 1; TRISAbits.TRISA0 = 1;

    DAC1CONLbits.DACEN = 1;
    DACCTRL1Lbits.DACON = 1;

DAC1CONL: DACEN, INSEL = input A (RA0), HYSSEL = 30 mV, IRQM = interrupt on both edges. DAC1DATH = output code. RA3 and RA0 are made analog inputs (ANSEL = 1, TRIS = 1) so the digital pin driver does not fight the analog signals. Slope compensation (SLP1CONH/L) is switched off. Finally the CMP1 interrupt is enabled at priority 3.

4. Writing a value.

inline void dacWrite(uint16_t v) { DAC1DATH = v & 0x0FFF; }      /* 0..4095 */
void dacWriteMv(long mv)
{
    if (mv < 0) mv = 0;
    if (mv > 3300) mv = 3300;
    dacWrite((uint16_t)(mv * 4095L / 3300L));
}

The mask & 0x0FFF keeps only 12 bits. dacWriteMv() clamps to 0..3300 mV first.

5. Read-back and linearity. readbackMv() averages 16 analogRead(A2) values (10-bit, 0..1023) and converts to mV with acc × 3300 / (16 × 1023). Averaging reduces noise. linearity() steps the code by 455 from 0 to 4095 (10 points), waits 5 ms for the output to settle, and prints code, expected mV, measured mV and the error.

6. Waveforms in loop().

    if (mode != DC && (long)(micros() - tNext) >= 0) {
        const unsigned long STEP_US = 1000000UL / (50UL * 64UL);   /* 50 Hz x 64 = 312 us */
        tNext += STEP_US;
        idx = (uint8_t)((idx + 1) & 63);
        if (mode == SINE) dacWrite((uint16_t)sineTab[idx]);
        else if (mode == TRI) dacWrite((uint16_t)(idx < 32 ? idx * 128 : (63 - idx) * 128));
        else dacWrite((uint16_t)((idx / 4) * 273));                 /* 16 steps of ~220 mV */
    }

Waveforms are paced with micros() in loop() (64 samples × 50 Hz). Lab 14 shows the zero-jitter DMA way. The sine table is filled once in setup() with 2047 + 2000 × sin(...), so the sine swings from code 47 to 4047 (about 0.1 V to 3.2 V). The triangle climbs in steps of 128 for 32 samples and falls for 32; the staircase holds each of 16 levels for 4 samples. Adding STEP_US to tNext (instead of “now + step”) keeps the average rate exact even if one update is late.

7. Comparator.

extern "C" void __attribute__((interrupt, no_auto_psv)) _CMP1Interrupt(void)
{
    cmpEdges++;
    IFS4bits.CMP1IF = 0;
}
...
    digitalWrite(LED_BUILTIN, DAC1CONLbits.CMPSTAT ? LED_ON : LED_OFF);

The ISR only counts edges. loop() copies the comparator output CMPSTAT (1 = input above the DAC) to the LED, and prints a line whenever cmpEdges has changed.

Key registers

DACCTRL1L0x80C0 (simulator read-back)DACON = 1 (bit 15, master on), CLKSEL = 3 (FPLLO), CLKDIV = 0, FCLKDIV = 0
DACCTRL2H / DACCTRL2L0x8A / 0x55SSTIME / TMODTIME, MCC defaults for slope mode (unused here)

DAC1CONL.CMPSTAT (bit 7)readcomparator output: 1 = input > DAC

Try it yourself

  1. Easy Make the sine 25 Hz instead of 50 Hz. Hint: STEP_US in loop() (and the copy inside the p branch) uses 50UL.
  2. Easy Make the staircase use 8 steps instead of 16. Hint: the (idx / 4) * 273 line; which divisor and step size give 8 levels from 0 to about 4095?
  3. Medium Add a sawtooth mode w: rise from 0 to 4095 over 64 samples, then jump back to 0. Hint: add a value to enum Mode, a branch in the waveform code, and a command in the Serial.read() section.
  4. Medium Change the hysteresis to the other HYSSEL values and turn the pot slowly through the threshold. Do you see more edges with less hysteresis? Hint: DAC1CONLbits.HYSSEL in dacBegin().
  5. Challenge Build a simple “window detector”: use the comparator to tell whether the pot is above 2.0 V, and the ADC on A2 (with the jumper moved to the pot) for whether it is below 1.0 V. Print LOW, OK or HIGH. Hint: CMPSTAT for the top limit, analogRead() for the bottom.

Check your understanding

What code gives 1.0 V, and what voltage does code 4095 give?

1000 × 4095 / 3300 ≈ 1240. Code 4095 gives 3.3 V × 4095 / 4096 ≈ 3.3 V (just under).

Why does the comparator need hysteresis?

When the input is close to the threshold, noise would make it cross back and forth many times, giving a burst of edges. Hysteresis requires the input to move about 30 mV past the threshold before the output changes, so each real crossing gives one edge.

Why is a comparator used as an over-current trip in motor control, instead of the ADC?

It reacts in nanoseconds in hardware. Reading the ADC and deciding in software takes microseconds or more, which can be too slow to protect a power stage.

The sine has 64 points and runs at 50 Hz. How often must the DAC be updated?

64 × 50 = 3200 times a second, every 312.5 µs (the sketch uses 312 µs).

The DAC output is weak (high impedance). Buffer it with an op-amp before driving a load.
Not verified on hardware: this device’s register file shows no separate DAC output-enable bit, so the lab assumes DACEN alone drives RA3. If J2-18 stays at 0 V, the DAC still works internally as the comparator threshold (k). The simulator confirms the registers (DACCTRL1L = 0x80C0, DAC1CONL = 0xE002, DAC1DATH = 2047) but does not model the analog output.

16Advanced PWM: motor-control generators, dead time, 3-phase sine

The “MC” in dsPIC33CK256MC005 stands for Motor Control: four dedicated PWM generators with complementary outputs and hardware dead time. Here three of them make a 3-phase sine, like the drive of a brushless motor.

advancedPG1–PG3complementarydead timecentre-alignedDDS sineinput capturePWM interruptoverride

Objectives

  • After this lab you can explain what complementary PWM is and why a half-bridge needs dead time.
  • After this lab you can set up a motor-control PWM generator (PGx) by writing its registers directly, without analogWrite().
  • After this lab you can calculate the period register for a centre-aligned PWM and the dead time in clock ticks.
  • After this lab you can explain how a phase accumulator and a sine table (DDS) turn a fixed PWM into a slowly changing sine.
  • After this lab you can measure a frequency with an SCCP input capture and use it to check your own clock assumptions.

Background

PWM (pulse-width modulation) switches a pin on and off very fast. The duty cycle – the share of time the pin is HIGH – sets the average voltage. You already used analogWrite() on D5–D8, which uses the simple SCCP timers. A motor drive needs more: two outputs per phase, exact timing between them, several phases locked together, and a way to switch everything off at once. That is what the four PWM generators PG1–PG4 of this chip do.

Half-bridge and complementary PWM. One motor phase is driven by two transistors in series between the supply and ground: a high-side switch and a low-side switch. The phase output is the point in the middle. When the high side is on, the output is at the supply; when the low side is on, it is at ground. The two switches must always be in opposite states, so the controller drives them with complementary signals: H is the PWM, L is its inverse.

+V ----+ | H --[ high-side switch ] | +-------- phase output (to the motor winding) | L --[ low-side switch ] | GND ----+ if H and L are ON at the same time: +V is shorted to GND = "shoot-through"

Dead time. Real transistors do not switch off instantly. If H goes LOW and L goes HIGH at the very same moment, for a short time both conduct and a large current flows straight from the supply to ground (shoot-through). It heats or destroys the transistors. The fix is dead time: a short gap at every edge where both outputs are LOW. The PWM generator inserts it in hardware by delaying the rising edge of each output (register PGxDTH for H, PGxDTL for L). This lab uses 500 ns, adjustable up to 2 µs.

Centre-aligned PWM. In the usual edge-aligned mode a counter counts up to the period and starts again at 0. In centre-aligned mode it counts up and down, and every pulse is centred in the period. The three phases then switch at different times, not all at the start of the cycle, which gives less electrical noise. The price: one up-down cycle takes twice as many clock ticks, so

f_pwm = f_clk / (2 × PER) PER = 100 MHz / (2 × 20 kHz) = 2500

Making a sine (DDS). If the duty cycle of one output changes slowly in a sine shape, the average voltage of that output is a sine. Filter it with a resistor and a capacitor and you see the sine itself. Three outputs whose sines are 120° apart form a 3-phase system, which makes a rotating magnetic field in a motor. The sketch uses direct digital synthesis (DDS): a 32-bit number (the phase accumulator) grows by a fixed step at every PWM period; its top 8 bits pick one of 256 entries in a sine table. A bigger step means a faster sine.

What is special on the dsPIC33CK. The PWM pins are fixed (no PPS remapping): PG1 owns RB14/RB15, PG2 RB12/RB13, PG3 RB10/RB11. Each generator can start its cycle on a trigger from another one (here all follow PG1), duty updates are taken over only at the start of a cycle (no half-changed pulses), and an override can force both pins to a fixed level at once – the same path a hardware fault input uses.

You need

10 kΩ resistor + 100 nF capacitor1 eachoptional: RC low-pass filter to see the sine on A0
Breadboard, jumper wires–

Wiring

The six PWM pins are fixed (no PPS):

GeneratorHigh sideLow sidePhase
PG1PWM1H RB14 J2-8PWM1L RB15 J2-9U (0°)
PG2PWM2H RB12 J2-6PWM2L RB13 J2-7V (120°)

Connect only what you need for the step you are doing:

SignalBoard pinOther end
Serial TXTX RC10 J5-2adapter RX

Scope / analyser CH2PWM1L RB15 J2-9probe tip

The RC filter (10 kΩ, 100 nF) has a corner frequency of about 160 Hz. It lets the slow 1–100 Hz sine through and smooths away most of the 20 kHz switching.

Step by step

  1. Select Tools → Clock = 100 MIPS, open Lab16_AdvancedPWM and upload it. Open the Serial Monitor at 115200. You see the title line, and about one second later a status line. It shows PER=2500 and the measured PWM frequency; it should read about 20000 Hz. The USER LED blinks at 2 Hz while the outputs are running.
  2. Read the measured= value carefully. The sketch assumes the PWM clock is FCY (100 MHz); this has not been checked on hardware yet. If the value is far from 20000 Hz, the line # NOTE: measured != 20 kHz ... appears. See the note at the end of this lab.
  3. Scope / logic analyser on J2-8 and J2-9: two 20 kHz signals, one the inverse of the other. Zoom in on an edge: for 500 ns both are LOW. That gap is the dead time. Send d2000: the gap widens to 2 µs. Send d0 to see the edges line up, then d500 to go back.
  4. Still on the scope, watch the pulse width of J2-8 slowly grow and shrink once per second (modulation 1 Hz, depth 80 %). That changing width is the sine, coded in the duty cycle.
  5. LEDs: wire the three LEDs to J2-8, J2-6 and J2-4 and send f1. The three LEDs fade up and down one after the other, 120° apart, like a rotating magnetic field. Send f5 and they chase faster; above about 20 Hz your eye sees only a steady glow.
  6. See the sine: build the RC filter from J2-8 to A0 (J2-15). Send f5, then a. Close the Serial Monitor and open the Serial Plotter: a smooth 5 Hz sine of raw ADC values. Any key you send stops the stream.
  7. Send m30 (after stopping the stream): the status line shows depth=30%. Start a again: the sine is smaller, centred on the same middle value. m0 gives a flat line at half the supply (50 % duty).
  8. Send s: the status says STOPPED, the LEDs go dark and both pins of every pair are held LOW by the override logic. The USER LED stops blinking. Send g to go again.
  9. Send ? at any time to repeat the status and a fresh frequency measurement.

Expected output

Lab 16 - 3-phase sine PWM on PG1..PG3 (J2-4..J2-9). f<hz> m<%> d<ns> s g a ?
# PER=2500 (expect 20000 Hz)  measured=20000.0 Hz  mod=1.0 Hz depth=80% dead=500 ns  RUNNING  isr/s~20000

These are the values the sketch is designed for, not a measurement: the simulator does not run the PWM generator, and the board has not been tried yet. If no PWM edges arrive, the status shows measured=no edges on RB14. isr/s~ is the number of PWM interrupts since the previous status line, so it equals the rate only when the lines are about one second apart. With command a the plotter receives one number per line (0…1023), every 5 ms.

How the code works

centre-aligned counter: /\/\/\/\ f_pwm = f_clk / (2 x PER) = 100 MHz / 5000 = 20 kHz PWM1H ___|‾‾‾‾‾‾|________|‾‾‾‾‾‾|___ PWM1L ‾‾|_|‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾|_|‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾|_|‾ <- complementary, with dead time (both LOW) at every edge duty(t) = PER/2 + PER/2 x depth x sin(phase + 0 / 120 / 240 deg)

Constants. The period register is computed from the assumed PWM clock at compile time:

#if FCY < 50000000UL
#error "Lab16 needs Tools > Clock = 100 MIPS"
#endif

const unsigned long PWM_HZ   = 20000;
const unsigned long PCLK_HZ  = FCY;            /* PWM master clock = FCY (MCLKSEL 00) */
const uint16_t      PER      = (uint16_t)(PCLK_HZ / (2UL * PWM_HZ));   /* centre-aligned */

PER = 100 000 000 / 40 000 = 2500. If the real PWM clock turns out to be different, PCLK_HZ is the one line to change.

One table of register pointers. PG1, PG2 and PG3 have identical register layouts, so the sketch stores pointers to them in an array and configures all three in a loop:

const PG pg[3] = {
    { &PG1CONL, &PG1CONH, &PG1STAT, &PG1IOCONL, &PG1IOCONH, ... &PG1DTL, &PG1DTH },
    { &PG2CONL, ... },
    { &PG3CONL, ... },
};

Setting up the generators (pwmBegin()):

PMD1bits.PWMMD = 0;                         /* power the PWM module */
PCLKCON = 0x0000;                           /* MCLKSEL = FCY, DIVSEL n/a */

for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    *pg[i].CONL   = 0;                      /* off while configuring */
    *pg[i].CONL   = CONL_CLK_MCLK | CONL_CENTER;
    *pg[i].CONH   = (i == 0 ? 0x0000u : CONH_SOC_PG1) | CONH_UPD_SOC;
    *pg[i].PER    = PER;
    *pg[i].DC     = PER / 2;                /* 50 % = sine zero */
    *pg[i].IOCONL = IOCONL_OVRENH | IOCONL_OVRENL;   /* start forced LOW */
    *pg[i].IOCONH = IOCONH_PENH | IOCONH_PENL;       /* PWM owns both pins, complementary */
    *pg[i].EVTH   = (i == 0) ? EVTH_IEVT_EOC : 0x0300u;   /* only PG1 interrupts */
}
setDeadTime(500);
  1. PMD1bits.PWMMD = 0 switches the module on (PMD = peripheral module disable; 1 would cut its power). PCLKCON = 0 selects FCY as the PWM master clock.
  2. PGxCONL: CLKSEL = 01 (use the master clock) and MODSEL = 100 (centre-aligned). The generator stays OFF while it is being set up.
  3. PGxCONH: PG2 and PG3 get SOCS = 0001 – they start each cycle when PG1 starts its cycle, so the three phases stay locked together. UPDMOD = 000 means new values are taken over at the start of a cycle.
  4. PGxDC = PER/2 = 50 % duty, which is the zero line of the sine.
  5. PGxIOCONH: PENH and PENL hand both pins to the PWM module, PMOD = 00 makes them complementary. PGxIOCONL starts with the override ON, so the pins stay LOW until everything is ready.
  6. PGxEVTH: PG1 interrupts at the end of each cycle (IEVTSEL = 00); PG2/PG3 have their interrupt off (IEVTSEL = 11).
IPC16bits.PWM1IP = 5;
IFS4bits.PWM1IF = 0;
IEC4bits.PWM1IE = 1;

/* clients first, master last, so they are already waiting for PG1's SOC */
*pg[2].CONL |= CONL_ON;
*pg[1].CONL |= CONL_ON;
*pg[0].CONL |= CONL_ON;
outputs(true);

The PG1 interrupt gets priority 5. PG3 and PG2 are switched on first and wait for PG1’s start-of-cycle; PG1 is switched on last, so all three begin together. Then outputs(true) removes the override.

Dead time (setDeadTime()) converts nanoseconds to clock ticks:

uint16_t ticks = (uint16_t)((uint32_t)ns * (PCLK_HZ / 1000000UL) / 1000UL);
if (ticks > 0x3FFF) ticks = 0x3FFF;
for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) { *pg[i].DTH = ticks; *pg[i].DTL = ticks; *pg[i].STAT |= STAT_UPDREQ; }

At 100 MHz one tick is 10 ns, so 500 ns = 50 ticks and 2000 ns = 200 ticks. The same value goes to the H and the L side.

The PWM interrupt runs once per PWM period (20 kHz) and computes three new duty cycles:

extern "C" void __attribute__((interrupt, no_auto_psv)) _PWM1Interrupt(void)
{
    phaseAcc += phaseInc;
    uint8_t idx = (uint8_t)(phaseAcc >> 24);              /* top 8 bits -> table */
    const uint8_t off[3] = { 0, 85, 171 };                /* 0, 120, 240 degrees */
    for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
        int32_t s = (int32_t)sineTab[(uint8_t)(idx + off[i])] * depthQ15 >> 15;
        uint16_t dc = (uint16_t)((PER / 2) + (((int32_t)(PER / 2) * s) >> 15));
        *pg[i].DC = dc;
    }
    PG1STATbits.UPDREQ = 1;
    PG2STATbits.UPDREQ = 1;
    PG3STATbits.UPDREQ = 1;
    pwmIsrCount++;
    IFS4bits.PWM1IF = 0;
}
  1. The sine table sineTab[256] is filled once in setup() with values from −32767 to +32767.
  2. Phase V reads 85 entries further on (85/256 × 360° ≈ 120°), phase W 171 entries (≈ 240°). Because idx + off[i] is cast to uint8_t, it wraps around from 255 to 0 by itself.
  3. depthQ15 is the depth as a fraction of 32768 (80 % = 26214). Multiplying and shifting right by 15 is a fast way to multiply by a fraction without floating point. At 80 % depth the duty swings from 250 to 2250 of 2500 (10 % to 90 %).
  4. New duty values are written to PGxDC. UPDREQ asks the hardware to load them at the next cycle start, never in the middle of a pulse, so there are no glitches.

Modulation frequency sets the phase step:

uint32_t inc = (uint32_t)(hz * 4294967296.0 / (double)PWM_HZ);
noInterrupts(); phaseInc = inc; interrupts();

One full turn of the accumulator is 232. With 20 000 steps per second, a step of f × 2³² / 20000 makes exactly f turns per second (1 Hz → step 214 748). The 32-bit write is protected with noInterrupts(), because the ISR could otherwise read half of an old and half of a new value.

Stop and go (outputs()) set or clear the override bits:

if (on) *pg[i].IOCONL &= (uint16_t)~(IOCONL_OVRENH | IOCONL_OVRENL);
else    *pg[i].IOCONL |= (IOCONL_OVRENH | IOCONL_OVRENL);

With OVRENH/OVRENL set, the pins show the override data (OVRDAT = 00, both LOW) instead of the PWM. The generator keeps running in the background, so g resumes at once.

Self-check (measurePwmHz()): SCCP2 is routed to RB14 through PPS (RPINR4bits.ICM2R = 46, RP46 = RB14) and set up as a 32-bit input capture that stores the timer value at every rising edge. The sketch collects 9 timestamps (8 periods) within 50 ms and computes

uint32_t span = t[8] - t[0];      /* 8 periods */
return span ? 8.0 * (double)FCY / (double)span : 0.0;

The capture timer counts at FCY, which is known for sure, so this tells you the real PWM frequency even if the PWM clock assumption is wrong.

loop() blinks the USER LED while running and reads single-letter commands. readNumber() collects the digits after the letter (it waits up to 50 ms for each next digit). Each command checks its range (f 1…100, m 0…100, d 0…2000) and then prints the status.

Key registers

Try it yourself

  1. Easy Change the default modulation and depth that the sketch starts with. Hint: the line double modHz = 1.0; int depthPc = 80; int deadNs = 500; and the matching depthQ15 = 26214 near the top.
  2. Easy Make the PWM 10 kHz instead of 20 kHz. Hint: PWM_HZ; PER and the DDS step follow automatically. Check the new value with ?.
  3. Medium Reverse the direction of the “rotating field” (the LEDs chase the other way). Hint: the off[3] array in _PWM1Interrupt() – swap the 85 and the 171.
  4. Medium Add a command p that prints the current phase index idx and the three duty values. Hint: copy the computation from the ISR into a function, read phaseAcc with interrupts off.
  5. Challenge Use the fourth generator PG4 for a fourth output, or add a soft start: let the depth ramp from 0 to 80 % over 2 s after g. Hint: change depthQ15 a little in loop() every few milliseconds, never jump.

Troubleshooting

SymptomLikely causeFix
Compile error Lab16 needs Tools > Clock = 100 MIPSClock menu set to 4 MIPSTools → Clock = 100 MIPS, upload again
measured=no edges on RB14PWM not running, outputs stopped (s), or something on J2-8 pulls the pinSend g; remove other wiring from J2-8; press RESET
