Check your understanding

Why must the high-side and low-side outputs never be HIGH at the same time?

The two switches are in series between the supply and ground. If both conduct, the supply is shorted through them (shoot-through), which can destroy the transistors. Dead time keeps both off for a short moment at every edge.

With centre-aligned mode and a 100 MHz clock, what PER gives 10 kHz?

PER = 100 000 000 / (2 × 10 000) = 5000. The factor 2 comes from the counter going up and down.

How many clock ticks are 1 µs of dead time, and what does d1000 write to PGxDTH?

At 100 MHz one tick is 10 ns, so 1 µs = 100 ticks; setDeadTime(1000) writes 100 to PGxDTH and PGxDTL.

Why does the sketch set UPDREQ instead of letting PGxDC change immediately?

A duty change in the middle of a pulse could make one pulse too short or too long (a glitch). With UPDREQ the hardware loads the new values only at the start of the next cycle, and all three generators load them together.

These are logic-level signals. Never connect them directly to MOSFETs or a motor. A real inverter needs gate drivers and a fault input. Also, RB10–RB12 are the Serial2/RS485 pins of Labs 21 and 24. The pins are 3.3 V outputs: keep the 1 kΩ resistors with the LEDs and do not connect 5 V to them.
Not verified yet: the MPLAB simulator does not model the PWM generator. It confirms the registers are set up (PG1CONL = 0x800C, PER = 2500, DC = 1250), but there is no output or interrupt. Whether the PWM really counts at FCY will only be known on the board, which is why the sketch measures and prints the frequency. If it shows 10 kHz or 40 kHz, the clock is FCY/2 or 2×FCY: scale PCLK_HZ to match.
Resources: the self-check borrows SCCP2 (the PWM of D6) for a moment each time the status is printed.

17EEPROM emulation in Flash

This chip has no data EEPROM. Make 256 bytes of EEPROM out of program Flash, with EEPwrite(address, data) and EEPread(address), so data survives power-off.

advancedEEPwrite / EEPreadEEPput / EEPgetNVM controllerpage erasedouble-word writewear levellingNVMKEY unlockpower-fail safe

Objectives

  • After this lab you can explain the difference between RAM, Flash and EEPROM, and why Flash cannot simply be overwritten byte by byte.
  • After this lab you can store and read settings that survive RESET and power-off with EEPwrite/EEPread and EEPput/EEPget.
  • After this lab you can explain how a log of entries spreads the wear over a whole Flash page (wear levelling).
  • After this lab you can describe the NVM unlock sequence (NVMCON, NVMADR, NVMKEY) that every Flash erase and write needs.
  • After this lab you can explain how the page swap survives a power cut at any moment.

Background

Three kinds of memory. RAM holds your variables; it is fast and can be written any number of times, but it forgets everything when the power goes. Flash holds the program; it keeps its content without power, but it is written in a special, slow way. EEPROM (electrically erasable programmable read-only memory) also keeps its content without power and can be changed one byte at a time; many small chips (like the ATmega of an Arduino Uno) have a few hundred bytes of it for settings. The dsPIC33CK256MC005 has no EEPROM. Real products therefore keep their settings in a reserved part of program Flash. This lab does exactly that.

Flash rules. An erased Flash cell reads as 1. Writing (“programming”) can only turn 1s into 0s. To get a 1 back you must erase, and an erase always clears a whole page at once. On this chip the smallest write is a double word (two 24-bit instruction words), and each word may be written only once per erase. So you cannot change byte 20 from 123 to 124 in place: you would have to erase the whole page, which also wipes all the other bytes.

RAMFlash (this chip)EEPROM (other chips)
Keeps data without powernoyesyes
Smallest write1 byte1 double word, only onto erased cells1 byte
Erasenot neededwhole page onlyper byte, automatic
Enduranceunlimitedabout 10 000 erases per pagetypically 100 000 or more

Wear levelling. Each erase wears the Flash a little; after about 10 000 erases a page may fail. If every EEPwrite erased a page, a setting saved once a second would kill the Flash in under three hours. The trick is a log: each write appends a small entry (“address 20 now holds 123”) to the next free place of a page. Only when the page is full is anything erased. The newest entry for an address wins. Spreading the writes over 511 places of a page like this is a simple form of wear levelling.

Power cuts. Settings must survive the power going away at the worst moment, even in the middle of an erase or a write. The library uses two pages: a page is only trusted when it has a valid header, and the header of a new page is written last. Each entry also stores its data byte twice (once inverted), so a half-written entry is recognised and ignored.

You need

PartQtyNotes
dsPIC33CK Nano board1any clock setting
USB-C supply / cable1power only; you will unplug it to test power-off
3.3 V USB-serial adapter1on J5, Serial Monitor at 115200

Wiring

Nothing to wire on the breadboard. Only the USB-serial adapter on J5. The USER button (RC12) and USER LED (RC13) are on the board.

SignalBoard pinOther end
Serial TXTX RC10 J5-2adapter RX
Serial RXRX RC11 J5-3adapter TX
GNDJ5-4adapter GND (leave J5-1 open)

The functions, in the FlashEEPROM.h tab

All the Flash code is in the second tab of the sketch, FlashEEPROM.h. It works like the Arduino EEPROM: 256 bytes, addresses 0…255, and a byte that was never written reads 255. To use it in your own sketch, copy FlashEEPROM.h into your sketch folder and add #include "FlashEEPROM.h".

#include "FlashEEPROM.h" EEPbegin(); // once, in setup() EEPwrite(20, 123); // store the byte 123 at address 20 byte x = EEPread(20); // x = 123, also after a reset or power-off struct Settings { uint8_t magic; uint8_t spare; uint16_t bootCount, blinkMs, userValue; } cfg; EEPput(0, cfg); // store a whole variable or struct (here addresses 0..7) EEPget(0, cfg); // read it back
FunctionWhat it does
EEPbegin()finds the two reserved Flash pages and loads the saved bytes; call once in setup()
EEPwrite(address, data)stores one byte; true = written and verified. A byte that already has that value is skipped (no wear).
EEPread(address)reads one byte (255 if never written)
EEPput(address, variable)stores any variable or struct, byte by byte, from address on
EEPget(address, variable)reads it back
EEPclear()erases everything: all bytes read 255
EEPdump()prints all 256 bytes as a hex table on Serial

Also readable (but do not write them): EEP_SIZE, eepActivePage, eepNextSlot, eepSeq (number of page swaps) and eepWrites (Flash writes since reset).

This sketch keeps its settings at addresses 0…7 (EEPput/EEPget). A magic byte tells it whether settings were ever saved. Addresses 16…255 are free for the w/r commands.

AddressFieldMeaning
0magic0x5A = “settings were saved before”
1spare0, unused
2–3bootCount+1 on every reset or power-up (low byte first)
4–5blinkMsLED blink period, 20…10000 ms
6–7userValueany number 0…65535 (v command or USER button)
8–15–not used
16–255freefor w / r
CommandAction
?show the settings
b<ms>set the blink period, e.g. b250 (saved at once)
v<num>set the user value, e.g. v1234 (saved at once)
w<addr> <n>EEPwrite one byte, e.g. w20 123
r<addr>EEPread one byte, e.g. r20
ddump all 256 bytes
ffactory reset (erase everything)
USER buttonuserValue + 1 and save

Step by step

  1. Upload Lab17_EEPROM, open the Serial Monitor at 115200. The first start prints no settings saved yet and bootCount=1, because all bytes still read 255 and the magic byte is not 0x5A. The LED blinks with the default 500 ms.
  2. Press RESET a few times: bootCount counts up. Unplug USB-C and plug it back in: it keeps counting. RAM was lost, but the Flash kept the value.
  3. Send w20 123 (= EEPwrite(20, 123)), then r20: it reads 123. Power-cycle and send r20 again: still 123. An address you never wrote, e.g. r30, reads 255 (the value of erased Flash).
  4. Send b100: the reply is # saved and the LED blinks fast. Power-cycle: still fast. Send v1234 to store a number; it comes back after a power-cycle too.
  5. Press the USER button: # userValue + 1, saved (button) and the new value are printed.
  6. Send d to see all 256 bytes. Bytes 02–03 are bootCount (low byte first), 04–05 blinkMs, and so on. The first line shows which page is active, the next free slot and the number of page swaps.
  7. Watch Flash writes this run. A reset that only changes bootCount costs 1 write, because the other 7 bytes are unchanged and skipped. Send w20 123 a second time: the count does not grow, because the byte already holds 123.
  8. Watch slot: it grows by one with each real write. When it reaches 512 the next write triggers a page swap: the dump then shows the other page and one more page swap.
  9. Send f (factory reset) then RESET: back to the defaults, and every byte reads 255.
  10. Finally, upload the sketch again: the settings are gone. Every new upload erases the emulated EEPROM (see the warning below).

Expected output

Lab 17 - EEPROM emulation in Flash.  ? b<ms> v<num> w<addr> <n> r<addr> d f
# boot counted and saved
bootCount=3  blinkMs=500  userValue=0
  page 0  slot 13/512  Flash writes this run 1
# EEPwrite(20, 123)
# EEPread(20) = 123

A dump with d looks like this (example values):

# EEPROM 256 bytes, page 0 @0x2A000, slot 14/512, page swaps 0
# 00: 5A 00 03 00 F4 01 00 00 FF FF FF FF FF FF FF FF
# 10: FF FF FF FF 7B FF FF FF FF FF FF FF FF FF FF FF
# 20: FF FF FF FF FF FF FF FF FF FF FF FF FF FF FF FF
...

F4 01 is 0x01F4 = 500 (blinkMs, low byte first) and 7B at address 0x14 = 20 is the 123 you wrote.

How the code works

Flash 0x2A000 page 0 [HDR seq][20:7B][02:01][02:02][02:03][ FFFF erased ... ] <- active, append here Flash 0x2A800 page 1 [ FFFF erased .............................................. ] <- spare entry = 1 double word: 0xA5 | address , data | ~data (512 slots per page = header + 511 entries) EEPbegin(): replay the entries in order into a 256-byte RAM copy -> the newest entry per address wins page full -> erase page 1, copy every byte != 255 there, header LAST, erase page 0
  1. Flash rules: Flash bits can only go 1→0 when written; only an erase sets them back to 1, and only a whole page at a time. The smallest write is a double word (2 instruction words), and each word can be written once per erase. So a byte can’t be overwritten in place.
  2. Log of entries: every EEPwrite appends one entry (address + data + inverted data) to the active page. EEPbegin() reads the page from the start into RAM, so later entries overwrite earlier ones and EEPread() is just a RAM read.
  3. Unlock: every erase or write sets NVMADR and NVMCON (NVMOP 0011 = page erase, 0001 = double word), loads the data latches through TBLPAG = 0xFA, then __builtin_write_NVM() writes 0x55/0xAA to NVMKEY and sets WR. Interrupts are masked (DISI) during the unlock. These are the same routines as the board’s bootloader.
  4. Page swap and power cuts: when a page is full, the other page is erased, every byte that is not 255 is copied there, and its header is written last. A page without a header is never trusted, so a power cut during the copy loses nothing. If both pages end up with a header (the cut came before the old page was erased), the higher sequence number wins. An entry whose inverted copy doesn’t match (half written) is ignored.
  5. Wear: a page survives about 10 000 erases and holds 511 writes, minus the bytes copied at each swap. With 20 bytes in use that is about 10 million byte writes. Still, only write when a value changes, not in every pass of loop().
  6. Where it lives: uint16_t eepArea[2048] __attribute__((space(prog), address(0x2A000), noload)). noload means the linker reserves the space but puts nothing in the .hex. That matters because the Serial bootloader checks a CRC of the application before every start, so data that changes must lie outside that range. A second noload block reserves the gap above 0x2B000, so the linker can’t place code up there, out of reach of short calls.

The sketch: setup(). It loads the EEPROM, reads the settings struct and checks the magic byte:

EEPbegin();
EEPget(SETTINGS_ADDR, cfg);
if (cfg.magic != MAGIC) {                  /* never saved: all bytes read 255 */
    Serial.println("# no settings saved yet - first start, using defaults");
    cfg.magic = MAGIC; cfg.spare = 0;
    cfg.bootCount = 0; cfg.blinkMs = 500; cfg.userValue = 0;
}
cfg.bootCount++;
Serial.println(saveSettings() ? "# boot counted and saved" : "# SAVE FAILED");

On a fresh chip every byte is 255, so magic is 0xFF, not 0x5A, and the defaults are used. saveSettings() is just EEPput(SETTINGS_ADDR, cfg).

loop() blinks the LED with (millis() / cfg.blinkMs) % 2, detects a USER button press (HIGH → LOW edge), and handles the commands. readNumber() skips a space, comma or = before a number and stops at one after it, so w20 123 gives two numbers; it returns −1 when no digits were typed.

The library: one write. EEPwrite() first compares with the RAM copy:

if (eepData[address] == data && eepActivePage >= 0) return true;   /* no change: no wear */
...
if (eepActivePage < 0 || eepNextSlot >= EEP_SLOTS) {
    if (eepNewPage()) return true;      /* new page: copies eepData[], which already holds the new value */
    continue;
}
if (eepWriteSlot(eepActivePage, eepNextSlot++, EEP_ENTRY_TAG | address,
                 data | ((uint16_t)(uint8_t)~data << 8)))
    return true;

An entry is two 16-bit words: 0xA500 | address and data | (~data << 8). The tag 0xA5 and the inverted copy let eepReplay() reject damaged entries. If a slot does not verify, it tries the next one, up to 3 times.

The library: one Flash operation.

NVMADRU = (uint16_t)(a >> 16);
NVMADR  = (uint16_t)a;
NVMCON  = EEP_NVMOP_WRITE_DW;            /* 0x4001: WREN | double-word program */
TBLPAG = EEP_NVM_LATCH_PAGE;             /* 0xFA: the write latches */
__builtin_tblwtl(0, w0); __builtin_tblwth(0, 0x00FF);
__builtin_tblwtl(2, w1); __builtin_tblwth(2, 0x00FF);
...
__builtin_disi(7);
__builtin_write_NVM();                   /* 0x55, 0xAA -> NVMKEY, then WR = 1 */
while (NVMCONbits.WR) { }
return !NVMCONbits.WRERR;

The data is loaded into the write latches first, then the unlock key starts the write. The key sequence must not be interrupted, which is why DISI blocks interrupts for a few cycles. The CPU waits until WR clears. Only the low 16 bits of each 24-bit instruction word are used; the upper byte stays 0xFF. Reading uses __builtin_tblrdl() with TBLPAG set to the upper address bits.

The library: page swap (eepNewPage()): erase the other page, write one entry for every byte that is not 255, write the header (0xEE5A + sequence number) last, and only then erase the old page.

Key registers

Register / bitValue usedMeaning
NVMCON0x4003WREN = 1 (writes allowed), NVMOP = 0011: page erase
NVMCON0x4001WREN = 1, NVMOP = 0001: program one double word
NVMCON.WRset by __builtin_write_NVM(), polled1 = operation running; hardware clears it when done
NVMCON.WRERRread1 = the operation failed
NVMADRU / NVMADRe.g. 0x0002 / 0xA000upper / lower part of the Flash address (0x2A000 = page 0, 0x2A800 = page 1)
NVMKEY0x55, then 0xAAunlock sequence; written by __builtin_write_NVM()
TBLPAG0xFAtable page of the write latches (for TBLWTL/TBLWTH)
TBLPAGaddress >> 16table page for reading Flash with TBLRDL; restored afterwards
DISI7disable interrupts for 7 instruction cycles during the unlock

Try it yourself

  1. Easy Add a new field uint16_t brightness to struct Settings and a command to set it. Hint: the struct grows to 10 bytes; change the magic value (e.g. 0x5B) so old saved data is not misread.
  2. Easy Store a whole float at address 100 with EEPput(100, f) and read it back after a power-cycle. Hint: add a command in loop() next to 'w'.
  3. Medium Count how many writes fit before a page swap: write alternating values to one address in a loop and print eepSeq and eepNextSlot after each one. Hint: the swap happens when eepNextSlot reaches EEP_SLOTS. Keep the loop short – every swap is one erase.
  4. Medium Add a checksum byte to the settings so a half-saved struct (power cut during EEPput) is detected. Hint: compute it over the other bytes before saveSettings() and check it after EEPget in setup().
  5. Challenge Save the settings only after nothing has changed for 5 s (a “lazy save”), so a user turning a knob does not cause hundreds of writes. Hint: set a dirty flag and a timestamp instead of calling saveSettings() in the b/v commands.

Troubleshooting

SymptomLikely causeFix
Settings gone after uploading againEvery upload (PICkit or Serial bootloader) erases the whole application area, including 0x2A000–0x2AFFFExpected; settings survive only RESET and power-off
bootCount goes up by more than 1 per resetThe board resets twice (e.g. plugging in the adapter), or the button bounced on RESETPress RESET once, firmly
# SAVE FAILED or # WRITE FAILEDFlash write did not verify (WRERR, or worn page)Try f and RESET; if it stays, report it – this has not been seen in the simulator
w20 123 replies with the usage textAddress or value out of range, or no space between the numbersAddress 0…255, value 0…255, e.g. w20 123
After a w to address 0…7 and a RESET, the settings look wrongAddresses 0…7 hold the settings struct; the sketch warns # note: addresses 0..7 hold the settings. The RAM copy cfg only changes at the next startUse addresses 16…255, or f + RESET
Link error “PC Relative branch out of range” in your own sketchCode placed above the reserved pagesKeep both noload blocks of FlashEEPROM.h unchanged

Check your understanding

Why can’t the library simply overwrite the byte at address 20 in Flash?

Writing can only change bits from 1 to 0, and each word can be written once per erase. Getting 1s back needs an erase, which clears a whole page. So the library appends a new entry instead, and the newest entry wins.

A reset changes only bootCount from 2 to 3. Why does that cost only one Flash write, although EEPput writes 8 bytes?

EEPput calls EEPwrite for each byte, and EEPwrite skips a byte that already holds the new value. Only the low byte of bootCount changed.

The power fails while the library copies data into the new page. What happens at the next start?

The new page has no header yet (the header is written last), so it is not trusted. EEPbegin() uses the old page, which is still complete.

What does an erased byte read, and why does the sketch use a magic byte?

255 (0xFF), because erased Flash bits are 1. Without a marker the sketch could not tell “never saved” from “saved as 255”; the magic value 0x5A at address 0 shows that real settings were stored.

The data survives RESET and power-off, but any new upload (PICkit or Serial bootloader) erases it, because both erase the whole application area. EEPput writes byte by byte: a power cut in the middle can leave a variable half old, half new, just like a real EEPROM.
Simulator-tested (MPLAB X): bootCount 1 → 2 → 3 across three resets. 3000 random EEPwrites over 48 addresses, checked against a copy after 12 simulated restarts: 0 errors, 6 page swaps. EEPput/EEPget of a struct with a float. Power cuts simulated before and after the new page’s header, and a half-written entry: no data lost. The .hex contains nothing in 0x2A000–0x2AFFF, in all three memory layouts.

18Power saving & reset sources: Doze, Idle, Sleep, POR, BOR, WDT

Find out why the chip started, and cut its power with the three low-power modes.

advancedRCONPOR / BORwatchdogDozeIdleSleepwake-uppersistent RAMRESET instruction

Objectives

  • After this lab you can read the RCON register and tell which event reset the chip: power-on, brown-out, RESET button, watchdog, software reset or a trap.
  • After this lab you can explain what the power-on reset, the brown-out reset and the watchdog protect against.
  • After this lab you can choose between Doze, Idle and Sleep, and say what keeps running in each mode.
  • After this lab you can wake the chip from Sleep with a pin interrupt.
  • After this lab you can keep a variable across a reset with __attribute__((persistent)).

Background

Why a product needs to know the reset reason. A microcontroller can restart for many reasons: the power was just switched on, the supply dipped, someone pressed RESET, the program hung and the watchdog stepped in, or the program restarted itself on purpose. For the user they all look the same – the device starts again. For you, the reason is a very useful clue: a log that says “watchdog reset” tells you the program got stuck. The dsPIC33CK keeps one flag per cause in the RCON (reset control) register. Hardware sets the flags; only software clears them.

RCON bitNameSet when…
0PORpower-on reset: VDD rose from about 0 V
1BORbrown-out reset: VDD dipped below the BOR trip point (also set together with POR at power-up)
2IDLEa RESET hit the device while it was in Idle
3SLEEPa RESET hit the device while it was in Sleep
4WDTOwatchdog time-out reset
6SWRsoftware RESET instruction
7EXTRexternal reset on the MCLR pin (RESET button, PICkit)
8VREGSnot a reset flag: keeps the voltage regulator on in Sleep (faster wake-up)
9CMconfiguration mismatch
14IOPUWRillegal opcode, or an uninitialised W register used as a pointer
15TRAPRtrap conflict reset

POR, BOR and the watchdog. A CPU needs a stable supply. The power-on reset (POR) holds the chip in reset while VDD is still rising. The brown-out reset (BOR) does the same whenever VDD later sags below a trip point, so the CPU never runs at a voltage where it might misread its own Flash. On this family the BOR is always on. The watchdog timer (WDT) is a separate timer with its own clock. The program must “feed” it regularly; if it ever stops doing that (an endless loop, a deadlock), the watchdog resets the chip. That is how a device far from any human recovers from a bug.

Saving power. The current a CMOS chip draws grows with its clock frequency. If the CPU has nothing to do, slowing or stopping the clock saves power. The dsPIC33CK has three ways:

  • Doze: only the CPU clock is divided (1:2 up to 1:128). Peripherals such as Timer1, the UART and the ADC keep full speed, so timing (millis(), baud rate) stays correct while the code runs slower.
  • Idle (PWRSAV #1): the CPU stops completely, the peripherals keep running. Any enabled interrupt wakes the CPU, which runs the ISR and continues after the PWRSAV instruction.
  • Sleep (PWRSAV #0): the whole clock system stops. Only events that need no clock can wake it: a pin change (change notification, CN), an INTx pin, or the watchdog. millis() does not advance while asleep.

Persistent RAM. At every start the C start-up code sets all global variables to zero. A variable marked __attribute__((persistent)) is skipped, so its value survives a reset. After a power-on its content is random, so the sketch clears it itself when POR is set.

You need

PartQtyNotes
dsPIC33CK Nano board1uses the on-board RESET and USER buttons and the USER LED
USB-C supply / cable1power only; you will unplug it for the power-on test
3.3 V USB-serial adapter1on J5, Serial Monitor at 115200
USB power meter (“USB doctor”) or multimeter on the mA range1optional: in series with the USB-C 5 V supply to see the current drop
Adjustable bench supply1optional, only for the brown-out test

Wiring

Nothing to wire on the breadboard. Only the USB-serial adapter on J5; optionally the power meter in the USB-C cable.

SignalBoard pinOther end
Serial TXTX RC10 J5-2adapter RX
Serial RXRX RC11 J5-3adapter TX
GNDJ5-4adapter GND (leave J5-1 open)
Supply current (optional)USB-C inputUSB power meter between the charger and the board
The board’s PWR LED (about 1.3 mA) and the LDO’s quiescent current stay in every reading, so the meter never shows the chip alone. Look at the differences between the modes. If you power the board from the adapter’s 3V3 instead, the readings are not comparable.

Step by step

  1. Upload Lab18_PowerReset, open the Serial Monitor at 115200. The first lines show RCON, the list of flags that are set, the reset reason and # starts since power-on. The LED blinks at 1 Hz.
  2. RESET button: press RESET. The report shows [EXTR MCLR pin] and MCLR pin: RESET button or programmer; the start counter goes up by one.
  3. Software reset: send r. The sketch prints executing RESET instruction... and restarts; the reason is SOFTWARE reset. The counter goes up again.
  4. Watchdog reset: send w. The sketch switches the watchdog on and then hangs in an endless loop without feeding it. About 1 s later the chip restarts with WATCHDOG reset.
  5. Power-on reset: unplug USB-C for 2 s and plug it back in. The reason is POWER-ON (POR and BOR are both set) and the counter starts again at 1, because persistent RAM is cleared on power-on.
  6. Send 1 (RUN): the sketch counts how many loop passes fit into 1 s. Note the number and, if you have the meter, the current.
  7. Send 2 (DOZE 1:128): for 3 s the LED still blinks at exactly 2 Hz, but the loop count is about 128× smaller than RUN × 3, and the current drops. Peripherals keep full speed; only the CPU is slowed.
  8. Send 3 (IDLE): the CPU stops between Timer1 ticks. It reports woke 3000 times in 3 s, one per 1 ms tick, and RCON.IDLE = 0 (only a reset during Idle sets that bit).
  9. Send 4 (SLEEP): everything stops (LED off, UART silent). Wait a few seconds, then press USER to wake it. millis() advanced only a few ms while you waited, because Timer1 was stopped too.
  10. Send ? at any time to print the reset report of this start again.
  11. Optional, brown-out: unplug USB-C and connect a bench supply to the 5V pin (J2-1) and GND (J2-2), set to 5 V. Turn the voltage down slowly: below the BOR threshold the chip is held in reset. Turn it up again and watch which flags the report shows. Never go above 5 V on J2-1.

Expected output (from the MPLAB simulator)

# RCON = 0x83 : [POR power-on] [BOR brown-out] [EXTR MCLR pin]
# reset reason: POWER-ON (POR+BOR are both set at power-up)
# executing RESET instruction...
# RCON = 0x40 : [SWR software]
# reset reason: SOFTWARE reset (RESET instruction)
# IDLE done, woke 3000 times (= 1 per Timer1 tick)
# RCON = 0x10 : [WDTO watchdog]
# reset reason: WATCHDOG reset - the program stopped feeding the WDT

Other lines you will see (the numbers are example values; loop counts depend on the clock setting):

Lab 18 - power modes and reset sources.  ? 1 2 3 4 w r
# starts since power-on: 1
# RUN: loops in 1 s = 2500000
# DOZE 1:128 for 3 s - the LED blink still has the right timing,
#   the loop counter is ~128x smaller. Measure the current now.
# DOZE done, loops in 3 s = 58000 (compare with RUN x3)
# IDLE for 3 s: the CPU sleeps between Timer1 ticks (1 ms).
# RCON.IDLE = 0 (0 is right: only a RESET during Idle sets it)
# SLEEP: everything stops. Press USER to wake up...
# woke up! millis() advanced only 3 ms while asleep (Timer1 was stopped)
# enabling the watchdog and NOT feeding it -> reset in about 1 s.

How the code works

CPU Timer1/millis UART ADC/PWM wakes on RUN full yes yes yes - DOZE 1:128 /128 yes (full) yes yes - (ROI=1: any interrupt ends Doze) IDLE off yes yes yes any enabled interrupt SLEEP off NO NO NO pin change (CN), INTx, WDT
  1. Reset reason: RCON collects a flag for every reset cause. The sketch reads it first in setup(), then clears it, so the next reset reports only its own cause. At power-up POR and BOR are both set.
  2. POR / BOR: the power-on reset holds the chip in reset until VDD is valid. The brown-out reset does the same whenever VDD sags below the BOR trip point, so the CPU never runs on a voltage too low to be reliable. On this family the BOR is always on.
  3. Watchdog: config bit FWDTEN = ON_SW lets software switch it on (WDTCONL.ON). If the program then stops feeding it (writing the key 0x5743 to WDTCONH), the WDT resets the chip. That’s how a product recovers from a hung loop. The period comes from config bit RWDTPS; this board uses 1:32768, nominally about 1 s. Lab 28 measures it and goes deeper (window mode, finding where a program hung).
  4. Doze: CLKDIV.DOZE = ratio, DOZEN = 1. Idle: Idle() = PWRSAV #1. Sleep: Sleep() = PWRSAV #0. The USER button wakes it because attachInterrupt() uses change notification, which needs no clock.
  5. Persistent RAM: __attribute__((persistent)) tells the C start-up code not to zero a variable, so it survives a reset (but not power-off).

setup(): read, then clear.

bootRcon = RCON;                    /* 1. read the reason FIRST ... */
RCON = 0;                           /* 2. ... then clear it for the next time */
...
printRcon(bootRcon);
attachInterrupt(digitalPinToInterrupt(BUTTON_BUILTIN), onButton, FALLING);

static unsigned int boots __attribute__((persistent));   /* survives reset, not power-off */
if (bootRcon & 0x0001) boots = 0;                         /* power-on: RAM content is random */
boots++;

If RCON were not cleared, the flags of earlier resets would pile up and the next reset would look like several at once. The button interrupt is set up here so it can later wake the chip from Sleep.

printRcon() prints the name of every flag that is set (bit 8, VREGS, is skipped because it is a setting, not a cause) and then picks the most likely single cause, in a fixed priority order:

if (r & 0x8000)      why = "TRAP CONFLICT reset";
else if (r & 0x4000) why = "ILLEGAL OPCODE / bad pointer reset";
else if (r & 0x0200) why = "CONFIGURATION MISMATCH reset";
else if (r & 0x0010) why = "WATCHDOG reset - the program stopped feeding the WDT";
else if (r & 0x0040) why = "SOFTWARE reset (RESET instruction)";
else if ((r & 0x0003) == 0x0003) why = "POWER-ON (POR+BOR are both set at power-up)";
else if (r & 0x0001) why = "POWER-ON reset";
else if (r & 0x0002) why = "BROWN-OUT reset - the supply dipped";
else if (r & 0x0080) why = "MCLR pin: RESET button or programmer";

The order matters: at power-up EXTR may be set as well (the simulator shows 0x83), but POR+BOR is checked first.

testDoze() divides the CPU clock and keeps blinking the LED from millis():

CLKDIVbits.ROI = 0;                 /* stay in Doze even when interrupts happen */
CLKDIVbits.DOZE = 7;                /* 1:128 */
CLKDIVbits.DOZEN = 1;
unsigned long n = 0, t0 = millis();
while (millis() - t0 < 3000) {      /* millis() is a peripheral (Timer1): still right */
    n++;
    digitalWrite(LED_BUILTIN, (millis() / 250) % 2 ? LED_ON : LED_OFF);
}
CLKDIVbits.DOZEN = 0;

Because Timer1 still runs at full speed, the 3 s and the 2 Hz blink stay exact; only n shows the slower CPU. Serial.flush() before Doze lets the last text leave the UART first.

testIdle() calls Idle() in a loop for 3 s. Each Timer1 interrupt (every 1 ms, the one behind millis()) wakes the CPU, the loop counts one wake-up and goes back to Idle: about 3000 in 3 s. With Timer1 running, Idle saves little; the CPU is woken 1000 times a second.

testSleep():

Serial.flush();                     /* let the last byte leave before the UART clock stops */
digitalWrite(LED_BUILTIN, LED_OFF);
unsigned long before = millis();
unsigned long w0 = wakeups;
while (wakeups == w0) {
    Sleep();                        /* = PWRSAV #0 */
}
unsigned long slept = millis() - before;

The ISR onButton() only increments wakeups. Any other wake-up (for example a glitch on a CN pin) leaves wakeups unchanged, so the loop goes straight back to Sleep. After waking, slept shows how little millis() moved.

testWatchdog() and testSoftwareReset():

WDTCONLbits.ON = 1;                 /* FWDTEN = ON_SW: software may switch it on */
for (;;) { }                        /* hang - like a bug that locks up the loop */
...
asm volatile ("reset");

The endless loop never feeds the watchdog, so it times out after its period. reset is a single CPU instruction that restarts the chip and sets SWR.

Key registers

Register / bitValue usedMeaning
RCONread in setup(), then 0reset flags (see the table in Background); cleared so the next reset reports only its own cause
RCON.IDLEread (0)1 only if a reset happened during Idle; a normal wake-up does not set it
CLKDIV.DOZE7CPU clock ratio 1:128 (0 = 1:1 … 7 = 1:128)
CLKDIV.DOZEN1, then 0Doze on / off
CLKDIV.ROI0an interrupt does not end Doze (1 would switch back to full speed on any interrupt)
PWRSAV #1 (Idle())–instruction: CPU off, peripherals on
PWRSAV #0 (Sleep())–instruction: all clocks off
WDTCONL.ON1switch the watchdog on (allowed because of FWDTEN = ON_SW)
WDTCONH0x5743 (not written here)the feed key; this sketch deliberately never writes it
Config FWDTENON_SWwatchdog off at start, software may switch it on
Config RWDTPSPS32768watchdog period, nominally about 1 s (set in system_config.c)

Try it yourself

  1. Easy Try other Doze ratios: change CLKDIVbits.DOZE = 7 in testDoze() to 3 (1:8) and compare the loop count with RUN.
  2. Easy Set CLKDIVbits.ROI = 1 in testDoze(). Timer1 interrupts now end Doze after the first millisecond: the loop count is almost the full RUN value. Explain why.
  3. Medium Make Idle save more: in testIdle(), switch Timer1’s interrupt off before the loop and wake with the USER button instead, like testSleep(). Hint: millis() will stop advancing too, so the 3 s loop condition needs changing.
  4. Medium Feed the watchdog: add a command that switches the WDT on and writes WDTCONH = 0x5743 in loop(). The board now keeps running; a second command that stops feeding causes the reset. Hint: look at Lab 28 for the full version.
  5. Challenge Store a short history of the last 8 reset reasons in a persistent array and print it with ?. Hint: shift the array and add bootRcon in setup(); clear it only on POR.

Troubleshooting

SymptomLikely causeFix
After 4 the board never wakes upUSER button not pressed hard enough, or the sketch was changed and the interrupt is not attachedPress USER firmly; if it still sleeps, press RESET
Garbage characters right before Sleep or DozeThe UART clock stopped (Sleep) while a byte was still being sentKeep the Serial.flush() before entering the mode
# starts since power-on does not restart at 1 after unpluggingThe adapter on J5 may keep the chip partly powered through the RX pin, so no real power-on happensAlso unplug the adapter for 2 s
Several flags in one reportRCON was not cleared in an earlier, different sketchNormal for the first start after another sketch; the next reset is clean
Current hardly changes in IdleTimer1 wakes the CPU 1000 times per secondExpected here; see the third exercise

Check your understanding

Why must setup() read RCON before anything else and then write 0 to it?

The flags stay set until software clears them. If they were not cleared, the next reset would show its own flag plus all the old ones, and the cause could not be told apart.

In Doze 1:128 the loop count drops by about 128×. Why is the LED blink still exactly 2 Hz?

Doze slows only the CPU. Timer1, which drives millis(), keeps running at full speed, so the time values the code reads are still correct.

Why can the USER button wake the chip from Sleep, but Timer1 cannot?

In Sleep all clocks stop, so Timer1 stops counting. The button uses change notification, which detects the pin edge without a clock.

The start counter survives RESET but not power-off. Why?

The variable is persistent: the start-up code does not zero it, so RAM keeps its value through a reset. Without power the RAM content is lost, and the sketch sets the counter to 0 when POR is set.

Simulator-tested: power-on, software reset and watchdog reset all produced the right RCON flags, and Idle woke exactly once per ms. Sleep and the current figures need the real board.

19RTOS: a preemptive real-time kernel from scratch

See what FreeRTOS does inside, by building a tiny version: tasks with their own stacks, preemption, priorities, sleep, a semaphore.

advancedcontext switchschedulerprioritiessemaphoreinline assemblyround-robinidle taskCPU load

Objectives

  • After this lab you can explain what a task, a task control block (TCB) and a task stack are.
  • After this lab you can describe how a preemptive scheduler picks the next task (priorities, round-robin, idle task).
  • After this lab you can explain step by step what a context switch saves and restores on a dsPIC33.
  • After this lab you can use a semaphore to let an interrupt wake a waiting task, and a lock to share Serial between tasks.
  • After this lab you can write your own tasks with rtosCreate(), rtosDelay() and rtosStart().

Background

Why an RTOS? In the earlier labs loop() did several jobs one after the other, checking millis() to decide what to do next (cooperative scheduling). That works as long as every job is short. If one job takes a long time – a big calculation, a slow print – everything else has to wait. An RTOS (real-time operating system) lets you write each job as its own endless loop, a task, and shares the CPU between them. A preemptive RTOS can take the CPU away from a task by force, at any moment, so an important task never waits for an unimportant one.

Tasks, stacks and the TCB. Each task has its own stack: the memory where its local variables, return addresses and saved registers live. While a task is not running, all its CPU registers are stored on its own stack. The kernel only has to remember where that stack ends – the saved stack pointer (W15 on a dsPIC). This and a few more facts (priority, state, wake-up time, run time) form the task control block (TCB).

Scheduling. Every task is in one of three states:

rtosDelay(ms) semTake(s), not given yet READY ------------------> SLEEPING READY ------------------------> BLOCKED ^ | ^ | +--- tick: wake time reached + +---- semGiveFromISR(s) -----------+

The scheduler runs at every 1 ms tick interrupt and whenever a task sleeps, blocks or yields. It always picks the highest-priority READY task. If several READY tasks share the top priority, they take turns, one tick each (round-robin). If nobody else is READY, the idle task (priority 0) runs. The time the idle task gets is the free CPU time; the rest is the CPU load.

Context switch. Changing from task A to task B means: save all of A’s registers on A’s stack, store A’s stack pointer in A’s TCB, load B’s stack pointer, restore B’s registers from B’s stack, and return from the interrupt. The return instruction (RETFIE) pops B’s program counter and status register, so B continues exactly where it was interrupted, as if nothing happened. This must be written in assembly, because C cannot change W15 under its own feet.

Semaphores and locks. A semaphore is a counter of “events”. A task that calls semTake() while the count is 0 is BLOCKED and uses no CPU; an interrupt or another task calls semGiveFromISR() and the waiting task becomes READY. A lock (mutex) protects a shared resource: only the task that holds it may use it. Here the shared resource is Serial – two tasks printing at once would mix their characters.

On the dsPIC33CK. The stack grows upwards in RAM, and a stack limit register (SPLIM) makes the CPU trap if W15 goes past it. The kernel uses SCCP2 as a 1 ms tick timer (priority 2) and the unused CRC interrupt (priority 1, the lowest) for the switch, in the same way ARM Cortex-M kernels use the PendSV exception.

You need

PartQtyNotes
dsPIC33CK Nano board1uses the on-board USER button and USER LED
USB-C supply / cable1power only
3.3 V USB-serial adapter1on J5, Serial Monitor at 115200

Wiring

Nothing to wire. Serial Monitor on J5.

SignalBoard pinOther end
Serial TXTX RC10 J5-2adapter RX
Serial RXRX RC11 J5-3adapter TX
GNDJ5-4adapter GND (leave J5-1 open)

The functions, in the MiniRTOS.h tab

The whole kernel (scheduler, tick interrupt, the assembly context switch, semaphore, Serial lock) is in the second tab of the sketch, MiniRTOS.h. Lab19_RTOS.ino only has the tasks and setup(), so it is easy to add or change a task. To use the kernel in your own sketch, copy MiniRTOS.h into your sketch folder and add #include "MiniRTOS.h".

#include "MiniRTOS.h" void tBlink(void) { // a task is a function that never returns for (;;) { digitalWrite(LED_BUILTIN, LED_ON); rtosDelay(50); // sleep 50 ms: other tasks run digitalWrite(LED_BUILTIN, LED_OFF); rtosDelay(200); } } void setup() { rtosCreate(tBlink, 2, "blink "); // function, priority (higher = more important), name rtosStart(); // last line: the kernel takes over, never returns } void loop() { } // not used
FunctionWhat it does
rtosCreate(task, prio, "name")adds a task (up to 5); priority 1…255, 0 is the idle task
rtosStart()adds the idle task, starts the 1 ms tick and switches into the first task
rtosDelay(ms)the task sleeps; the CPU goes to the next READY task
rtosYield()lets another task of the same priority run now
rtosTicks()milliseconds since rtosStart()
semInit(s, n), semTake(s), semGiveFromISR(s)semaphore: wait for an event; give it from an interrupt or another task
lockSerial() / unlockSerial()only one task prints at a time
rtosCpuLoad(), rtosPrintTasks()CPU load in % since the last call / a table of all tasks

The demo has these tasks (higher number = more important):

PriorityTaskWhat it does
3tButtonwaits on a semaphore given by the USER-button interrupt, then prints the press
2tBlinkUSER LED 50 ms on, 200 ms off
1tWorkercounts primes. Light mode: works 20 ms, sleeps 80 ms. Heavy mode (w): never sleeps
1tReportonce a second: statistics and the task table; reads the w command
0idleadded by rtosStart(); runs only when nothing else can

Step by step

  1. Upload Lab19_RTOS, open the Serial Monitor at 115200. The title line appears, the LED blinks (task blink), and every second report prints a table of all the tasks.
  2. Read the first line of each report: t= is the kernel time in ms, switches= the number of context switches so far, primes= the worker’s progress.
  3. Watch load=: about 20–30 % with the worker in light mode. The worker works 20 ms out of every 100 ms; the report task adds the rest.
  4. Look at the state column. Most of the time blink is SLEEPING (in rtosDelay), button is BLOCKED (waiting for the semaphore) and report is READY (it is the task printing the table).
  5. Press USER: [button] press #1 handled at tick … appears at once. The button task has the highest priority and preempts everything.
  6. Send w: the worker goes HEAVY (never sleeps). Load jumps to 100 %, idle stops gaining time, worker and report share the CPU round-robin, and the LED still blinks on time (higher priority). That is real-time scheduling.
  7. While the worker is HEAVY, press USER again: the reaction is still immediate. Send w once more to go back to light mode.
  8. Look at stack used/512: every task has its own stack, and the table shows how much of it was ever used. report needs the most, because it calls the Serial.print functions.
  9. Watch ran … ms: at every tick, the task that is running gets 1 ms added. In HEAVY mode worker and report gain almost all the time and idle stops growing.

Expected output (from the simulator)

t=1001 ms  switches=53  primes=954  load=21%  worker=light
   blink  prio 2 SLEEPING ran 0 ms  stack 90/512
   button prio 3 BLOCKED  ran 0 ms  stack 90/512
   worker prio 1 SLEEPING ran 230 ms  stack 102/512
   report prio 1 READY    ran 286 ms  stack 166/512
   idle   prio 0 READY    ran 800 ms  stack 72/512

(report uses a lot of CPU in the simulator because Serial.print waits for the UART. On the board at 115200 baud expect a few %. The ran times can add up to more than t: t is printed first and each task line later, while the tasks keep running, and in the simulator printing the table takes about 0.3 s.)

A button press adds a line like this (example values):

[button] press #1 handled at tick 3412

blink shows ran 0 ms because its run time is counted only when a tick lands while it is running, and it runs for just a few microseconds at a time.

How the code works

The application (Lab19_RTOS.ino). setup() creates the semaphore and the four tasks, attaches the button interrupt and starts the kernel:

semInit(buttonSem, 0);
rtosCreate(tBlink,  2, "blink ");
rtosCreate(tButton, 3, "button");
rtosCreate(tWorker, 1, "worker");
rtosCreate(tReport, 1, "report");
attachInterrupt(digitalPinToInterrupt(BUTTON_BUILTIN), onButton, FALLING);

rtosStart();                           /* never returns */

loop() is empty and never called: once rtosStart() runs, the kernel owns the CPU.

void onButton() { presses++; semGiveFromISR(buttonSem); }

void tButton(void)
{
    for (;;) {
        semTake(buttonSem);                /* sleeps until the ISR gives it */
        uint32_t t = rtosTicks();
        lockSerial();
        Serial.print("[button] press #"); ...
        unlockSerial();
    }
}

The ISR does almost nothing; the real work happens in the task. This is the usual RTOS pattern: keep interrupts short, let a task do the rest.

if (!workerHeavy && rtosTicks() - burstStart >= 20) {
    rtosDelay(80);                 /* light mode: 20 ms on, 80 ms off */
    burstStart = rtosTicks();
}

Inside its burst the worker never yields. Only the tick interrupt can take the CPU away from it – that is preemption.

How a context switch works

task A running -- 1 ms tick ISR (SCCP2, IPL2): wake sleepers, pick best READY task, pend switch \- switch ISR (CRC vector, IPL1 = lowest, like PendSV on ARM) push W0-W14, RCOUNT, TBLPAG, DSRPAG, DSWPAG, CORCON, MODCON, ACCA, ACCB, DO regs tasks[A].sp = W15 SPLIM = 0xFFFF; W15 = tasks[B].sp; SPLIM = B's limit pop all of B's registers RETFIE --> task B continues where it was interrupted
  1. TCB: each task has a saved stack pointer, a stack limit, a priority, a state (READY / SLEEPING / BLOCKED), a wake-up tick and a run-time counter.
  2. Scheduler: picks the highest-priority READY task. Among equal priorities it takes the next one after the current task (round-robin). The idle task is always READY.
  3. Switch in assembly: it runs at the lowest interrupt priority, so it never splits another ISR. It raises its own CPU priority to 7 while it works, and switches SPLIM together with W15, so a stack overflow traps instead of corrupting the next task.
  4. Idle task: rtosStart() adds it by itself at priority 0. It only runs when no other task can, so the time it gets is the free CPU time, and rtosCpuLoad() is 100 % minus its share.
  5. New task: rtosCreate() builds a fake “interrupted” frame (PC = task function, SR = IPL0, 32 zeroed registers) so the first RETFIE “returns” into the task.
  6. rtosDelay(ms): marks the task SLEEPING until kTicks + ms and switches away. semTake() marks it BLOCKED. semGiveFromISR() (called by the button’s attachInterrupt) makes it READY and requests a switch.
  7. Serial lock: two tasks printing at once would mix characters. lockSerial() waits with rtosDelay(1), not just a yield. A high-priority task that only yielded would be picked again immediately, the low-priority owner would never finish, and the system would deadlock (priority inversion).

The TCB in MiniRTOS.h:

struct TCB {
    volatile uint16_t sp;                  /* saved W15 - MUST be the first member */
    uint16_t splim;                        /* stack limit for this task            */
    uint8_t  prio, state;
    volatile uint32_t wakeTick;
    volatile uint32_t runTicks;            /* ticks this task was running          */
    const char *name;
};

sp must be first because the assembly reads it as [w0] and splim as [w0+2].

The scheduler:

for (uint8_t k = 1; k <= nTasks; k++) {
    uint8_t i = (uint8_t)((current + k) % nTasks);
    if (tasks[i].state == READY && (best < 0 || tasks[i].prio > tasks[best].prio)) best = i;
}

The search starts at the task after the current one and only replaces best with a strictly higher priority. So among equals, the first one after the current task wins – that gives round-robin for free. requestSwitch() then sets nextTCB and pends the switch with IFS3bits.CRCIF = 1.

The tick:

extern "C" void __attribute__((interrupt, no_auto_psv)) _CCT2Interrupt(void)
{
    IFS1bits.CCT2IF = 0;
    kTicks++;
    tasks[current].runTicks++;
    for (uint8_t i = 0; i < nTasks; i++)
        if (tasks[i].state == SLEEPING && (int32_t)(kTicks - tasks[i].wakeTick) >= 0)
            tasks[i].state = READY;
    requestSwitch();
}

The signed difference (int32_t)(kTicks - wakeTick) >= 0 stays correct when the 32-bit counter wraps around.

The switch itself (excerpt of __CRCInterrupt):

    push.d  w0
    ...
    push    _DOENDH
    mov     _currentTCB, w0
    mov     w15, [w0]                  /* currentTCB->sp = W15              */
    mov     _nextTCB, w0
    mov     w0, _currentTCB            /* currentTCB = nextTCB               */
    setm    w1
    mov     w1, _SPLIM                 /* SPLIM = 0xFFFF (no limit) ...      */
    nop
    mov     [w0], w15
    mov     [w0+2], w1
    mov     w1, _SPLIM                 /* ... then this task's own limit     */
    nop
    pop     _DOENDH
    ...
    pop.d   w0
    retfie

SPLIM is opened fully before W15 moves, because the new stack may lie above the old limit; then the new task’s own limit is set. The nops are needed because the CPU must not use W15 in the cycle right after an SPLIM write.

Semaphore:

void semTake(Sem &s)
{
    noInterrupts();
    if (s.count > 0) { s.count--; interrupts(); return; }
    s.waiter = (int8_t)current;
    tasks[current].state = BLOCKED;
    requestSwitch();
    interrupts();                          /* sleeps here until semGive... */
}

Interrupts are off while the count is checked, so the button ISR cannot slip in between the test and the state change. When interrupts() runs, the pended switch happens at once and the task stops right there; it continues on the next line after semGiveFromISR() made it READY. This simple semaphore remembers only one waiting task.

Start: rtosStart() sets SCCP2 to a 1 ms period (at 100 MIPS: prescaler 1:4, period 25 000 counts), sets the CRC interrupt to priority 1, saves the running setup() into a dummy TCB that is never scheduled again, and pends the first switch.

Key registers

Register / bitValue usedMeaning
PMD2.CCP2MD0SCCP2 powered
CCP2CON1L.TMRPS1 at 100 MIPS (0 at 4 MIPS)timer prescaler 1:4 (1:1)
CCP2PRL24999 at 100 MIPS (3999 at 4 MIPS)period: one tick per 1 ms
CCP2CON1L.CCPON1start the tick timer
IPC6.CCT2IP2tick priority: above the switch, below millis()/Serial
IFS1.CCT2IF / IEC1.CCT2IEcleared / 1tick interrupt flag / enable
IPC12.CRCIP1context switch at the lowest priority
IFS3.CRCIF (bit 3)set by software“pend a switch”; cleared at the start of the switch
IEC3.CRCIE1switch interrupt enabled
SR bits 5–7 (IPL)set to 7 in the switchCPU priority 7: nothing interrupts the switch; RETFIE restores the task’s own SR

SPLIM0xFFFF, then the task’s limitstack limit; going past it causes a stack error trap

Try it yourself

  1. Easy Change the blink pattern to 100 ms on, 900 ms off. Hint: the two rtosDelay() calls in tBlink().
  2. Easy Give tWorker priority 2 (the same as blink) and switch it to HEAVY. What happens to the LED timing now, and why? Hint: rtosCreate(tWorker, 1, ...) in setup().
  3. Medium Add a fifth task that prints analogRead(A0) every 500 ms. Hint: write it like tReport, with lockSerial()/unlockSerial() around the prints. Up to 5 tasks of your own fit.
  4. Medium Remove the lockSerial()/unlockSerial() pair from tButton() and press USER many times while the report prints. You will see mixed-up lines. Put the lock back.
  5. Challenge Write semGive(s) for use between tasks, and let tReport wake a new task through it once per report. Hint: it can wrap semGiveFromISR() between noInterrupts() and interrupts().

Troubleshooting

SymptomLikely causeFix
Nothing after the title line, LED does not blinkA task returned, or a new task overflowed its stack and trappedEvery task must be an endless for (;;) loop; keep big arrays out of tasks (512 bytes of stack each)
Lines are mixed togetherA task prints without lockSerial()Put every group of prints between lockSerial() and unlockSerial()
A new task never runsrtosCreate() returned −1 (more than 5 tasks), or a higher-priority task never sleepsCheck the return value; make high-priority tasks call rtosDelay()
System locks up when a task waits for SerialWaiting with rtosYield() in a high-priority task starves the owner (priority inversion)Wait with rtosDelay(1), as lockSerial() does
analogWrite(6, ...) or NanoTimer Timer2 stops workingThe kernel uses SCCP2 as its tickUse another PWM pin or timer in RTOS sketches

Check your understanding

Why does every task need its own stack?

When a task is switched out, all its registers, local variables and return addresses must stay where they are until it runs again. With one shared stack, the next task would overwrite them.

Why does the context switch run at the lowest interrupt priority?

So it never interrupts another ISR. It runs only after all other interrupts are finished, and then changes the stack of the task, not of an interrupt in progress.

The worker is HEAVY (100 % load). Why does the LED still blink on time?

tBlink has priority 2, higher than the worker’s 1. When its sleep ends, the tick makes it READY and the scheduler switches to it at once, preempting the worker.

How does the kernel measure CPU load?

Each tick is counted for the task that is running. The idle task only runs when nothing else can, so its share of the ticks is the free time; rtosCpuLoad() returns 100 % minus that share.

Resources: SCCP2 (D6’s PWM) is the kernel tick and the unused CRC interrupt is the switch vector. Simulator-tested: preemption, round-robin, sleeping, blocking, stack use and the load figure all behave as described. Timer1/millis() keep running underneath.
This is a teaching kernel. For a product use a proven RTOS, e.g. the official FreeRTOS dsPIC33 port, which does the same things with many more safety checks.
After moving the kernel into MiniRTOS.h the simulator gives the same figures as before (task switches, primes, load, stack use).

28Watchdog, software reset and oscillator switching

Let the watchdog rescue a program that hangs and find out where it hung, choose your own timeout with WDTset(), use window mode, restart on purpose and remember why, and change the CPU clock while the program runs.

advancedWDTWDTset / WDTclearwindow watchdogRESET instructionRCONpersistent RAMOSCCONPLLLPRCREFCLKO

Objectives

  • After this lab you can switch the watchdog on, feed it in the right place, and let it reset a program that hangs.
  • After this lab you can use WDTset(ms) / WDTclear() from the Watchdog.h tab to get a watchdog with the timeout you choose.
  • After this lab you can read RCON after a reset and tell a power-on, RESET button, watchdog and software reset apart.
  • After this lab you can keep data through a reset with a persistent variable, for example a checkpoint that says where the program hung.
  • After this lab you can switch the CPU clock at run time (PLL, FRC, FRC/2, LPRC), re-time millis() and Serial, and see the clock on a pin.

Background

Why a watchdog. A program can hang in ways you never tested: a sensor that never answers, a loop that waits for a flag that is never set, a pointer that overwrites the wrong memory. In a product nobody is there to press RESET. The watchdog timer (WDT) is a counter that runs on its own oscillator, the 32 kHz LPRC (low-power RC oscillator), independent of the CPU clock. The program must “feed” (clear) it regularly. If the program stops feeding it, the counter runs out and the watchdog resets the chip. Even a completely stuck CPU gets restarted.

LPRC 32 kHz --[ prescaler 1:32768 (config bit RWDTPS) ]--> counter runs out after ~1 s (nominal) ^ | WDTCONH = 0x5743 (feed) | v loop() "still alive" ---+ RESET, RCON.WDTO = 1

Where to feed it. Feed it in one place in the main loop, never in an interrupt. An interrupt keeps running while loop() is stuck and would hide the hang. On the dsPIC33CK, feeding means writing the key 0x5743 to WDTCONH, so a random wrong write cannot feed it by accident.

The period is fixed, and not exact. The watchdog period is set by the configuration bit RWDTPS when the chip is programmed. On this board it is 1:32768 of the 32 kHz LPRC, about 1 s nominal. The program cannot change it; WDTCONL.RUNDIV only reports the setting. The LPRC is a simple RC oscillator, accurate only to a few percent. That is why the sketch measures the real period with the h test. Other configuration bits on this board: FWDTEN = ON_SW (off after reset, software switches it on with WDTCONL.ON), WINDIS = ON (window mode not forced; WDTWINEN switches it on) and WDTWIN = WIN25 (window = last 25 %).

WDTset(ms) / WDTclear(). Because the chip’s period is fixed, the Watchdog.h tab adds a second, adjustable watchdog in front of it. A 1 ms check interrupt (SCCP3 timer, lowest priority) compares millis() with the time of the last WDTclear(). If WDTclear() was missing for the timeout, the check saves a note in RAM and resets the chip at once, accurate to about 1 ms. Otherwise it feeds the chip’s WDT. The check interrupt is the only thing that feeds the chip’s WDT, so if even the interrupts stop (stuck with interrupts off), the hardware still resets the chip about 1 s later.

loop() --WDTclear()--> lastClear = millis() SCCP3 interrupt, every 1 ms: millis() - lastClear >= timeout ? -> save note (persistent RAM 0x4F20), RESET instruction (RCON.SWR) otherwise -> feed the chip's WDT chip WDT (~1 s): fed ONLY by that interrupt (RCON.WDTO)

Window mode. A normal watchdog only catches a program that feeds it too late. A program stuck in a short loop that keeps feeding it far too often looks healthy. In window mode feeding is only allowed in the last 25 % of the period; an early feed also resets the chip.

0 % 75 % 100 % |------------- closed: feed = RESET --------|---- open ------| no feed = RESET ^ the sketch feeds at 7/8 = 87.5 %

Reset reasons and persistent RAM. After any reset, the register RCON tells why: POR (power-on), BOR (brown-out), EXTR (MCLR pin: RESET button or programmer), WDTO (watchdog), SWR (software reset instruction). The bits stay set until the program clears them, so the sketch reads RCON first thing and then clears it. A reset does not clear RAM, but the start-up code normally zeroes all variables. A variable marked __attribute__((persistent)) is not zeroed, so it carries information into the next run. A magic number tells whether its contents are valid (after a power-off RAM is random).

Clock switching. The CPU clock comes from one of several sources. OSCCON.NOSC selects the new source, OSWEN = 1 starts the switch, and the hardware clears OSWEN when it is done (the config bit FCKSM = CSECMD allows switching). Both halves of OSCCON are protected by unlock sequences, written with __builtin_write_OSCCONH / __builtin_write_OSCCONL. The PLL multiplies the 8 MHz FRC up to FOSC 200 MHz; FCY (instruction clock) = FOSC / 2. The PLL may only be reprogrammed while the CPU is not running from it.

NOSC 0 = FRC 8 MHz 1 = FRC + PLL 5 = LPRC 32 kHz 7 = FRC / FRCDIV PLL 8 MHz / N1 1 x M 100 = FVCO 800 MHz / N2 2 / N3 1 = FPLLO 400 MHz, FOSC = FPLLO / 2 = 200 MHz command source FOSC FCY (MIPS) D9 = FOSC / 2000 1 FRC + PLL 200 MHz 100 100 kHz 2 FRC 8 MHz 4 4 kHz 3 FRC / 2 4 MHz 2 2 kHz 4 LPRC 32 kHz 0.016 16 Hz (5 s, then back)

What breaks after a switch. The core works out many settings from FCY at compile time. After a switch they are wrong. The sketch re-times the two things it uses: Timer1 (millis(), delay(): PR1 and prescaler) and UART1 (Serial: U1BRG). Still at compile-time speed after a switch: micros(), delayMicroseconds(), analogWrite() and tone() frequencies, the ADC clock, NanoTimer periods. The reference clock output (REFCLKO) puts FOSC / 2000 on D9, so you can see the real clock with a meter.

WDTset() and WDTclear(), in the Watchdog.h tab

A watchdog with the timeout you choose. Call WDTclear() in loop(); if it is missing for longer than the timeout, the chip resets. To use it in your own sketch, copy the Watchdog.h tab into it.

#include "Watchdog.h" void setup() { uint16_t rcon = RCON; RCON = 0; // reset reason, first thing in setup() if (WDTwasTimeout(rcon)) { // the last reset was a WDTset() timeout Serial.print("no WDTclear() for "); Serial.print(WDTlastLate()); Serial.println(" ms"); } WDTset(1000); // reset if WDTclear() is missing for 1000 ms } void loop() { WDTclear(); // "still alive" ... }
FunctionWhat it does
WDTset(ms)watchdog on with a timeout of 1 ms … 1 hour
WDTclear()restart the timeout; call it regularly, in one place
WDTstop()watchdog off
WDTisOn(), WDTgetTimeout()running? / the timeout in ms
WDTwasTimeout(rcon), WDTlastLate(), WDTlastTimeout()after the reset: was it this watchdog? / how many ms WDTclear() was missing / which timeout was set
wdtHwStart(window), wdtHwStop(), wdtHwFeed()lower level: the chip’s own fixed-period WDT (used by the w W e h commands)
Why two layers: the chip’s watchdog period is fixed by the config bit RWDTPS when the chip is programmed (this board: about 1 s); WDTCONL.RUNDIV only reports it. So WDTset(ms) adds a 1 ms check interrupt (SCCP3). If WDTclear() is late, the check resets the chip at once, to about 1 ms, and leaves a note in RAM for after the reset. The check interrupt is also the only thing that feeds the chip’s own watchdog. So if even the interrupts stop (stuck with interrupts off), the hardware resets the chip about 1 s later anyway. SCCP3 is also used by NanoTimer Timer3, analogWrite(D7) and NanoServo, so don’t combine them with WDTset().

Step by step

  1. Upload Lab28_WatchdogClock and open the Serial Monitor at 115200. It prints the reset reason (POWER-ON reset the first time, or MCLR after the RESET button or an upload with the programmer), the clock and the watchdog setup. The USER LED blinks at 1 Hz: proof that millis() runs at the right speed.
  2. Status: send ?. You read the clock source, FCY and the expected D9 frequency, whether WDTset and the watchdog are on, RUNDIV = 15 (1:32768, about 1024 ms nominal), and how many starts there were since power-on. This counter lives in persistent RAM and grows with every reset.
  3. Watchdog: send w. The watchdog is on now and loop() feeds it every 100 ms, so nothing happens. Send w again to switch it off.
  4. Hang: send h. The program gets stuck in while(1), stops feeding the watchdog, and restarts by itself. After the restart it prints WATCHDOG reset, where it was stuck (last checkpoint) and how long the hang lasted. That time is the real watchdog period of your chip; the sketch stores it for window mode.
  5. WDTset: send t: WDTset(1000) is on, and loop() calls WDTclear() on every pass, so nothing happens. Now send T: loop() keeps running (the LED keeps blinking) but no longer calls WDTclear(). Exactly 1 s later the board restarts and prints WATCHDOG reset by WDTset(1000): no WDTclear() for 1000 ms. RCON shows 0x40 (SWR), because the check uses the reset instruction. After the restart WDTset is off again; send t to switch it on, and t again to switch it off.
  6. Window mode: send W. Now loop() feeds the watchdog only at 7/8 of the measured period, inside the open window, so it keeps running. Send e to feed it early: it resets at once, and the checkpoint says window test: fed too early. (Do step 4 first; without a measured period the sketch uses 1024 ms.)
  7. Software reset: send r. The board restarts, and RCON says SOFTWARE reset with the reason the program saved before the reset.
  8. Clock: send s (speed test), then 3 (2 MIPS) and s again: about half the loop passes per ms. Send 1 (100 MIPS) and s: about 25× more than at 4 MIPS. Serial and the 1 Hz blink keep working at every clock. 2 returns to 4 MIPS.
  9. Send 4: 5 seconds on the 32 kHz LPRC oscillator. Serial is silent, the USER LED toggles every 0.5 s, an LED on D9 flickers at 16 Hz. Then it switches back by itself and reports that millis() did not count during those 5 s. A watchdog that was on is switched off for the demo and on again afterwards.
  10. On the board: measure D9 in each mode. It must read 100 kHz at 100 MIPS, 4 kHz at 4 MIPS, 2 kHz at 2 MIPS. That proves the PLL really makes FOSC = 200 MHz.

And the t / T test (100 MIPS build):

On a real chip the hang time should be near 1000 ms instead of 8192 ms, and the window feed time 7/8 of that; check it on your board.

How the code works

1. Data that survives a reset. The Saved structure sits at a fixed RAM address near the top of RAM, above anything the serial bootloader uses. The start-up code does not clear it.

struct Saved {
    uint16_t magic;                         /* 0xC0DE = contents are valid */
    uint16_t boots;                         /* starts since power-on */
    uint16_t swReason;                      /* why we did a software reset */
    uint16_t checkpoint;                    /* where the program was last */
    unsigned long hangMs;                   /* how long the hang lasted */
    unsigned long wdtPeriodMs;              /* measured watchdog period, 0 = not yet */
};
Saved saved __attribute__((persistent, address(0x4F00)));

2. setup(): reset reason first. RCON is read before anything else, then cleared so the next reset shows only its own flags. WDTwasTimeout() checks the note left by the WDTset check. After a power-on (or an invalid magic) the saved data is initialised.

bootRcon = RCON;                        /* read the reset reason FIRST ... */
RCON = 0;                               /* ... then clear it for next time */
wdtTimeout = WDTwasTimeout(bootRcon);   /* was it a WDTset() timeout? */
if ((bootRcon & 0x0001) || saved.magic != 0xC0DE) {   /* power-on: RAM is random */
    saved.magic = 0xC0DE; saved.boots = 0; ...
}
saved.boots++;

reportBoot() then decodes the flags in this order: WDTO (0x0010) with the checkpoint (and, after the hang test, the hang time, which becomes the measured period), a WDTset timeout, SWR (0x0040) with the saved reason, POR (0x0001), EXTR (0x0080). Finally refoBegin() starts the clock output and status() prints the state.

3. loop(). It writes the checkpoint, calls WDTclear() if WDTset is on (unless T was sent), lets wdtService() feed the chip’s WDT in w/W mode, blinks the LED from millis(), and handles one command.

saved.checkpoint = CP_LOOP;
if (WDTisOn() && !forgetClear) WDTclear();   /* "still alive" */
wdtService();
digitalWrite(LED_BUILTIN, (millis() / 500) % 2 ? LED_ON : LED_OFF);   /* 1 Hz if millis is right */

4. Feeding. wdtService() feeds every 100 ms in normal mode, and only after 7/8 of the period in window mode. The period is the measured one, or 1024 ms if h was not run yet.

if (since >= (wdtWindow ? wdtPeriod() * 7 / 8 : 100)) { wdtFeed(); lastFeed = millis(); }

In Watchdog.h, wdtHwStart() changes the window bit only while the WDT is off, and does not feed in window mode, because a feed right after the start would already be “too early”.

inline void wdtHwFeed(void) { WDTCONH = 0x5743; }    /* the feed key */
void wdtHwStart(bool window)
{
    WDTCONLbits.ON = 0;                     /* change the mode only while it is off */
    WDTCONLbits.WDTWINEN = window;
    WDTCONLbits.ON = 1;
    if (!window) wdtHwFeed();               /* window mode: a feed NOW would be "too early" */
}

5. The bugs on purpose. h switches the watchdog on, sets the checkpoint and spins in a loop that keeps writing the elapsed time into persistent RAM, so after the reset the last value is the hang time. e feeds twice inside the closed part of the window, then hangs.

saved.checkpoint = CP_HANG;
unsigned long t0 = millis();
for (;;) { saved.hangMs = millis() - t0; }   /* the "bug" */

6. The WDTset check (Watchdog.h). WDTset() sets SCCP3 up as a 32-bit timer at FCY with a 1 ms period, priority 1 (lowest), and starts the chip’s WDT as the backup. The interrupt does the check:

unsigned long since = millis() - wdtLastClear;
if (since >= wdtTimeoutMs) {            /* WDTclear() missing for too long */
    wdtNote.magic = 0x5744;
    wdtNote.fired = 1;
    ...
    asm volatile ("reset");
}
wdtHwFeed();                            /* all fine: keep the chip's WDT quiet */

WDTclear() writes the 32-bit time with interrupts off, so the check never sees half of it. WDTwasTimeout() returns true only for SWR without POR/BOR and with a valid note, then clears the note. The check uses millis(), so the timeout stays right after a clock switch; only how often it checks changes.

7. Software reset. r stores the reason, flushes Serial (so the last text leaves), and executes the reset instruction.

saved.swReason = SW_COMMAND;
asm volatile ("reset");

8. Clock switching. oscSwitch() writes NOSC and OSWEN with the unlock sequences and waits until the hardware clears OSWEN. For the PLL, setClock() first programs the dividers while running from FRC, then switches and waits for LOCK. Before every switch Serial.flush() lets the last byte leave at the old baud rate.

void oscSwitch(uint8_t nosc)
{
    __builtin_write_OSCCONH(nosc);
    __builtin_write_OSCCONL(OSCCON | 0x01); /* OSWEN = 1: go */
    while (OSCCONbits.OSWEN) { }            /* hardware clears it when done */
}
...
CLKDIVbits.PLLPRE = 1;          /* N1 = 1 (on this family the field IS the divider) */
PLLFBDbits.PLLFBDIV = 100;      /* M  = 100 */
PLLDIVbits.POST1DIV = 2;        /* N2 = 2 */
PLLDIVbits.POST2DIV = 1;        /* N3 = 1 */
oscSwitch(1);
while (!OSCCONbits.LOCK) { }    /* wait for the PLL to lock */

9. Re-timing. retime() gives Timer1 a new period for a 1 ms tick (prescaler 1:1, 1:8 or 1:64 depending on FCY) and UART1 a new baud divider. The UART is left on while U1BRG changes; switching it off and on would also need the TX/RX enables set again.

else                        { T1CONbits.TCKPS = 2; PR1 = fcy / 64000UL - 1; }       /* 1:64, as the core */
...
unsigned long brg = (fcy + BAUD / 2) / BAUD;    /* fractional baud generator, as the core */
U1BRG  = (uint16_t)brg;
U1BRGH = (uint16_t)(brg >> 16);

10. LPRC demo. At 16 kIPS a 1 ms Timer1 interrupt would come every 16 instructions and Serial cannot run, so lprcDemo() switches off the Timer1 interrupt and both watchdog modes, lets Timer1 count freely, and toggles the LED every 8000 counts (0.5 s). After 10 toggles it switches back with setClock() and restores the watchdog.

11. Clock output. refoBegin() selects FOSC as the source (so it follows every switch), sets the divider RODIV = 1000 (output = FOSC / 2000), loads it with ROSWEN (bounded wait), and routes REFCLKO to RP36 = RB4 = D9 with PPS.

Try it yourself

  1. Easy Change the WDTset timeout: in command(), case 't', change WDTset(1000) to WDTset(250) (and the text). Send t, then T, and check the reported late time.
  2. Easy Add your own checkpoint: add a name to CP_NAME[] and the enum, set saved.checkpoint before a slow part of your code, and see it after a watchdog reset (the check saved.checkpoint < 4 in reportBoot() must grow too).
  3. Medium Simulate a sensor that never answers: add a command that waits while (digitalRead(BUTTON_BUILTIN) == HIGH) { } with WDTset(2000) on. Press USER within 2 s and nothing happens; wait longer and the board resets.
  4. Medium Count resets by type: add counters for watchdog and software resets to the Saved structure (it is in persistent RAM) and print them in status().
  5. Challenge Test the second layer: in a new command, call WDTset(1000), then noInterrupts() and hang. The check interrupt cannot run, so the chip’s own WDT must reset the board after its fixed period, with RCON = WDTO instead of SWR.

Check your understanding

Why should you not feed the watchdog from a timer interrupt?

An interrupt keeps running while loop() is stuck. The watchdog would be fed forever and never reset the hung program. WDTset() feeds the chip’s WDT from an interrupt only because that interrupt itself checks that loop() still calls WDTclear().

What does window mode catch that a normal watchdog misses?

A program stuck in a short loop that feeds the watchdog far too often. In window mode a feed in the first 75 % of the period resets the chip too.

After a T timeout, RCON shows 0x40 (SWR), not WDTO. Why?

The WDTset check resets the chip with the reset instruction, which sets SWR. It leaves a note in persistent RAM, and WDTwasTimeout() uses that note to tell this reset from an ordinary software reset.

After switching from 100 MIPS to 2 MIPS, which still work correctly in this sketch, and which do not?

millis()/delay() and Serial work, because retime() set Timer1 and U1BRG again. micros(), delayMicroseconds(), analogWrite()/tone() frequencies, the ADC clock and NanoTimer periods are still calculated for the compile-time FCY and are wrong.

WDTset simulator-tested: T resets after 1000 ms at 100 MIPS, and after 1001 ms after switching to 4 MIPS. With interrupts switched off and the program stuck, the chip’s own watchdog takes over (RCON = WDTO).
Simulator-tested (4 MIPS build): watchdog reset with checkpoint and hang time, window mode (fed at 7/8 for 30 s without a reset, an early feed resets), software reset with a saved reason, persistent data through every reset, switching to FRC / 2, LPRC, FRC + PLL and back with Serial working each time (speed 152 / 75 / 3843 passes per ms at 4 / 2 / 100 MIPS).
Check on the board: (1) the watchdog period. The simulator gives 8192 ms, but the nominal value for 1:32768 on a 32 kHz LPRC is about 1 s. The h test prints the real value. (2) The D9 clock output: the simulator does not model the reference clock (ROSWEN never clears there), so the sketch prints a warning in the simulator and goes on.

Application Labs 20–27, 29 and 30 · real projects, modules and vehicle / industrial buses

20Mini data logger (combines the Basics labs 01–09)

Timed multi-channel sampling, statistics, an alarm, button control and CSV output – a small but complete instrument built only from the Arduino functions you already know.

applicationmillis schedulingCSVstatisticsanalogReadbutton edgetoneSerial Plotter

Objectives

  • After this lab you can sample several analog inputs at a fixed rate with millis(), without delay().
  • After this lab you can keep minimum, maximum and average values of a measurement while it runs.
  • After this lab you can print data as CSV and open it in a spreadsheet or the Serial Plotter.
  • After this lab you can combine a button, serial commands, an alarm LED and a buzzer in one loop() that never blocks.
  • After this lab you can explain why (long)(millis() - nextSample) >= 0 stays correct when millis() wraps around.

Background

What a data logger does. A data logger measures signals at regular times and records them, so you can look at how they change later: temperature over a day, light over an hour, a battery voltage while it discharges. Its parts are always the same: sensors that turn something physical into a voltage, an ADC (analog-to-digital converter) that turns the voltage into a number, a clock that decides when to measure, some processing (here: min, max, average and an alarm), a user interface (button, LED, buzzer, commands) and an output (here: text on Serial).

pot ----> A0 \ +--> CSV line on Serial --> spreadsheet / Plotter LDR ----> A1 >- analogRead() x3 ----+--> min / max / sum --> 's' prints the statistics any ----> A2 / every 250 ms +--> CH0 > 2.5 V ? --> LED solid + beep on D9 ^ millis() ------------+ USER button: logging on/off Serial 'r' / 's': reset / print stats

How the pieces combine. Each part comes from a basic lab: digitalWrite for the LED, digitalRead with edge detection for the button, analogRead for the pot (as in Lab 04) and the light sensor, Serial for output and commands, tone() for the buzzer, and millis() for timing. The new idea is how they share one loop(): no part is allowed to wait. Every pass of loop() checks the button, checks for a serial command, and asks “is it time for the next sample yet?”. Only when the answer is yes does it measure. This is cooperative scheduling: each job does a little work and returns quickly, so all of them seem to run at the same time. It is the pattern behind all the advanced labs (Lab 19 shows the preemptive alternative).

CSV. CSV (comma-separated values) is plain text with one record per line and the values separated by commas. The first line names the columns. Every spreadsheet program can open it, and the Arduino Serial Plotter can draw it.

Statistics without storing every sample. The board does not keep the samples. For each channel it keeps only three numbers: the smallest value so far, the largest, and the sum. The average is sum / samples. That needs the same small memory whether you log for one minute or one week.

On this board. The ADC is 12-bit inside, and analogRead() scales the result to 0…1023 like a classic Arduino. With a 3.3 V reference one step is 3.3 V / 1023 ≈ 3.2 mV. tone() works on any pin; it uses SCCP4 and a timer interrupt that toggles the pin.

Breadboard, jumper wires–

Wiring

ChannelBoardPart
CH0A0 RA0 J2-15pot wiper (as Lab 04); pot ends to 3V3 (J3-1) and GND (J3-2)
CH1A1 RA1 J2-16LDR from 3V3 to RA1, 10 kΩ RA1 to GND
CH2A2 RA2 J2-17anything 0–3.3 V (open = noise)
buzzerD9 RB4 J3-15optional: piezo + to J3-15, − to GND
Serial TXTX RC10 J5-2adapter RX
