GNDJ5-4adapter GND (leave J5-1 open)
The analog inputs accept 0…3.3 V only. Power the pot and the LDR divider from 3V3 (J3-1), never from +5V (J2-1). Use a passive piezo directly on the pin; a magnetic buzzer draws too much current and needs a transistor.

Step by step

  1. Upload Lab20_DataLogger, open the Serial Monitor at 115200. You see the title line, the CSV header time_ms,ch0_V,ch1_V,ch2_V, and then data lines.
  2. Four CSV rows per second appear: the time in ms and three voltages with 3 decimals. The LED toggles at each sample, so it blinks at 2 Hz while logging.
  3. Turn the pot: ch0_V follows, from about 0.000 to 3.300.
  4. Cover the LDR with your hand and watch ch1_V change. Shine a light on it: the voltage moves the other way. (Less light = higher LDR resistance = lower voltage on RA1 with this divider.)
  5. Look at ch2_V with nothing connected: the value wanders. An open input “floats” and picks up noise. Connect J2-17 to GND and it reads 0.000.
  6. Turn the pot above 2.5 V: LED solid + beep = alarm. The buzzer beeps (2 kHz, 60 ms) at every sample as long as CH0 stays above 2.5 V.
  7. Press USER: # logging OFF, the rows stop and the LED goes off. Press again: # logging ON and the rows continue.
  8. Send s: the number of samples and min/max/average of each channel. Turn the pot end to end, send s again: min and max have spread. Send r (# stats reset) to start the statistics again.
  9. Close the Monitor and open the Serial Plotter to watch the channels as graphs.
  10. Copy the CSV text from the Serial Monitor into a text file log.csv (remove the lines starting with #), open it in a spreadsheet and draw a chart of the columns.

Expected output

time_ms,ch0_V,ch1_V,ch2_V
1250,1.204,2.611,0.387
1500,1.206,2.598,0.402
# samples=40
# CH0 min=1.200 max=1.212 avg=1.205

The full start and the other messages look like this (example values):

# Lab 20 - data logger. USER = start/stop, r = reset, s = stats
time_ms,ch0_V,ch1_V,ch2_V
0,1.203,2.605,0.391
250,1.204,2.611,0.387
...
# logging OFF
# logging ON
# samples=40
# CH0 min=1.200 max=1.212 avg=1.205
# CH1 min=2.590 max=2.615 avg=2.603
# CH2 min=0.350 max=0.420 avg=0.389
# stats reset

How the code works

Instead of delay(250), the loop checks (long)(millis() - nextSample) >= 0 (correct even when millis() wraps). So the button and serial commands are handled continuously between samples. This “cooperative scheduler” pattern is used by every advanced lab.

Settings at the top. All the numbers you may want to change are constants:

const uint8_t  CH[]        = { A0, A1, A2 };
const int      NCH         = 3;
const unsigned long PERIOD = 250;     /* ms between samples (4 Hz) */
const double   ALARM_V     = 2.5;
const uint8_t  BUZZER_PIN  = 9;

The channel list is an array, so every loop over the channels uses for (int i = 0; i < NCH; i++). Adding a channel means adding one entry and changing NCH.

Statistics.

int  minV[NCH], maxV[NCH];
long sumV[NCH];

double toVolts(int raw) { return raw * 3.3 / 1023.0; }

void resetStats()
{
    samples = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < NCH; i++) { minV[i] = 1023; maxV[i] = 0; sumV[i] = 0; }
}

The minimum starts at the highest possible value (1023) and the maximum at the lowest (0), so the first sample replaces both. The values are kept as raw ADC numbers (integers) and converted to volts only for printing. sumV is a long: 4 samples per second × 1023 would overflow a 16-bit int after a few seconds.

setup() sets the LED as output and the button as input, starts Serial, clears the statistics and prints the title and the CSV header line.

loop(), part 1: the button.

static int lastBtn = HIGH;
int btn = digitalRead(BUTTON_BUILTIN);
if (btn == LOW && lastBtn == HIGH) {
    logging = !logging;
    Serial.println(logging ? "# logging ON" : "# logging OFF");
    delay(30);
}
lastBtn = btn;

The button reads LOW when pressed. Reacting only to the change from HIGH to LOW (an edge) means one press toggles once, however long you hold it. The short delay(30) skips the contact bounce right after the press.

Part 2: commands. r calls resetStats(), s calls printStats(). Each one is a single character, so reading it never waits.

Part 3: timed sampling.

if (logging && (long)(millis() - nextSample) >= 0) {
    nextSample = millis() + PERIOD;
    int v[NCH];
    for (int i = 0; i < NCH; i++) {
        v[i] = analogRead(CH[i]);
        if (v[i] < minV[i]) minV[i] = v[i];
        if (v[i] > maxV[i]) maxV[i] = v[i];
        sumV[i] += v[i];
    }
    samples++;
    ...

millis() is an unsigned long that wraps to 0 after about 49.7 days. A test like millis() >= nextSample would fail right at the wrap. The difference millis() - nextSample is still right across the wrap, and casting it to long makes “not yet” a negative number. nextSample starts at 0, so the first sample is taken at once.

Serial.print(millis());
for (int i = 0; i < NCH; i++) {
    Serial.print(",");
    Serial.print(toVolts(v[i]), 3);
}
Serial.println();

One CSV line: the time, then a comma and a value with 3 decimals for each channel.

bool alarm = toVolts(v[0]) > ALARM_V;
if (alarm) {
    digitalWrite(LED_BUILTIN, LED_ON);
    tone(BUZZER_PIN, 2000, 60);
} else {
    digitalWrite(LED_BUILTIN, (samples & 1) ? LED_ON : LED_OFF);
}
...
if (!logging) digitalWrite(LED_BUILTIN, LED_OFF);

In alarm the LED stays on and tone() starts a 60 ms beep that ends by itself, so the loop does not wait. Without alarm the LED follows the lowest bit of the sample counter: on, off, on, off – a 2 Hz blink that shows the logger is alive. When logging is off, the LED is held off.

printStats() prints the sample count and, for each channel, min, max and avg in volts. The average is sumV[i] / samples as a whole number of ADC steps, converted to volts; with no samples it prints 0.

Try it yourself

  1. Easy Log once per second instead of four times. Hint: PERIOD at the top.
  2. Easy Make the alarm trigger at 1.5 V and beep at 1 kHz. Hint: ALARM_V, and the tone(BUZZER_PIN, 2000, 60) line.
  3. Medium Stop the timing from drifting. nextSample = millis() + PERIOD starts each period from the moment the sample was taken, so any delay adds up. Change it to nextSample += PERIOD and compare the time_ms column after a few minutes.
  4. Medium Add hysteresis to the alarm: switch on above 2.5 V, but off only below 2.3 V, so it does not flicker near the limit. Hint: make alarm a static bool and change it with two separate tests.
  5. Challenge Add a fourth channel and a command p<ms> that changes the sample period while running. Hint: CH[]/NCH, the CSV header in setup(), and make PERIOD a normal variable; read the number like Lab 17’s readNumber().

Troubleshooting

SymptomLikely causeFix
ch0_V stays at 0.000 or 3.300Pot wiper not on J2-15, or one pot end not connectedCheck: ends to J3-1 (3V3) and GND, wiper to J2-15
ch1_V hardly changesLDR and 10 kΩ not forming a divider, or the room light does not change muchLDR between 3V3 and J2-16, 10 kΩ between J2-16 and GND; cover the LDR completely
ch2_V jumps aroundInput open (floating)Expected; connect a source or GND
No beep in alarmMagnetic or active buzzer, or wrong pinPassive piezo on J3-15 (D9) to GND
Data stops, LED offLogging was paused with USERPress USER again (# logging ON)
Plotter graphs are squashed flatThe time_ms column grows without end and sets the scaleIgnore or hide that series in the Plotter, or print without the time for plotting

Check your understanding

Why does the sketch not use delay(250) between samples?

During delay() nothing else runs: button presses and serial commands would be noticed late or missed. Checking millis() lets loop() handle them all the time and measure only when the period is over.

Why does minV start at 1023 and maxV at 0?

So the first real sample is always smaller than the start minimum and larger than the start maximum, and replaces both.

How long can the logger run before sumV overflows?

A long holds up to about 2.1 billion. At the worst case 1023 per sample and 4 samples per second, that is about 2 100 000 000 / 4092 ≈ 525 000 s, roughly 6 days. Send r before that, or use unsigned long long.

What does one ADC step mean in volts here?

toVolts() uses 3.3 V / 1023, so one step is about 3.2 mV. Smaller changes cannot be seen.

Resources: tone() uses SCCP4, which is also the analogWrite() channel of D8, so the two cannot be used together.

21GPS logger (NMEA parser on UART2)

Read a GPS module on the second hardware UART, check every NMEA sentence with its checksum, pull out time and position, and log one CSV row per second.

applicationSerial2NMEAparsingchecksumCSV logging

Objectives

  • After this lab you can use a second hardware UART (Serial2, from the NanoSerial2 library) next to the normal Serial.
  • After this lab you can explain what an NMEA sentence is and read the fields of $GxRMC and $GxGGA.
  • After this lab you can compute and check an NMEA XOR checksum.
  • After this lab you can assemble text lines from a byte stream and split them into fields without copying.
  • After this lab you can convert NMEA ddmm.mmmm coordinates into decimal degrees for a map.

Background

Why a second UART? A UART (Universal Asynchronous Receiver/Transmitter) sends bytes one bit at a time over a single wire, with no clock wire. Both ends must agree on the baud rate – the number of bits per second. On this board Serial (UART1, on J5) is already busy talking to your PC through the USB-serial adapter. The GPS needs its own UART, so the lab uses UART2, wrapped by the NanoSerial2 library as Serial2. By default its RX is RB10 = D15 J2-4 and its TX is RB11 = D16 J2-5. The dsPIC33CK has PPS (Peripheral Pin Select): UART2 is not tied to fixed pins, the library connects it to these pins in software. Received bytes are stored by an interrupt in a 128-byte ring buffer, so nothing is lost while loop() is busy for a short time.

NMEA 0183 is the text format almost every GPS module speaks. The module sends a few lines (“sentences”) every second at 9600 baud. Each sentence starts with $, then a 5-letter address, then comma-separated fields, then * and a two-digit hex checksum, and ends with CR LF. The first two letters are the talker: GP = GPS only, GN = several satellite systems combined (GPS + GLONASS/BeiDou/Galileo). The last three letters are the sentence type. This lab uses two types:

SentenceFields used by the sketch
$GPRMC / $GNRMC – “recommended minimum”1 UTC time hhmmss.ss, 2 status A = valid / V = not valid, 3–4 latitude + N/S, 5–6 longitude + E/W, 7 speed in knots, 9 date ddmmyy
$GPGGA / $GNGGA – “fix data”6 fix quality (0 none, 1 GPS, 2 DGPS …), 7 number of satellites, 8 HDOP, 9 altitude in metres
$GNRMC,083015.00,A,1345.37986,N,10030.10590,E,0.162,,111126,,,A*6F f[0] f[1] f[2] f[3] f[4] f[5] f[6] f[7] f[8] f[9] checksum type time ok lat ddmm.mmmm lon dddmm.mmmm knots date ddmmyy

Checksum. A long cable or a loose jumper can flip bits. The checksum lets the receiver catch that: XOR (exclusive OR, bit by bit “different = 1”) all characters between $ and *, and compare the 8-bit result with the two hex digits after *. A tiny example: for $AB* the XOR is 'A' ^ 'B' = 0x41 ^ 0x42 = 0x03, so the full sentence would be $AB*03. If one bit of the text changes, the XOR changes too, and the sentence is dropped.

Coordinates. NMEA does not send decimal degrees. Latitude is ddmm.mmmm (degrees and minutes) and longitude dddmm.mmmm. 1345.37986,N means 13° 45.37986′ north = 13 + 45.37986 / 60 = 13.756331°. South and West are written as negative numbers. HDOP (horizontal dilution of precision) is a quality number: around 1 is good, above 5 is poor.

Fix. A GPS needs signals from at least 4 satellites to compute a position (a “fix”). After power-up with no stored data (“cold start”) this can take 1–5 minutes with a clear view of the sky. Until then the module still sends sentences, but with status V and empty fields.

You need

PartQtyNotes
dsPIC33CK Nano board1any Clock setting
USB-C cable + 5 V supply1power only
3.3 V USB-serial adapter1on J5, for the CSV log at 115200 baud
NMEA GPS module, 9600 baud, 3.3 V logic1u-blox NEO-6M/7M/M8N breakout, Quectel L80, ATGM336H … with its antenna
Jumper wires4female-female or via breadboard

Work near a window or outdoors: GPS signals do not pass well through concrete.

Wiring

SignalBoard pinGPS module
Power3V3 J3-1 (or 5V J2-1 – only if the module has its own regulator and a 3.3 V TX pin)VCC
GroundGND J3-2GND
Serial2 RX (data from GPS)RB10 = D15 J2-4TX
Serial2 TX (optional)RB11 = D16 J2-5RX – only needed to configure the module; this sketch never sends to it
Log outputJ5-2 TX, J5-3 RX, J5-4 GNDUSB-serial adapter RX, TX, GND (leave J5-1 open)
The board is 3.3 V logic. Some GPS breakouts are sold as “5 V” modules: they have a regulator, and on most of them TX is still 3.3 V, but check the datasheet or measure TX against GND with a multimeter before you connect it to J2-4. If TX swings to 5 V, use a divider (e.g. 1 kΩ in series, 2 kΩ to GND) or a level shifter. Remember TX of the GPS goes to RX of the board – the wires cross.

Step by step

  1. Wire the GPS as in the table. Connect the USB-serial adapter to J5 and power the board. Most GPS modules have their own LED: it lights or blinks once the module has power.
  2. Upload Lab21_GPSLogger. Open the Serial Monitor at 115200 baud. You should read the two header lines: # Lab 21 - GPS logger. USER = start/stop logging and the CSV column names.
  3. Look at the USER LED. Off = no valid sentence in the last 3 seconds. If it stays off, the monitor prints # no GPS data - check GPS TX -> J2-4 and 9600 baud. good=0 bad=0 once a second. good=0 bad=0 means not a single $ line arrived: check the TX wire and power.
  4. If bad keeps rising while good stays 0, bytes are arriving but they are garbage: almost always a wrong baud rate (some modules default to 4800 or 38400) – change GPS_BAUD.
  5. With good sentences but no fix yet, the LED blinks slowly (0.5 s on, 0.5 s off) and rows are printed with status 0: fix is 0, and lat/lon stay 0.000000. Put the antenna near a window and wait 1–5 minutes.
  6. When the module has a fix, the LED is solid on. The fix column becomes 1 (or 2 for DGPS), sats shows how many satellites are used and lat/lon show your position.
  7. Press USER: the monitor prints # logging OFF and rows stop. Press again: # logging ON. The parser keeps running in both cases, so the LED status is always current.
  8. Copy some rows into a text file, save it as track.csv and open it in a spreadsheet, or paste the lat/lon pairs into an online map tool. Walk around with the board on a power bank and a laptop to record a track.
  9. Compare the utc column with your clock: it is UTC, not local time. Bangkok, for example, is UTC + 7 h.

Expected output

# Lab 21 - GPS logger. USER = start/stop logging
utc,date,lat,lon,fix,sats,hdop,alt_m,speed_kmh
083015.00,111126,13.756331,100.501765,1,7,1.2,12.4,0.3

Without a GPS connected you see instead (example values):

# no GPS data - check GPS TX -> J2-4 and 9600 baud. good=0 bad=0

How the code works

1. Setup. Two UARTs are started: Serial for the log, Serial2 for the GPS on its default pins.

Serial.begin(115200);
Serial2.begin(GPS_BAUD);                  /* RX RB10 (J2-4), TX RB11 (J2-5) */
Serial.println("# Lab 21 - GPS logger. USER = start/stop logging");
Serial.println("utc,date,lat,lon,fix,sats,hdop,alt_m,speed_kmh");

GPS_BAUD is 9600. Serial2.begin() computes the baud generator from FCY, so the lab works with both Clock menu settings.

2. Line assembly. feedGps() is called at the start of every loop(). It empties the receive buffer and builds one line in line[96].

while (Serial2.available() > 0) {
    char c = (char)Serial2.read();
    if (c == '$') lineLen = 0;            /* resynchronise on every start */
    if (c == '\r' || c == '\n') {
        if (lineLen > 6) { line[lineLen] = 0; parseSentence(line); }
        lineLen = 0;
    } else if (lineLen < sizeof(line) - 1) {
        line[lineLen++] = c;
    } else {
        lineLen = 0;                       /* too long: drop it */
    }
}

A $ always starts a new line, so if a byte is lost in the middle, the broken half never mixes into the next sentence. CR or LF ends the line; very short lines (6 characters or less) are ignored, and a line that would overflow the buffer is thrown away.

3. Checksum.

bool checksumOk(const char *s)
{
    if (s[0] != '$') return false;
    uint8_t x = 0;
    const char *p = s + 1;
    while (*p && *p != '*') x ^= (uint8_t)*p++;
    if (*p != '*' || hexVal(p[1]) < 0 || hexVal(p[2]) < 0) return false;
    return x == (uint8_t)(hexVal(p[1]) * 16 + hexVal(p[2]));
}

The loop XORs every character after $ up to *. hexVal() turns a hex digit (0–9, A–F, also lower case) into 0–15, or −1 if it is not a hex digit. A line with no * or a broken checksum is rejected. parseSentence() counts the result in goodSentences or badChecksums; only good sentences update gps.lastSentenceMs.

4. Splitting into fields.

int splitFields(char *s, char *f[], int maxF)
{
    int n = 0;
    char *star = strchr(s, '*');
    if (star) *star = 0;
    f[n++] = s;
    while (*s && n < maxF) {
        if (*s == ',') { *s = 0; f[n++] = s + 1; }
        s++;
    }
    return n;
}

Instead of copying each field, the function writes a string terminator (0) over every comma and stores a pointer to the character after it. f[0] is "$GNRMC", f[1] the time, and so on. Two commas in a row give an empty string "", so field numbers never shift. (The standard strtok() would skip empty fields – a classic NMEA bug.)

5. Using the fields.

const char *type = f[0] + 3;             /* skip "$GP" / "$GN" talker */
if (strcmp(type, "RMC") == 0 && n >= 10) {
    strncpy(gps.utc, f[1], sizeof(gps.utc) - 1);
    gps.valid = (f[2][0] == 'A');
    gps.lat = nmeaToDeg(f[3], f[4][0]);
    gps.lon = nmeaToDeg(f[5], f[6][0]);
    gps.speedKmh = atof(f[7]) * 1.852;   /* knots -> km/h */
    strncpy(gps.date, f[9], sizeof(gps.date) - 1);
} else if (strcmp(type, "GGA") == 0 && n >= 10) {
    gps.fixQuality = atoi(f[6]); ...

Skipping 3 characters ignores the talker, so $GPRMC and $GNRMC are handled the same. All other sentence types (GSV, GSA, VTG …) pass the checksum and are counted but otherwise ignored. One knot is 1.852 km/h.

double raw = atof(v);
int deg = (int)(raw / 100.0);
double minutes = raw - deg * 100.0;
double d = deg + minutes / 60.0;
return (hemi == 'S' || hemi == 'W') ? -d : d;

nmeaToDeg() splits ddmm.mmmm: dividing by 100 gives the whole degrees, the rest is minutes. An empty field returns 0.0.

6. The loop. After feedGps() the loop checks the USER button for a press (HIGH → LOW edge) and toggles logging. Then it sets the LED:

bool hearing = (millis() - gps.lastSentenceMs) < 3000 && goodSentences > 0;
bool fix = hearing && gps.valid && gps.fixQuality > 0;
if (fix)          digitalWrite(LED_BUILTIN, LED_ON);
else if (hearing) digitalWrite(LED_BUILTIN, (millis() / 500) % 2 ? LED_ON : LED_OFF);
else              digitalWrite(LED_BUILTIN, LED_OFF);

Finally, once per LOG_PERIOD_MS (1000 ms) it prints either the “no GPS data” message or printRow(). printRow() prints lat/lon with 6 decimals (about 0.1 m resolution – far finer than the GPS accuracy of a few metres) and writes fix as 0 whenever the RMC status is not A. Empty time or date fields are printed as -.

Try it yourself

  1. Easy Log every 5 seconds instead of every second. Change LOG_PERIOD_MS at the top.
  2. Easy Print local time: in printRow(), take the hours from gps.utc[0..1], add your time zone and wrap at 24.
  3. Medium Add a column for the number of bad checksums, so you can see how clean the link is. Print badChecksums at the end of printRow() and add it to the header line in setup().
  4. Medium Parse $GxVTG (course and speed) or the course field f[8] of RMC, and print the heading in degrees. Add a branch in parseSentence().
  5. Challenge Compute the distance travelled: keep the previous lat/lon and add the distance between two fixes (equirectangular approximation: dx = Δlon × cos(lat), dy = Δlat, both in radians × 6371 km). Only add when fix is true and speed > 1 km/h, otherwise GPS noise adds up.

Troubleshooting

SymptomLikely causeFix
good=0 bad=0 forever, LED offGPS TX not on J2-4, GPS not powered, or TX/RX swappedGPS TX → J2-4. Check the module’s own LED. Check GND is shared.
bad rises, good stays 0wrong baud ratetry GPS_BAUD 4800 or 38400; see the module datasheet
LED blinks for many minutes, fix stays 0no sky view, antenna missing or indoorsgo outdoors or to a window; connect the antenna; wait up to 5 minutes for a cold start

Check your understanding

Why does the sketch reset lineLen whenever it sees a $?

Because $ always marks the start of a sentence. If bytes were lost and the previous line never got its CR LF, the broken part is discarded instead of being glued in front of the next sentence.

What does $GNRMC,...,V,... tell you?

Status V means the data is not valid: the module is running but has no fix yet. The sketch sets gps.valid = false and prints fix as 0.

Convert 10030.10590,E to decimal degrees.

100° + 30.10590 / 60 = 100.501765°, positive because it is East.

Why can’t the GPS use Serial?

Serial (UART1) is already connected to J5 and the USB-serial adapter for the log output. A UART RX pin can only listen to one transmitter, so the GPS gets its own UART2 (Serial2).

22WS2812B addressable RGB LEDs via SPI

Generate the strict 800 kHz single-wire WS2812B protocol with the SPI peripheral instead of fragile bit-banging, then animate a strip.

applicationSPI as waveform generatorbit encodingtiming100 MIPS only

Objectives

  • After this lab you can explain how a WS2812B LED receives 24 bits of colour on one data wire, using pulse width.
  • After this lab you can use an SPI peripheral as a waveform generator: one LED bit = four SPI bits.
  • After this lab you can pre-encode a frame into a buffer and send it without timing gaps.
  • After this lab you can calculate the SPI clock from the baud-rate register and say why the lab needs 100 MIPS.
  • After this lab you can power a LED strip safely and handle the 3.3 V / 5 V level question.

Background

Addressable LEDs. A WS2812B (often sold as “NeoPixel”) is a red, a green and a blue LED plus a tiny controller chip in one 5×5 mm package. The LEDs are chained: data goes into DIN of the first LED, comes out of its DOUT and goes into the next one. Each LED keeps the first 24 bits it receives (8 bits green, 8 red, 8 blue – in that order, GRB) and passes everything after that down the chain. When the line stays LOW for more than about 50 µs (newer chips: 280 µs) (“reset” or “latch”), every LED shows its new colour at once.

The bit code. There is no clock wire. Every bit is a pulse of about 1.25 µs (800 kHz), and the width of the HIGH part says whether it is 0 or 1:

|<------- 1.25 us ------->| LED '0' ‾‾‾‾‾|____________________| 0.40 us high + 0.85 us low (+-150 ns) LED '1' ‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾|_____________| 0.80 us high + 0.45 us low (+-150 ns) reset __________________________ ... >= 50 us low = latch

±150 ns is very tight. Toggling the pin in software (“bit-banging”) means counting CPU instructions, and any interrupt in the middle ruins the timing.

The trick: SPI as a waveform generator. SPI (Serial Peripheral Interface) is meant for talking to chips: it shifts bytes out on the MOSI pin, one bit per clock, with perfect timing done by hardware. We ignore the clock pin and use only MOSI. If one SPI bit lasts 300 ns, then four SPI bits are 1.2 µs – close enough to one LED bit:

SPI at 3.333 MHz: 1 SPI bit = 300 ns, 4 SPI bits = 1.2 us = 1 LED bit LED '0' -> SPI 1000 (300 ns high, 900 ns low) spec: 400 +-150 ns high -> OK LED '1' -> SPI 1110 (900 ns high, 300 ns low) spec: 800 +-150 ns high -> OK 2 LED bits = 8 SPI bits = 1 SPI byte: 00 -> 1000 1000 = 0x88 01 -> 1000 1110 = 0x8E 10 -> 1110 1000 = 0xE8 11 -> 1110 1110 = 0xEE PAIR[] = {0x88,0x8E,0xE8,0xEE} 1 colour byte = 8 LED bits = 32 SPI bits = 4 SPI bytes example: 0x27 = 00 10 01 11 -> 0x88 0xE8 0x8E 0xEE

Why 100 MIPS only. The SPI library sets the clock with SPI1BRGL = FCY / (2 × f) − 1, and the SPI clock is FCY / (2 × (BRG + 1)). At 100 MIPS (FCY = 100 MHz) a request for 3.2 MHz gives BRG = 100 000 000 / 6 400 000 − 1 = 14 (integer division), so the real clock is 100 MHz / 30 = 3.333 MHz – the 300 ns bit we need. At 4 MIPS (FCY = 4 MHz) the fastest possible SPI clock is FCY / 2 = 2 MHz, and the formula would not even give a valid BRG. So the sketch stops the build with #error if FCY is below 50 MHz.

Power. Each LED draws up to about 60 mA at full white (20 mA per colour). 8 LEDs at full white = 480 mA, which is about the limit for a USB supply. The sketch scales every colour with BRIGHTNESS = 40 out of 255 (about 16 %), so the current stays far lower.

You need

PartQtyNotes
dsPIC33CK Nano board1Tools → Clock = 100 MIPS (the sketch does not compile at 4 MIPS)
USB-C cable + 5 V supply1power only; also powers the strip through J2-1
3.3 V USB-serial adapter1on J5, optional (prints the effect number)
WS2812B strip, ring or stick18 LEDs by default (NUM_LEDS)
330 Ω resistor1in series with DIN, close to the strip
470–1000 µF electrolytic capacitor, ≥ 6.3 V1across 5V/GND at the strip, observe polarity

Wiring

SignalBoard pinStrip
Data (SPI1 MOSI)MOSI RC5 = D26 J3-5 → 330 ΩDIN (the input end – arrow pointing away from it)
Power5V J2-15V / VCC (≤ 8 LEDs from USB)
GroundGND J2-2GND – common ground is mandatory
SCKRC4 = D25 J3-6not connected (it toggles, but the LEDs do not need it)
Capacitor470–1000 µF between 5V and GND at the strip, + leg to 5V
A 5 V WS2812B wants VIH ≥ 0.7 × VDD = 3.5 V on DIN, but our data is 3.3 V. It usually works with short wires. If it flickers: use a 74AHCT125 level shifter, or power the strip at about 4.5 V. Never connect the strip’s 5 V to a signal pin, and keep brightness low on USB power: 60 mA per LED at full white.

Step by step

  1. Set Tools → Clock = 100 MIPS. Try once to compile at 4 MIPS: you get the error Lab22 needs Tools > Clock = 100 MIPS (SPI must run at 3.3 MHz). That is the #error line doing its job. Switch back to 100 MIPS.
  2. Wire the strip with power off: capacitor across 5V/GND at the strip first, then GND, then 5V, then the data wire with the 330 Ω resistor. Make sure you use the DIN end.
  3. Upload Lab22_WS2812B. The Serial Monitor (115200) shows Lab 22 - WS2812B on MOSI RC5 (J3-5). USER = next effect. All LEDs are first set to off, then a rainbow moves along the strip (effect 0).
  4. The USER LED blinks while the animation runs (about 0.6 s on, 0.6 s off). It shows that loop() is running even if the strip stays dark.
  5. Press USER: effect 1 – a single orange dot runs along the strip.
  6. Press again: effect 2 – all LEDs “breathe” in blue, slowly brighter and darker.
  7. Press again: effect 3 – the colour test. LED 0 must be red, LED 1 green, LED 2 blue, then the pattern repeats. If red and green are swapped, your strip is RGB-order, not GRB.
  8. Press again: back to effect 0, the rainbow.
  9. If your strip is longer, change NUM_LEDS. Keep BRIGHTNESS low as long as the strip runs from USB.

Expected output

Lab 22 - WS2812B on MOSI RC5 (J3-5). USER = next effect
effect 1
effect 2
effect 3
effect 0

How the code works

1. Compile-time check and storage.

#define NUM_LEDS   8
#define BRIGHTNESS 40          /* 0..255, keep low on USB power */

#if FCY < 50000000UL
#error "Lab22 needs Tools > Clock = 100 MIPS (SPI must run at 3.3 MHz)"
#endif

uint8_t leds[NUM_LEDS][3];     /* G, R, B - the WS2812B wire order */
static const uint8_t PAIR[4] = { 0x88, 0x8E, 0xE8, 0xEE };   /* 00 01 10 11 */

FCY comes from the Clock menu. leds[] stores the colours already in wire order, 3 bytes per LED. PAIR[] is the table from the Background: two LED bits in, one SPI byte out.

2. setPixel() scales the colour by brightness and stores it in G, R, B order:

leds[i][0] = (uint8_t)((g * BRIGHTNESS) >> 8);
leds[i][1] = (uint8_t)((r * BRIGHTNESS) >> 8);
leds[i][2] = (uint8_t)((b * BRIGHTNESS) >> 8);

>> 8 divides by 256, so a full 255 becomes (255 × 40) / 256 = 39.

3. show() – encode first, then send.

static uint8_t buf[NUM_LEDS * 3 * 4];
int k = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < NUM_LEDS; i++)
    for (int c = 0; c < 3; c++) {
        uint8_t v = leds[i][c];
        buf[k++] = PAIR[(v >> 6) & 3];
        buf[k++] = PAIR[(v >> 4) & 3];
        buf[k++] = PAIR[(v >> 2) & 3];
        buf[k++] = PAIR[v & 3];
    }

Each colour byte is cut into four 2-bit pieces, most significant first, and each piece is looked up in PAIR[]. For 8 LEDs the buffer is 8 × 3 × 4 = 96 bytes. All the slow work (loops, shifts, lookups) happens before transmission, so the sending loop only has to feed bytes.

SPI.beginTransaction(SPISettings(3200000, MSBFIRST, SPI_MODE0));
noInterrupts();            /* a millis() tick in the middle would stretch a bit */
for (int j = 0; j < k; j++) SPI.transfer(buf[j]);
interrupts();
SPI.endTransaction();
delayMicroseconds(300);    /* latch */

SPISettings(3200000, ...) asks for 3.2 MHz and gets 3.333 MHz (BRG = 14). MSBFIRST sends the top bit of each byte first, which matches the order of the PAIR patterns. Interrupts are switched off so that no timer interrupt can pause the stream. Sending 96 bytes takes about 96 × 8 × 0.3 µs ≈ 230 µs plus small gaps (calculated), so millis() loses nothing noticeable.

The gap between bytes. SPI.transfer() waits for each byte to finish, so there is a short pause between bytes (a few hundred ns at 100 MIPS – estimated from the code, not measured with a scope). During that pause MOSI stays at the last bit, and every encoded byte ends with a 0 SPI bit. So the gap only makes a LOW phase a bit longer, which the LED tolerates as long as it stays well below the ~5 µs reset threshold. At the end, 300 µs of LOW latches the colours.

4. Effects in loop(). A counter t (0–255, wraps around) drives all effects:

case 0:  /* rainbow */
    wheel((uint8_t)(t + i * 256 / NUM_LEDS), &r, &g, &b);
case 1:  /* running dot */
    if (i == (t / 8) % NUM_LEDS) { r = 255; g = 80; }
case 2:  /* breathing blue */
    b = (t < 128) ? t * 2 : (255 - t) * 2;
default: /* red / green / blue test - check colour order */
    if (i % 3 == 0) r = 255; else if (i % 3 == 1) g = 255; else b = 255;

wheel() maps 0–255 to a colour circle red → green → blue → red. Each LED gets a position shifted by 256 / NUM_LEDS, so the strip shows one full rainbow. After each frame the loop calls show(), increments t and waits 20 ms, giving roughly 50 frames per second. A USER press (HIGH → LOW edge) moves to the next of the 4 modes.

Try it yourself

  1. Easy Make the running dot green and faster: in case 1 change the colour, and use t / 4 instead of t / 8.
  2. Easy Your strip is RGB order? Swap the indices in setPixel() so that leds[i][0] gets red and leds[i][1] gets green, then check with effect 3.
  3. Medium Add a fifth effect, “theatre chase”: every third LED on, shifting by one each 100 ms. Add a case 3: before default and set MODES to 5.
  4. Medium Control the brightness with a potentiometer on A0: replace the BRIGHTNESS constant in setPixel() by a global variable set from analogRead(A0) / 4 in loop(). Watch the current.
  5. Challenge The SK6812 RGBW LED uses 32 bits per LED (G, R, B, W) with the same timing. Change leds[][3] to 4 colours and the loop in show() to c < 4; size buf[] accordingly.

Troubleshooting

SymptomLikely causeFix
Compile error Lab22 needs Tools > Clock = 100 MIPSClock menu on 4 MIPSTools → Clock = 100 MIPS
Strip completely dark, USER LED blinkswired to DOUT, no common GND, or no 5 V at the stripuse the DIN end; connect GND J2-2 to strip GND; check 5 V
Random colours, flicker3.3 V data below the strip’s VIH, long data wireshorten the wire, 330 Ω near the strip, or a 74AHCT125 level shifter
Red and green swapped in effect 3strip is RGB orderswap the indices in setPixel()
Board resets when the LEDs get brightsupply overloadedlower BRIGHTNESS, add the capacitor, or use a separate 5 V supply (shared GND)

Check your understanding

Which SPI byte sends the LED bits 1 0?

0xE8 = 1110 1000: the first four SPI bits (1110) are a long HIGH = LED ‘1’, the next four (1000) a short HIGH = LED ‘0’.

Why does every PAIR value end with a 0 bit, and why does that matter?

Each LED bit ends LOW, so the last SPI bit of every byte is 0. The pause between two SPI bytes therefore only stretches a LOW phase, which the LED tolerates. If a byte ended HIGH, the pause would stretch a HIGH pulse and turn a ‘0’ into a ‘1’.

Why does the sketch refuse to build at 4 MIPS?

At FCY = 4 MHz the fastest SPI clock is 2 MHz (500 ns per SPI bit), so the 300 ns SPI bit needed for the 1000 / 1110 patterns is impossible. The #error stops the build instead of producing a sketch that sends wrong colours.

How many bytes does show() send for a 30-LED strip, and roughly how long does that take?

30 × 3 × 4 = 360 SPI bytes. At 0.3 µs per SPI bit: 360 × 8 × 0.3 µs ≈ 0.86 ms, plus the small gaps and the 300 µs latch.

A 5 V WS2812B wants VIH ≥ 3.5 V; 3.3 V data usually works with short wires. If it flickers: 74AHCT125 level shifter, or power the strip at ~4.5 V.

23OLED display: SSD1306 graphics driver from scratch

Initialise the SSD1306 controller, keep a frame buffer in RAM, draw pixels, lines, rectangles and text with your own 5×7 font, and stream the whole picture over I2C.

applicationSSD1306I2Cframe bufferBresenhambitmap fontring buffer

Objectives

  • After this lab you can explain how the SSD1306 stores 128×64 pixels in 8 pages of 128 bytes.
  • After this lab you can send commands and display data to an I2C display using the control byte (0x00 / 0x40).
  • After this lab you can draw into a frame buffer: pixels, Bresenham lines, rectangles and scaled text.
  • After this lab you can read a bitmap font table and design your own character.
  • After this lab you can estimate how long one frame takes on a 400 kHz I2C bus.

Background

The display. The common 0.96″ OLED module has 128×64 tiny organic LEDs that each light up by themselves – no backlight, very good contrast. A controller chip, the SSD1306, sits on the glass. It has its own 1024-byte display RAM (GDDRAM) and refreshes the pixels from it all the time. We only have to write that RAM over I2C.

Pages, not rows. The RAM is not organised in rows of pixels. It is 8 pages of 128 bytes. Each byte is one column of 8 pixels stacked vertically, bit 0 at the top. So one pixel lives in exactly one bit:

SSD1306 RAM = 8 pages x 128 columns, 1 byte = 8 vertical pixels (bit0 = top) x = 0 1 2 ... 127 page 0 [b0 ] [b0 ] rows 0..7 byte index 0..127 [ : ] [ : ] [b7 ] [b7 ] page 1 rows 8..15 byte index 128..255 ... page 7 rows 56..63 byte index 896..1023 pixel(x,y) -> fb[(y/8)*128 + x] bit (y%8) whole screen = 1024 bytes

Frame buffer. We cannot read pixels back from the SSD1306 over I2C, and changing one bit needs a whole byte. So the sketch keeps a copy of the screen in the dsPIC’s RAM, fb[1024], called a frame buffer. All drawing only changes this array. When a picture is finished, oledShow() copies the whole array to the display in one go. This also avoids flicker, because the display never shows a half-drawn picture for long.

I2C and the control byte. I2C uses two wires: SDA (data) and SCL (clock), both with pull-up resistors (the module has them on board). Every transfer starts with the 7-bit device address – usually 0x3C. The SSD1306 then expects a control byte that says what follows: 0x00 = commands, 0x40 = display data.

I2C: [addr 0x3C] [0x00 = commands follow] cmd cmd ... [addr 0x3C] [0x40 = data follows] 16 bytes of fb x 64 transactions

The board’s Wire library has a 32-byte transmit buffer, so the frame is sent in 64 pieces of 1 control byte + 16 data bytes. At 400 kHz each byte takes 9 clock bits (8 data + ACK), so one frame needs about 1024 × 9 / 400 000 ≈ 23 ms, plus address bytes and gaps – around 25–30 ms in total (calculated estimate). That is about 30 frames per second.

Fonts. A bitmap font stores each character as a small picture. Here every character is 5 columns × 7 rows, stored as 5 bytes, with bit 0 = top row – the same layout as the display pages. For example 'A' is {0x7E,0x11,0x11,0x11,0x7E}. The table covers the 96 printable ASCII characters 32–127. Each character cell is 6 pixels wide (one empty column as spacing), so 21 characters fit in one line. For bigger text the sketch simply draws each font pixel as a size×size square.

Lines. Drawing a straight line between two points on a pixel grid needs to choose which pixels to light. Bresenham’s algorithm does this with integer additions only: it keeps an error term and steps in x, in y or in both, whichever keeps the line closest to the ideal one. No division, no floating point – fast on any microcontroller.

You need

PartQtyNotes
dsPIC33CK Nano board1any Clock setting
USB-C cable + 5 V supply1power only
3.3 V USB-serial adapter1on J5, for status and frame time messages
0.96″ SSD1306 OLED, 128×64, I2C14 pins: GND VCC SCL SDA (the 128×32 version also works: set OLED_H to 32)
10 kΩ potentiometer1optional, same as Lab 04
Jumper wires7

Wiring

SignalBoard pinOther end
GroundGND J3-2OLED GND
Power3V3 J3-1OLED VCC
I2C clockRB8 = SCL1 J3-8OLED SCL (sometimes labelled SCK)
I2C dataRB9 = SDA1 J3-7OLED SDA
Pot wiperA0 RA0 J2-15middle pin of the potentiometer
Pot ends3V3 / GNDouter pins of the potentiometer
Power the OLED from 3V3, not 5 V. Most modules have a regulator and accept 5 V on VCC, but then their on-board pull-ups may pull SDA/SCL up to 5 V, which is above the board’s 3.3 V logic. With VCC = 3V3 the pull-ups go to 3.3 V and everything is safe. Pin order differs between modules (GND-VCC or VCC-GND first): read the labels.

Step by step

  1. Wire the display and run Lab 08 (I2C scanner) first. It should find a device at 0x3C. Some modules use 0x3D; then change OLED_ADDR at the top of the sketch.
  2. Upload Lab23_OLED and open the Serial Monitor at 115200. You read Lab 23 - SSD1306 OLED on I2C (SDA RB9 J3-7, SCL RB8 J3-8) and then # OLED found. USER = next screen.
  3. The display shows “Hello!” in double size and “Lab 23 - OLED” below it for one second.
  4. Then the dashboard appears: a title line, the pot voltage as a big number with “V”, a bar, and at the bottom the uptime in seconds and the button counter.
  5. Turn the pot: the big number goes from 0.00 to about 3.30 and the bar grows from empty to full. Without a pot, A0 floats and the number wanders.
  6. Press USER: the graph screen, “A0 history”. Turn the pot and watch the curve scroll from right to left – the last 128 samples.
  7. Press again: the font page, all characters of the font at size 1, “Size 2” in double size and the frame rate fps. Press again to return to the dashboard; the btn counter has gone up by 3.
  8. The USER LED blinks while frames are sent (it toggles every 8 frames). In the Serial Monitor a line # frame time NN ms appears every 50 frames: about 30 ms at 400 kHz I2C, so about 30 frames per second.
  9. Unplug the SDA wire and press RESET: the monitor prints # no OLED at 0x3C - check wiring, run Lab 08, try OLED_ADDR 0x3D and the USER LED blinks fast. The sketch checks for an ACK before it starts.

Expected output

Lab 23 - SSD1306 OLED on I2C (SDA RB9 J3-7, SCL RB8 J3-8)
# OLED found. USER = next screen
# frame time NN ms

NN is the time for one frame in milliseconds, about 30 at 400 kHz.

The dashboard screen (rendered on the PC from the sketch’s own drawing code)

How the code works

1. Low level: one command.

bool oledCmd(uint8_t c)
{
    Wire.beginTransmission(OLED_ADDR);
    Wire.write(0x00);                      /* control byte: command */
    Wire.write(c);
    return Wire.endTransmission() == 0;
}

Each command goes in its own small I2C transaction: address, control byte 0x00, command. endTransmission() returns 0 when the display acknowledged.

2. Initialisation. oledBegin() first sends only the address and checks for an ACK (“is anyone there?”). Then it sends the init list from the SSD1306 datasheet:

0xAE,                    /* display OFF                                   */
0xD5, 0x80,              /* clock divide ratio / oscillator frequency     */
0xA8, OLED_H - 1,        /* multiplex ratio = number of rows - 1          */
0xD3, 0x00,              /* display offset 0                              */
0x40,                    /* start line 0                                  */
0x8D, 0x14,              /* charge pump ON (needed at 3.3 V)              */
0x20, 0x00,              /* memory mode: horizontal addressing            */
0xA1,                    /* segment remap: column 127 = SEG0              */
0xC8,                    /* COM scan direction: remapped (not mirrored)   */
0xDA, (OLED_H == 64) ? 0x12 : 0x02,   /* COM pins configuration            */
0x81, 0xCF,              /* contrast                                      */
...
0xAF,                    /* display ON                                    */

The OLED pixels need about 7–15 V. The charge pump (0x8D, 0x14) is a small voltage converter inside the SSD1306 that makes this from 3.3 V – without it the screen stays black. Horizontal addressing means: after each data byte the column moves right, and after column 127 it jumps to the next page, so 1024 bytes in a row fill the whole screen. Segment remap and COM scan direction flip the picture left-right and top-bottom, so that it is not mirrored on the usual modules.

3. Sending the frame buffer.

static const uint8_t win[] = { 0x21, 0, OLED_W - 1,  0x22, 0, OLED_H / 8 - 1 };
oledCmds(win, sizeof(win));
for (unsigned i = 0; i < sizeof(fb); i += CHUNK) {
    Wire.beginTransmission(OLED_ADDR);
    Wire.write(0x40);                  /* control byte: data */
    for (int k = 0; k < CHUNK; k++) Wire.write(fb[i + k]);
    Wire.endTransmission();
}

Command 0x21 sets the column range 0–127 and 0x22 the page range 0–7, which also puts the write pointer back to the top-left corner. Then the 1024 bytes go out in chunks of CHUNK = 16 bytes, each with the 0x40 control byte. 17 bytes per transaction fit easily in the 32-byte Wire buffer.

4. Drawing a pixel.

void pixel(int x, int y, bool on = true)
{
    if (x < 0 || x >= OLED_W || y < 0 || y >= OLED_H) return;
    uint8_t m = (uint8_t)(1u << (y & 7));
    if (on) fb[(y >> 3) * OLED_W + x] |= m; else fb[(y >> 3) * OLED_W + x] &= (uint8_t)~m;
}

y >> 3 is y / 8 (the page), y & 7 is y % 8 (the bit). Points outside the screen are simply ignored (“clipping”), so the drawing functions never write past the end of fb. All other drawing functions are built on pixel().

5. Lines and rectangles.

int dx = abs(x1 - x0), sx = x0 < x1 ? 1 : -1;
int dy = -abs(y1 - y0), sy = y0 < y1 ? 1 : -1;
int err = dx + dy;
for (;;) {
    pixel(x0, y0);
    if (x0 == x1 && y0 == y1) break;
    int e2 = 2 * err;
    if (e2 >= dy) { err += dy; x0 += sx; }
    if (e2 <= dx) { err += dx; y0 += sy; }
}

This Bresenham version works for lines in every direction. err measures how far the drawn pixels are from the ideal line; depending on its sign the next pixel steps in x, in y, or diagonally. rect() draws four lines, or fills the area pixel by pixel when fill is true.

6. Text.

int drawChar(int x, int y, char c, int size = 1)
{
    if (c < 32 || c > 127) c = '?';
    const uint8_t *g = FONT[c - 32];
    for (int col = 0; col < 5; col++)
        for (int row = 0; row < 7; row++)
            if (g[col] & (1 << row))
                for (int a = 0; a < size; a++) for (int b = 0; b < size; b++)
                    pixel(x + col * size + a, y + row * size + b);
    return x + 6 * size;
}

The character code minus 32 is the row of the FONT table. For every set bit a size×size block is drawn. The function returns the x position of the next character, so text() just calls it in a loop. Size 1 = 6×8 cell, size 2 = 12×16, size 3 = 18×24 (used for the big number). Text can start at any y, not only on page boundaries, because it is drawn pixel by pixel.

7. Numbers without floating point.

long mv = (long)raw * 3300L / 1023L;
buf[0] = (char)('0' + mv / 1000); buf[1] = '.';
buf[2] = (char)('0' + (mv / 100) % 10); buf[3] = (char)('0' + (mv / 10) % 10); buf[4] = 0;

fmtVolts() turns the 10-bit ADC value into millivolts with integer maths and writes the digits directly, e.g. 2470 mV → "2.47". utoa10() does the same for unsigned numbers (uptime, counter, fps). This is faster and smaller than printf with floats.

8. The loop.

int raw = analogRead(A0);
graph[gHead] = (uint8_t)(raw * 47L / 1023L);     /* ring buffer of 128 samples */
gHead = (uint8_t)((gHead + 1) % GRAPH_N);

unsigned long t0 = millis();
clear();
if (screen == 0) drawDashboard(raw);
else if (screen == 1) drawGraph();
else drawFontPage();
oledShow();
frameMs = millis() - t0;

Every pass reads the pot and stores it, scaled to 0–47 pixels, in a ring buffer of 128 entries: gHead always points to the oldest sample, which is overwritten next. drawGraph() walks from the oldest to the newest and connects neighbours with lines, inside a frame from y = 10 to 63. Then the whole picture is redrawn from scratch: clear(), draw the current screen, oledShow(). frameMs measures drawing + sending; the font page shows 1000 / frameMs as fps. A USER press (HIGH → LOW edge) moves to the next of the 3 screens and increments presses.

Try it yourself

  1. Easy Put your name in the title line: change the string in text(0, 0, "dsPIC33CK Nano", 1) in drawDashboard(). Maximum 21 characters at size 1.
  2. Easy Invert the display: in the init list, replace 0xA6 (normal) with 0xA7 (inverted).
  3. Medium Draw your own character: change the last FONT entry (code 127, now a full block {0x7F,...}) into a small heart or a degree sign. Draw it on squared paper first: one byte per column, bit 0 at the top. Show it with drawChar(x, y, 127, 2).
  4. Medium Add a circle(cx, cy, r) function using the midpoint circle algorithm (integers only, like Bresenham), and draw a round gauge on the dashboard.
  5. Challenge Make the frame faster: only send the pages that changed. Keep a second copy of fb, compare page by page in oledShow(), and set the window (0x21/0x22) for each changed page only. Compare # frame time before and after.

Troubleshooting

SymptomLikely causeFix
# no OLED at 0x3C, LED blinks fastSDA/SCL swapped, no power, or address 0x3Drun Lab 08; SCL → J3-8, SDA → J3-7; try OLED_ADDR 0x3D
Found, but screen stays blackcharge pump not enabled, or a different controller (SH1106)keep 0x8D, 0x14 in the init list; SH1106 modules (1.3″) need page-by-page writes
Picture mirrored or upside downmodule mounted the other waychange 0xA1 ↔ 0xA0 and/or 0xC8 ↔ 0xC0
Only the top half shows, every second line empty128×32 module with OLED_H 64 (or the other way round)set OLED_H to match the module
Picture shifted by 2 columns, garbage at the edgeSH1106 controller (132 columns)the sketch is for SSD1306; SH1106 needs a column offset of 2
Big number jumps aroundno pot, A0 floatingconnect the pot, or ignore it

Check your understanding

Which byte and bit of fb hold the pixel (x = 10, y = 20)?

Page = 20 / 8 = 2, bit = 20 % 8 = 4. Byte index = 2 × 128 + 10 = 266, bit 4.

What is the difference between the control bytes 0x00 and 0x40?

0x00 tells the SSD1306 that the following bytes are commands (init, window); 0x40 says they are display data that go into the RAM.

Why does the sketch keep a frame buffer instead of writing pixels directly to the display?

The display RAM cannot be read back over I2C, and each byte holds 8 pixels. To change one pixel without destroying its 7 neighbours you need to know the old byte, so a copy in the dsPIC’s RAM is needed. It also lets you draw a full picture first and send it at once.

Why is the frame sent in chunks of 16 data bytes?

The Wire library buffers at most 32 bytes per transmission. 1 control byte + 16 data bytes fits; 1024 bytes need 64 transactions.

The drawing code was checked by running the same algorithms on the PC: the screen above is the real 128×64 frame buffer. That caught the layout and the font, not the I2C link, which needs a real display.

24Modbus RTU over RS485 (master + slave)

A real industrial fieldbus: half-duplex RS485 physical layer, binary Modbus RTU frames, CRC-16, timeouts and exception replies – master and slave in one sketch.

applicationRS485Modbus RTUCRC-16protocol stateSerial2half duplex

Objectives

  • After this lab you can explain how RS485 sends data over a twisted pair and why it needs direction control (DE).
  • After this lab you can read and build Modbus RTU frames for function 03 (read holding registers) and 06 (write single register).
  • After this lab you can compute the CRC-16/MODBUS and explain why it is sent low byte first.
  • After this lab you can detect the end of a frame by silence (the 3.5-character rule) and handle timeouts.
  • After this lab you can connect the board to a PC Modbus tool and read its registers.

Background

RS485 – the physical layer. A normal UART signal (0 V / 3.3 V against GND) only works over short distances, because noise on long cables adds to the signal. RS485 sends each bit as a difference between two wires, A and B: if A is higher than B it is one logic level, if B is higher it is the other. Noise hits both wires of a twisted pair equally, so the difference survives. That is why RS485 works over hundreds of metres in factories. Up to 32 standard nodes share the same pair. At each end of a long cable a 120 Ω resistor (termination) across A-B stops reflections.

Half duplex and DE. All nodes share one pair, so only one may drive it at a time. A transceiver chip (SP3485, THVD1500, MAX485 …) converts between UART and RS485. It has four logic pins:

PinMeaning
DI (driver in)UART TX goes in here
RO (receiver out)received data comes out here, to UART RX
DE (driver enable)HIGH = drive the bus (transmit)
/RE (receiver enable, active LOW)LOW = receiver on

With DE and /RE tied together, one pin chooses the direction: HIGH = transmit, LOW = receive. The NanoSerial2 library does this for you: Serial2.write() sets DE HIGH before the first byte, and Serial2.flush() waits until the last stop bit has left the pin (the UART’s TRMT flag) and then sets DE LOW. Releasing DE too early would cut off the end of the CRC; releasing it too late would collide with the answer of the other node.

Modbus RTU – the protocol. Modbus is a very common industrial protocol: one master asks, slaves answer. A slave never talks unless asked. Data lives in numbered 16-bit holding registers. Every frame is binary:

request (fn 03): [01][03][00 00][00 05][CRC lo][CRC hi] id, function, start reg, quantity response : [01][03][0A][r0 hi][r0 lo] ... [r4 lo][CRC lo][CRC hi] 0A = 10 data bytes request (fn 06): [01][06][00 02][00 01][CRC lo][CRC hi] write value 1 into reg 2 response : identical echo of the request = success exception : [01][83][02][CRC lo][CRC hi] fn | 0x80, code 01 bad function / 02 bad address / 03 bad value

16-bit values inside a frame are sent high byte first. Register numbers like “40001” are the traditional names: 4xxxx means holding register, and 40001 is address 0 in the frame.

CRC-16/MODBUS. The last two bytes are a cyclic redundancy check over all bytes before them. It catches almost every transmission error, much better than a simple sum. Start with 0xFFFF; for each byte, XOR it into the low byte, then 8 times: shift right, and if the bit that fell out was 1, XOR with 0xA001 (the reflected form of the polynomial 0x8005). The CRC is sent low byte first – the one exception to the high-byte-first rule. A well-known example: 01 03 00 00 00 01 has the CRC 0x0A84, so the full frame is 01 03 00 00 00 01 84 0A. A frame with a wrong CRC is silently ignored.

Framing by silence. RTU frames have no start or end character. A frame ends when the line has been quiet for 3.5 character times. The sketch counts 11 bits per character, so at 9600 baud: 3.5 × 11 / 9600 = 4.0 ms (T35_US = 4010 µs). Above 19200 baud the spec fixes it at 1.75 ms.

DI and DE are inputs of the transceiver; a 5 V MAX485 usually accepts the board’s 3.3 V HIGH there (check its VIH). Many cheap modules already have 120 Ω on board: with only two modules on a short cable, that is fine. Some modules label A/B the other way round (D+/D−); if nothing works, swap A and B at one end – it does no harm.

Step by step

  1. Upload Lab24_ModbusRS485 to both boards. The role is chosen at RESET by the USER button.
  2. Board A: just press RESET (USER released) → SLAVE id 1. Its Serial Monitor shows Lab 24 - Modbus RTU SLAVE id 1 (registers 0..4). Its LED blinks slowly (1 s on, 1 s off) = “alive, waiting”.
  3. Board B: hold USER while pressing RESET, then release USER → MASTER. Open its Serial Monitor: Lab 24 - Modbus RTU MASTER (polling slave 1). The sketch waits until you release USER, so this press is not taken as a command.
  4. The master reads the 5 registers twice a second and prints one line each time. Its LED flashes briefly (20 ms) on every good reply. req= counts the requests the slave has accepted – it goes up by about 2 per second.
  5. Turn the pot on the slave’s A0: A0= changes (0–1023). Hold the slave’s USER: btn=1.
  6. Press the master’s USER: it prints write LED=1 ok and the slave’s LED turns on (and stops blinking). The next lines show led=1. Press again: write LED=0 ok, LED off.
  7. Unplug the A wire: read failed: timeout (check A/B, DE wiring, slave powered?) every 500 ms. That is how a fieldbus master detects a dead node: no answer within 200 ms. Plug it back: the lines return, and the fail counter shows how many polls were lost.
  8. Optional: if you see read failed: CRC error (noise? termination? baud?), bytes arrived but were damaged – check termination, GND and cable length.
  9. Optional PC test: connect a USB-RS485 dongle instead of the master. In the Modbus tool choose 9600 baud, 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit, slave id 1, function 03, address 0, quantity 5. Write 1 to register 2 with function 06 to switch the slave’s LED.

Expected output (master)

Lab 24 - Modbus RTU MASTER (polling slave 1)

write LED=1 ok
slave1: A0=515 btn=0 led=1 up=15s req=29  (ok 28 / fail 0)

Note that req on the slave counts every valid request, including the write, while ok on the master counts only successful reads.

Slave register map

ModbusRegMeaningAccess
400010analogRead(A0)R

400032LED 0/1R/W
400043uptime sR

How the code works

1. Setup and role.

isMaster = (digitalRead(BUTTON_BUILTIN) == LOW);
Serial2.begin(MB_BAUD, SERIAL2_DEFAULT_RX, SERIAL2_DEFAULT_TX, PIN_DE);

The USER button is read once at start. The fourth argument of Serial2.begin() is the DE pin (RB12); with it, the library switches the transceiver direction automatically. Without it (as in Lab 21) DE is not used.

2. CRC-16.

uint16_t crc16(const uint8_t *b, uint16_t n)
{
    uint16_t crc = 0xFFFF;
    while (n--) {
        crc ^= *b++;
        for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) crc = (crc & 1) ? (uint16_t)((crc >> 1) ^ 0xA001) : (uint16_t)(crc >> 1);
    }
    return crc;
}

This is the bit-by-bit version of the algorithm described above: 8 shift steps per byte. It is short and fast enough for 9600 baud (a table-driven version would be faster but needs 512 bytes of table).

3. Sending a frame.

uint16_t c = crc16(f, n);
f[n++] = (uint8_t)(c & 0xFF);       /* CRC low byte first */
f[n++] = (uint8_t)(c >> 8);
Serial2.write(f, n);                /* DE goes HIGH on the first byte */
Serial2.flush();                    /* waits for the last stop bit, then DE LOW */

sendFrame() appends the CRC to the buffer, so every caller only fills in the bytes before it. The buffers are always 2 bytes larger than the message for this reason.

4. Receiving a frame.

while (Serial2.available() == 0) {
    if (millis() - t0 >= waitMs) return 0;
}
uint16_t n = 0;
unsigned long last = micros();
while (micros() - last < T35_US) {
    if (Serial2.available() > 0) {
        int c = Serial2.read();
        if (n < maxLen) f[n++] = (uint8_t)c;
        last = micros();
    }
}
return n;

receiveFrame() first waits up to waitMs for the first byte (200 ms for the master, 0 for the slave, so the slave’s loop never blocks). Then it collects bytes and restarts the silence timer after each one. When 4.0 ms pass without a byte, the frame is complete. crcOk() recomputes the CRC over all bytes except the last two and compares.

5. The slave. slavePoll() first refreshes registers 0, 1, 3 and 4 from the pot, the button, millis() and the request counter. Then:

if (!crcOk(f, n) || f[0] != SLAVE_ID) return;   /* not for us / corrupt: stay silent */
if (n != 8) { slaveException(f[1], 0x03); return; }   /* fn 03 and 06 requests are 8 bytes */
requests++;
...
if (fn == 0x03) {                                /* Read Holding Registers */
    if (qty < 1 || qty > 125) { slaveException(fn, 0x03); return; }
    if ((uint32_t)addr + qty > NREGS) { slaveException(fn, 0x02); return; }
    ...
} else if (fn == 0x06) {                         /* Write Single Register */
    if (addr != 2) { slaveException(fn, 0x02); return; }   /* only the LED is writable */
    regs[2] = val ? 1 : 0;
    digitalWrite(LED_BUILTIN, regs[2] ? LED_ON : LED_OFF);
    sendFrame(f, 6);                             /* echo request = success */
} else {
    slaveException(fn, 0x01);                    /* illegal function */
}

A corrupt frame, or a frame for another address, gets no answer – as the spec requires. Otherwise every problem gets an exception reply: function code | 0x80 plus an exception code. Reading registers 3..7, for example, gives exception 02 (illegal data address) because only 0..4 exist. The read answer contains qty × 2 data bytes, each register high byte first. In loop() the slave LED blinks slowly until the master has written a 1 into register 2 once; after that it follows register 2.

6. The master.

uint8_t f[8] = { id, 0x03, (uint8_t)(addr >> 8), (uint8_t)addr, (uint8_t)(qty >> 8), (uint8_t)qty };
while (Serial2.available()) Serial2.read();     /* flush stale bytes */
sendFrame(f, 6);
uint8_t r[64];
uint16_t n = receiveFrame(r, sizeof(r), 200);
if (n == 0) return 1;
if (!crcOk(r, n)) return 2;
if (r[1] & 0x80) { *exc = r[2]; return 3; }

masterReadRegs() builds the request, drops any old bytes, sends, and waits up to 200 ms. The return value says what happened: 0 ok, 1 timeout, 2 CRC error, 3 exception. masterPoll() calls it every 500 ms and prints the line or the reason for the failure, and counts ok / fail. On a USER press it calls masterWriteReg(SLAVE_ID, 2, ledCmd) with ledCmd toggled between 0 and 1.

Try it yourself

  1. Easy Poll faster: change 500 in masterPoll() to 100 and watch req rise faster. How fast can you go before frames start to fail?
  2. Easy Provoke an exception: in masterPoll() read 6 registers instead of NREGS. The master prints read failed: exception from slave (code 02). Print exc too.
  3. Medium Add a sixth register, e.g. a writable blink period. Increase NREGS, add it in slavePoll(), and allow writes to address 5 in the function 06 branch.
  4. Medium Use two slaves: give the second board SLAVE_ID = 2 and let the master poll id 1 and id 2 in turn. All three boards share the same A/B pair.
  5. Challenge Implement function 16 (0x10, Write Multiple Registers) in the slave. The request is longer than 8 bytes, so the n != 8 check must be changed to check the length per function.

SymptomLikely causeFix

read failed: CRC error now and thennoise, missing termination, long cabletwisted pair, 120 Ω at both ends, common GND
Master sees nothing, but a PC tool shows the slave’s replymaster’s RO not reaching RB10, or 5 V RO not dividedcheck RO → J2-4 and the divider

PC tool shows “illegal data address”tool uses 1-based numbers or another register rangeaddress 0 (= 40001), quantity 5, holding registers

Check your understanding

Why must Serial2.flush() wait for the last stop bit before DE goes LOW?

The UART still shifts out the last byte after it was written to the transmit buffer. If DE dropped earlier, the transceiver would stop driving the bus and the end of the CRC would be lost, so the slave would reject the frame.

The slave receives a frame with a correct CRC but address 5. What does it do?

Nothing. A Modbus slave only answers frames with its own address; others are ignored without any reply, otherwise several slaves would talk at once.

How long is one byte at 9600 baud 8N1, and why is the frame gap 4.0 ms?

8N1 = 10 bits, so about 1.04 ms per byte. The sketch uses the spec’s 3.5 character times with 11 bits per character: 3.5 × 11 / 9600 ≈ 4.0 ms of silence ends a frame.

The master sends 01 06 00 02 00 01 + CRC. What is the reply if all goes well?

The same 8 bytes, echoed back: for function 06 an exact copy of the request means success.

25LIN bus: master and slave at 19200 baud

The low-cost single-wire car body bus: break, sync, protected ID, data and checksum, built byte by byte on UART2, with a schedule table and echo checking.

applicationLIN 2.xbreak / syncPID parityclassic & enhanced checksumschedule tableSerial2

Objectives

  • After this lab you can name the parts of a LIN frame (break, sync, PID, data, checksum) and say who sends each part.
  • After this lab you can generate a LIN break with the UART’s break override bit.
  • After this lab you can compute the protected identifier (PID) parity bits and the classic and enhanced checksums by hand.
  • After this lab you can explain echo checking on a single-wire bus and how it finds bit errors.
  • After this lab you can describe a schedule table and why only the master starts frames.

Background

What LIN is for. A modern car has dozens of small electronic units: window lifters, mirrors, seat motors, rain sensors, ambient lights. CAN would be too expensive for each of them. LIN (Local Interconnect Network) is the cheap answer: one signal wire plus ground, up to about 16 nodes, 19200 baud at most, and it can be built on an ordinary UART. One node is the master (for example the door control unit); the others are slaves.

The physical layer. The LIN wire is pulled up to the battery voltage (VBAT, about 12 V) in the master by 1 kΩ + a diode. Any node can pull it down to 0 V (“dominant” = logic 0); when nobody pulls, it floats up to 12 V (“recessive” = logic 1, also the idle state). A LIN transceiver (MCP2003B, TJA1021, TLE7259) translates between this 12 V wire and the microcontroller’s TXD/RXD logic pins. Every node always hears the wire, including what it sends itself.

The frame. In LIN only the master starts a frame. It sends the header; then whichever node “publishes” that ID sends the response (this can be the master itself or one slave):

|<-- BREAK >= 13 bits low -->|del| SYNC 0x55 | PID | D0 | D1 | ... | Dn | CHECKSUM | \______________ header (always sent by the MASTER) _____/\_____ response (publisher) _____/ PID = ID(6 bits) + P0 = ID0^ID1^ID2^ID4 + P1 = !(ID1^ID3^ID4^ID5) 0x10 -> 0x50, 0x3C -> 0x3C checksum = ~(sum with carry wrap) classic: data only enhanced (LIN 2.x): PID + data
FieldPurpose
BREAKat least 13 bit times LOW, followed by a 1-bit HIGH “delimiter”. No normal byte has that many 0 bits in a row (a 0x00 byte is only 9 bits low including the start bit), so every slave knows: a new frame starts.
SYNC 0x550101 0101 – with start and stop bit an alternating pattern. Slaves with a cheap RC oscillator measure the edges and adjust their own baud rate (“auto-baud”).
PID6-bit frame ID (0–63) + 2 parity bits. The ID says what the frame contains, not who sends it.
Data1 to 8 bytes; the length is fixed per ID and known to all nodes.
Checksum8-bit sum with carry wrap-around, inverted.

PID worked example. ID 0x10 = 01 0000 binary, so only ID4 = 1. P0 = ID0^ID1^ID2^ID4 = 0^0^0^1 = 1. P1 = NOT(ID1^ID3^ID4^ID5) = NOT(0^0^1^0) = 0. PID = 0x10 + P0 × 0x40 + P1 × 0x80 = 0x50. For ID 0x20 (only ID5 = 1): P0 = 0, P1 = NOT(1) = 0, PID = 0x20.

Checksum worked example. “Sum with carry wrap” means: add the bytes; whenever the sum goes above 0xFF, subtract 0xFF (= drop the 0x100 and add 1). Classic checksum of 4A 55 93 E5: 4A + 55 = 9F; 9F + 93 = 132 → 33; 33 + E5 = 118 → 19; inverted: E6. The classic checksum (LIN 1.x) covers the data only; the enhanced checksum (LIN 2.x) also includes the PID. Both ends must use the same kind, or every frame is rejected.

Timing at 19200 baud. One bit = 52 µs, one byte (start + 8 + stop) = 521 µs. A frame with 4 data bytes has a header of about 34 bit times and a response of 50 bit times, roughly 4.4 ms in total – it fits easily into the 50 ms slots of this lab’s schedule.

On the dsPIC33CK. The sketch uses UART2 (via NanoSerial2) in plain 8N1 mode and builds the frame by hand. The break comes from the BRKOVR bit in U2MODE, which forces the TX pin LOW for as long as it is set. The receiver sees this long LOW as a 0x00 byte with a framing error (the stop bit was missing). The UART also has a hardware LIN mode (MOD = 1100) that automates break, sync and checksum; this lab does not use it, so every field stays visible.

You need

Wiring

SignalBoardTransceiver
UART2 TXRB11 = D16 J2-5TXD
UART2 RXRB10 = D15 J2-4RXD (open drain, internal pull-up on)
Enable3V3 J3-1EN / CS
GroundGND J3-2GND, also to the 12 V supply GND

Test 1: just jumper J2-5 → J2-4. Test 2: EN/CS → 3V3, VBAT → 12 V, LIN wires joined, GND common, master: 1 kΩ + diode LIN→VBAT.
The LIN wire and VBAT carry 12 V. Never connect them to any board pin – only TXD, RXD and EN of the transceiver go to the board. Check that the transceiver’s RXD is open drain (pulled up to 3.3 V by the board) or 3.3 V push-pull, not 5 V. Switch the 12 V supply on last and off first.

Step by step

  1. Test 1, one board. Put a jumper from J2-5 (TX) to J2-4 (RX). Upload Lab25_LIN and open the Serial Monitor at 115200, USER released at RESET = MASTER. You read Lab 25 - LIN 19200 baud, MASTER (schedule 0x10 / 0x20) and # PID(0x10)=0x50 PID(0x20)=0x20 – compare with the worked example above.
  2. Every 2 seconds the master prints # no answer to 0x20 (single board + jumper: expected - no slave). Frames are still echo-checked: followed by the statistics. That message is expected: there is no slave to answer frame 0x20.
  3. Look at bitErrors=0: every byte the master sent came back unchanged through the jumper, exactly as on a real LIN wire. noResponse rises by about 10 per second (one 0x20 slot every 100 ms). Send ? at any time to print the statistics.
  4. Pull the jumper out: bitErrors now rises quickly, because the master no longer hears its own bytes. Put it back.
  5. Test 2, two boards. Wire both transceivers as in the table. Start board B with USER held during RESET, then release it = SLAVE: Lab 25 - LIN 19200 baud, SLAVE (answers ID 0x20, listens to 0x10). Board A is the master (USER released).
  6. The master now prints slave 0x20: A0=… btn=… alive=… about every half second. Turn the pot on the slave: A0 follows. Hold the slave’s USER: btn=1. alive counts up with every answer and wraps at 255.
  7. Press USER on the master: # LED command -> 1. Frame 0x10 carries the LED command and the slave’s LED turns on. Press again: off.
  8. Send c to the master (classic checksum). The slave still expects enhanced, so frames no longer match: the master prints the “no answer” message with badChecksum rising, and the LED command no longer reaches the slave. Send e to switch back to enhanced and everything works again.

Expected output (master, two boards)

Lab 25 - LIN 19200 baud, MASTER (schedule 0x10 / 0x20)
# PID(0x10)=0x50  PID(0x20)=0x20
slave 0x20: A0=512 btn=0 alive=17
# LED command -> 1

One board with the jumper (example values):

Lab 25 - LIN 19200 baud, MASTER (schedule 0x10 / 0x20)
# PID(0x10)=0x50  PID(0x20)=0x20
# no answer to 0x20 (single board + jumper: expected - no slave). Frames are still echo-checked:
# ok=0 noResponse=20 badChecksum=0 bitErrors=0  checksum=ENHANCED (LIN 2.x)

How the code works

1. Setup.

isMaster = digitalRead(BUTTON_BUILTIN) == HIGH;
Serial2.begin(LIN_BAUD);                            /* RX RB10 (J2-4), TX RB11 (J2-5) */
pinMode(SERIAL2_DEFAULT_RX, INPUT_PULLUP);          /* LIN transceiver RXD is open drain */

Note the role is the opposite of Lab 24: here USER released = master. The internal pull-up on RB10 is needed because the transceiver’s RXD can only pull LOW. BIT_US = 1 000 000 / 19200 = 52 µs (integer).

2. PID and checksum.

uint8_t p0 = ((b >> 0) ^ (b >> 1) ^ (b >> 2) ^ (b >> 4)) & 1;
uint8_t p1 = (~((b >> 1) ^ (b >> 3) ^ (b >> 4) ^ (b >> 5))) & 1;
return (uint8_t)(id | (p0 << 6) | (p1 << 7));
...
uint16_t s = enh ? pid : 0;
for (uint8_t i = 0; i < n; i++) { s += d[i]; if (s > 0xFF) s -= 0xFF; }   /* add with carry */
return (uint8_t)~s;

linPid() shifts each needed ID bit down to bit 0, XORs them and keeps only bit 0. linChecksum() starts with the PID for the enhanced checksum, 0 for classic, and subtracts 0xFF on every overflow – the carry wrap from the Background.

3. The break.

Serial2.flush();                                   /* previous byte fully out */
U2MODEbits.BRKOVR = 1;                             /* force TX low ... */
delayMicroseconds(13 * BIT_US);                    /* ... 13 bit times */
U2MODEbits.BRKOVR = 0;
delayMicroseconds(BIT_US);                         /* break delimiter (1 bit high) */
delayMicroseconds(2 * BIT_US);
flushRx();                                         /* drop the 0x00/framing-error byte the break produced */
U2STAbits.FERR = 0;

The break lasts 13 × 52 = 676 µs, then TX is released (HIGH) for the delimiter plus a little extra. The master hears its own break as a 0x00 byte and throws it away. The slave, in contrast, uses exactly that 0x00 byte to find the start of the frame.

4. Echo check.

bool txEcho(uint8_t b)
{
    Serial2.write(b);
    unsigned long t0 = micros();
    while (Serial2.available() == 0) if (micros() - t0 > 20 * BIT_US) { bitErrors++; return false; }
    int e = Serial2.read();
    if (e != b) { bitErrors++; return false; }
    return true;
}

Every byte sent is also received. If it does not come back within 20 bit times, or comes back different, someone else was driving the wire (or the wire is broken): a bit error. This is how LIN nodes detect collisions without any extra hardware.

5. Master: publishing and requesting.

void masterHeader(uint8_t id)
{
    sendBreak();
    txEcho(0x55);                                      /* SYNC */
    txEcho(linPid(id));
}
...
int got = rxBytes(buf, n + 1, 1400 * BIT_US / 100);   /* response window ~ 1.4 x nominal */
if (got < n + 1) { noResponse++; return false; }
if (buf[n] != linChecksum(linPid(id), buf, n, enhanced)) { badChecksum++; return false; }

masterPublish() sends the header and then the data and checksum itself (frame 0x10: LED command and a counter). masterRequest() sends only the header and then waits for n data bytes + 1 checksum from a slave (frame 0x20: 4 bytes). rxBytes() gives up when no new byte arrives within 1400 × 52 / 100 = 728 µs; the timer restarts after each byte, so this is a gap timeout between bytes.

6. Schedule table.

if (millis() - last >= 50) {                        /* schedule table: one slot every 50 ms */
    last = millis();
    slot = !slot;
    if (slot) {
        uint8_t d[2] = { ledCmd, counter++ };
        masterPublish(0x10, d, 2);
    } else {
        ... masterRequest(0x20, d, 4) ...

Every 50 ms the master runs the next slot, alternating 0x10 and 0x20, so each frame repeats every 100 ms. Real cars use exactly this: a fixed list of frames that the master plays in a loop, so every signal arrives at a known rate. The result of 0x20 is printed at most every 500 ms; the “no answer” message and stats() at most every 2 s. At the end of the loop the master reads c, e or ? from Serial.

7. Slave.

int c = Serial2.read();
if (c != 0x00) return;                              /* not a break - ignore */
uint8_t h[2];
if (rxBytes(h, 2, 20 * BIT_US) < 2 || h[0] != 0x55) return;
uint8_t pid = h[1], id = pid & 0x3F;
if (pid != linPid(id)) { badChecksum++; return; }   /* parity error */

The slave waits for a 0x00 byte (the break), then expects SYNC 0x55 and a PID with correct parity. For ID 0x10 it receives 2 data bytes + checksum and sets its LED from the first byte. For ID 0x20 it reads A0 and the button, waits 2 bit times (the “response space”) and sends 4 bytes + checksum, each one echo-checked with txEcho(). Other IDs are ignored.

Key registers

Register / bitValue usedMeaning
U2MODE.BRKOVR1 for 676 µs, then 0break override: forces the TX pin LOW (set directly by the sketch)
U2STA.FERRcleared to 0framing error flag, set by the break (no stop bit seen)
U2STA.TRMTpolled by Serial2.flush()1 = transmit shift register empty, last stop bit sent
U2MODE.MOD0000 (library default)plain asynchronous 8-bit mode; 1100 would be the hardware LIN mode, not used here
U2MODEH.BCLKMOD / U2BRG1 / FCY / 19200fractional baud generator, set by the library: 5208 at 100 MIPS, 208 at 4 MIPS (calculated)

Try it yourself

  1. Easy Compute the PID of ID 0x3C by hand and check it: add a Serial.print(linPid(0x3C), HEX) in setup(). It should print 3C.
  2. Easy Make the schedule slower: change the 50 in loop() to 200 ms and watch alive count more slowly.
  3. Medium Add a third frame to the schedule: ID 0x30, published by the master, carrying 1 byte with a PWM brightness for the slave’s LED. Use a slot counter 0/1/2 instead of the bool, and add an id == 0x30 branch in slavePoll().
  4. Medium Let the slave also accept c/e from its own Serial Monitor: copy the Serial.available() block of the master into the slave branch of loop().
  5. Challenge Implement LIN “sleep”: when the master sends the diagnostic frame ID 0x3C with first data byte 0x00, the slave turns its LED off and ignores frames until it sees a new break after a pause of more than 1 s.
