Check your understanding

Why is the break at least 13 bits long?

A normal byte can be LOW for at most 9 bit times (start bit + eight 0 data bits, then the stop bit is HIGH). 13 LOW bits can never appear in normal data, so every node recognises the start of a frame without doubt.

Who sends the data bytes of frame 0x20 in this lab, and who decides when it is sent?

The slave publishes the data, but only after the master has sent the header for 0x20. The master alone decides the timing through its schedule table.

What PID does the master send for ID 0x3C?

0x3C: P0 = ID0^ID1^ID2^ID4 = 0^0^1^1 = 0, P1 = NOT(ID1^ID3^ID4^ID5) = NOT(0^1^1^1) = 0, so no parity bits are added.

Why does the master throw away the first byte it receives after the break, while the slave looks for it?

The break produces a 0x00 byte with a framing error in every receiver. The master knows it just sent a break, so that byte is useless to it. For the slave, this 0x00 byte is the signal that a new frame starts.

The PID and checksum functions were checked against known values (ID 0x3C → PID 0x3C; classic checksum of 4A 55 93 E5 = E6). The UART also has a hardware LIN mode (MOD = 1100) that automates break/sync/checksum. This lab builds the frame by hand so every field is visible. Hardware test pending.

26CAN FD controller: frames, filters, loopback, a real bus

The bus used in cars and machines: set the bit timing, send frames through a transmit queue, receive them into a FIFO behind an acceptance filter, and watch the error counters.

applicationCAN 2.0B / CAN FD500 kbit/sbit timingarbitrationmessage RAMfiltersTEC/RECerror confinementPPS

Objectives

  • After this lab you can explain how CAN nodes share two wires, and why the frame with the lowest ID always wins arbitration without losing any time.
  • After this lab you can work out a CAN bit timing (time quanta, TSEG1, TSEG2, SJW, sample point) for 500 kbit/s from a 20 MHz CAN clock.
  • After this lab you can set up the dsPIC33CK CAN FD controller: message RAM, transmit queue, a receive FIFO, one filter and one mask.
  • After this lab you can test CAN code on a single board with internal loopback, then move to a real bus with a transceiver and 120 Ω terminations.
  • After this lab you can read the error counters TEC/REC and say whether a node is error-active, error-passive or bus-off.

Background

What CAN is. CAN (Controller Area Network) is a serial bus that lets many controllers (“nodes”) talk over one twisted pair, called CANH and CANL. A car has dozens of nodes (engine, brakes, doors, dashboard) on a few CAN buses. There is no master: any node may start sending when the bus is idle. A message does not carry a destination address. It carries an identifier (ID) that says what the data is (for example “engine speed”), and every node decides for itself whether it wants that ID. Classic CAN (CAN 2.0) carries 0–8 data bytes per frame. CAN FD (“flexible data rate”) allows up to 64 bytes and a faster data phase. The dsPIC33CK has a CAN FD controller; this lab uses it for classic CAN 2.0 frames with 11-bit IDs.

Dominant and recessive. The transceiver chip turns the controller’s TX logic level into a voltage difference on the pair. A logic 0 is dominant: the transceiver drives CANH up and CANL down. A logic 1 is recessive: the transceiver lets go, and the two 120 Ω terminating resistors pull CANH and CANL together. If one node sends dominant and another recessive at the same time, dominant wins (a “wired-AND”). Every node also listens to the bus while it sends.

Arbitration. When two nodes start a frame at the same moment, both send their ID bit by bit, most significant bit first, and compare what they read back. A node that sends a recessive 1 but reads a dominant 0 knows a more important frame is on the bus, stops sending and becomes a receiver. The winner never notices anything, so no time is lost. Result: the lowest ID has the highest priority. For this to work, two nodes must never send the same ID with different data.

ID bit: 10 9 8 7 6 5 4 ... node A 0x123 : 0 0 1 0 0 1 0 keeps sending (wins) node B 0x150 : 0 0 1 0 1 <-- sends 1 (recessive), reads 0 (dominant): stops, now a receiver bus : 0 0 1 0 0 1 0 ... = node A's frame, undamaged classic CAN data frame (11-bit ID): SOF | ID (11) | RTR | IDE | r0 | DLC (4) | data 0..8 bytes | CRC (15) | ACK | EOF (7) ^ any receiver drives this bit dominant

ACK, CRC and stuffing. Every frame ends with a CRC check. Every receiver that got the frame correctly drives the ACK bit dominant. A sender that sees no ACK knows nobody received the frame and repeats it. That is why a CAN node alone on a bus cannot send successfully, and why this lab starts in loopback, where the controller acknowledges its own frames. After five equal bits in a row the sender adds one opposite “stuff” bit, so there are always edges on the bus for the receivers to synchronise to.

Bit timing. All nodes must agree on the bit rate, here 500 kbit/s, so one bit lasts 2 µs. The controller divides each bit into small steps called time quanta (tq). A bit is: one sync quantum, where an edge is expected, then TSEG1 (propagation + phase 1), then the sample point, where the bit value is read, then TSEG2 (phase 2). SJW (synchronisation jump width) is how many tq the controller may stretch or shrink a bit to stay in step with a node whose clock is slightly different. Here: CAN clock 20 MHz, 1 tq = 50 ns, 40 tq per bit = 2 µs, sample point at 32 / 40 = 80 %.

CAN clock: FVCO 400 MHz / 4 = 100 MHz / 5 = 20 MHz -> 1 tq = 50 ns 1 bit = 40 tq = 2 us = 500 kbit/s |sync|<------------ TSEG1 = 31 tq ------------>|<-- TSEG2 = 8 tq -->| | 1 | ^ sample point (1 + 31) / 40 = 80 % SJW = 8 tq: a bit may be moved by up to 8 tq to follow another node's clock

Error confinement. Each node has a transmit error counter (TEC) and a receive error counter (REC). A detected error adds to the counter (8 for a transmit error), a good frame subtracts 1. Below 128 the node is error-active (healthy, may signal errors loudly). From 96 the controller raises a warning. At 128 or more it becomes error-passive: it still works but signals errors only quietly. When TEC passes 255 the node goes bus-off and disconnects itself. This way one broken node cannot block the whole bus.

TEC / REC 0 .......... 96 .......... 128 .................. 255 | 256 state error-active (warning) error-passive | BUS-OFF (TEC only)

What is special on the dsPIC33CK. The CAN FD controller (CAN1) keeps its transmit and receive buffers in normal data RAM, the message RAM. The program reserves an array (canRam) and tells the controller its address in C1FIFOBA. The controller then uses it as a transmit queue (TXQ, 4 objects here) followed by FIFO1 (8 receive objects). Filters decide which IDs get into which FIFO. The CAN clock comes from the PLL (FVCO/4), so this lab needs Tools > Clock = 100 MIPS; the sketch stops with an #error otherwise. The TX and RX pins are chosen with PPS (peripheral pin select).

Wiring

Step 1 (internal loopback): nothing to wire except the USB-serial adapter on J5. Step 2 (real bus): one transceiver per board.

SignalBoardOther end
CAN TXRC6 = D27 J2-22transceiver TXD
CAN RXRC7 = D28 J3-18transceiver RXD
Transceiver power5V J2-1, GND J2-2VCC / VDD. MCP2562: VDD = 5 V, VIO = 3V3 J3-1
Standby–STBY (or S / RS) → GND = normal mode
BusCANH ↔ CANH, CANL ↔ CANL, 120 Ω between CANH and CANL at both ends
SerialJ5-2 TX, J5-3 RX, J5-4 GNDadapter RX, adapter TX, GND (leave J5-1 open)
3.3 V logic: the transceiver’s RXD drives RC7 directly. Use a transceiver whose logic side runs at 3.3 V (SN65HVD230 is a 3.3 V part, MCP2562 has a separate VIO pin for it). A 5 V-only transceiver would put 5 V on RXD. Connect the grounds of all nodes.

Step by step

  1. Set Tools > Clock = 100 MIPS, upload Lab26_CAN, open the Serial Monitor at 115200. You read the banner and a status line with mode=INTERNAL LOOPBACK. If you see CAN did not enter the requested mode!, the controller did not leave configuration mode (see Troubleshooting).
  2. Watch for a few seconds. Every 500 ms the board sends ID 0x123 and, in internal loopback, receives it back at once. You read one rx id=0x123 dlc=8 : … line every 500 ms, and the USER LED toggles each time, because it follows bit 0 of the counter in byte 0.
  3. Look at the data bytes: byte 0 counts up, bytes 1–2 are the A0 reading (high, low), byte 3 is 1 while the USER button is held, bytes 4–5 are always CA FE. Hold USER: byte 3 becomes 01. Touch A0 (J2-15) or connect it to GND or 3V3: bytes 1–2 change.
  4. Send ? (or e). You read the mode, the TX/RX counters, how often the queue was full, and TEC/REC. TEC=0 REC=0 error-active means a healthy node. Send s to send one extra frame at once.
  5. Power off and wire the transceivers (step 2 table) on two boards, with a 120 Ω resistor at each end. Upload the sketch to both. Both start in loopback and each still sees only its own frames.
  6. Send n on both boards. You read # NORMAL mode - needs another node to ACK and the status line with NORMAL CAN 2.0. In normal mode a controller does not receive its own frames, so each board now prints the other board’s frames, and its LED follows the other board’s counter.
  7. With a USB-CAN adapter on the bus: send ID 0x120 with one data byte 01, then 00. The board’s LED switches on and off: that is CAN remote control. Send an ID outside 0x100–0x1FF (for example 0x220): nothing is printed, because the filter rejects it in hardware.
  8. Send n on one board only, with no other node in normal mode (or unplug the bus). Nobody acknowledges its frames. Send ? a few times: TEC climbs in steps of 8 and the state changes to warning and then error-passive. That is fault confinement at work. Plug the bus back in: every good frame lowers TEC by 1, and the node returns to error-active.
  9. Send l to go back to internal loopback.

Expected output

Lab 26 - CAN 500 kbit/s. TX RC6 (J2-22), RX RC7 (J3-18). n l s e ?
# mode=INTERNAL LOOPBACK  tx=0 (queue full 0)  rx=0  TEC=0 REC=0  error-active
rx id=0x123 dlc=8 : 00 01 FF 00 CA FE 00 00
rx id=0x123 dlc=8 : 01 01 FE 00 CA FE 00 00
# mode=INTERNAL LOOPBACK  tx=1 (queue full 0)  rx=0  TEC=0 REC=0  error-active

Bytes 1–2 (01 FF, 01 FE) are the A0 reading and the counters in the last line are example values: they depend on what is on A0 and on when you send ?. This output was not captured from a running board (see the note at the end).

How the code works

1. Clock check and pins. The sketch refuses to compile at 4 MIPS, because the CAN clock is taken from the PLL.

#if FCY < 50000000UL
#error "Lab26 needs Tools > Clock = 100 MIPS (CAN clock = FVCO/4 from the PLL)"
#endif
const uint8_t CAN_TX_PIN = 27;     /* RC6 */
const uint8_t CAN_RX_PIN = 28;     /* RC7 */
const uint16_t MY_ID = 0x123;

2. Message RAM. The controller’s buffers are a plain array. Each object is 4 words of 32 bits: two header words (ID, then DLC and flags) and 8 data bytes.

#define TXQ_N   4
#define RX_N    8
#define OBJ_W   4                  /* 32-bit words per object: T0, T1, data[0..3], data[4..7] */
static uint32_t canRam[(TXQ_N + RX_N) * OBJ_W] __attribute__((aligned(4)));

3. canBegin(): clock, pins, configuration mode. The module is powered (PMD), given a 20 MHz clock, and its pins are mapped with PPS: output function 21 (CAN1TX) on RC6, and the CAN1RX input reads RC7. TX starts HIGH (recessive) and RX has a pull-up, so a board without a transceiver looks like an idle bus. Then the module is switched on and asked for configuration mode (4), the only mode in which timing and FIFOs may be changed.

PMD1bits.C1MD = 0;                         /* power the module */
CANCLKCONbits.CANCLKSEL = 5;               /* FVCO/4 */
CANCLKCONbits.CANCLKDIV = 4;               /* divide by 5 */
CANCLKCONbits.CANCLKEN = 1;
...
ppsOut(rpTx, 21);
_CAN1RXR = (uint16_t)rpRx;
...
C1CONLbits.CON = 1;                        /* module on (stays in config mode) */
if (!setMode(4)) return false;             /* 4 = configuration mode */

setMode() writes the request into REQOP and waits up to 50 ms until the controller reports the same value in OPMOD. The change only happens at a quiet moment on the bus, so it is not instant.

4. Bit timing. The register fields hold “value − 1”: TSEG1 = 30 means 31 tq, TSEG2 = 7 means 8 tq, BRP = 0 means the 20 MHz clock is divided by 1. The data-phase timing (used only by CAN FD with bit-rate switch) is set to the same values.

C1NBTCFGH = (0u << 8) | 30u;               /* BRP = 0, TSEG1 = 30 */
C1NBTCFGL = (7u << 8) | 7u;                /* TSEG2 = 7, SJW = 7  */

5. TXQ and FIFO1. The base address of canRam goes into C1FIFOBA. The transmit queue gets 4 objects with 8-byte payloads and 3 transmit attempts (TXAT, honoured because RTXAT = 1). FIFO1 is a receive FIFO with 8 objects and an interrupt when it is not empty.

C1TXQCONH = (uint16_t)(((TXQ_N - 1) << 8) | (1u << 5) | 0u);   /* FSIZE, TXAT=01, PRI 0 */
C1TXQCONL = 0x0080;                        /* TXEN must be 1 for the TXQ */
C1FIFOCON1H = (uint16_t)((RX_N - 1) << 8); /* FSIZE, PLSIZE = 8 bytes */
C1FIFOCON1L = 0x0001;                      /* TXEN = 0 (receive), TFNRFNIE: not empty IRQ */

6. Filter and mask. A received ID is accepted when (ID & mask) == (filter & mask). Mask 0x700 compares only ID bits 10–8; filter 0x100 wants them to be 001. So IDs 0x100…0x1FF pass, everything else is dropped by the hardware, without costing CPU time. MIDE makes the filter also check the IDE bit, so only standard 11-bit frames match.

C1FLTOBJ0L = 0x100; C1FLTOBJ0H = 0;        /* SID = 0x100, standard frame */
C1MASK0L   = 0x700; C1MASK0H = (1u << 14); /* compare SID bits 10..8, MIDE: match IDE */
C1FLTCON0L = 0x0080 | 0x01;                /* FLTEN0, buffer pointer = FIFO1 */
ID 0x123 = 001 0010 0011 & 0x700 = 001 0000 0000 = 0x100 -> accepted ID 0x220 = 010 0010 0000 & 0x700 = 010 0000 0000 = 0x200 -> rejected

Finally the CAN interrupt is enabled (priority 3) and the controller is asked for loopback (2) or normal CAN 2.0 (6).

7. Receive interrupt. While FIFO1 is not empty, C1FIFOUA1L tells where the next object is. The interrupt copies ID, DLC and the 8 bytes into a 16-entry ring buffer for loop(), then sets UINC to hand the object back to the controller.

while (C1FIFOSTA1 & 0x0001) {              /* TFNRFNIF: FIFO1 not empty */
    volatile uint32_t *o = objPtr(C1FIFOUA1L);
    uint32_t r0 = o[0], r1 = o[1];
    ...
    f.id = (uint16_t)(r0 & 0x7FF);
    f.dlc = (uint8_t)(r1 & 0x0F);
    ...
    C1FIFOCON1Lbits.UINC = 1;              /* release the object */
}

objPtr() handles an open question: if the value in the “user address” register lies inside canRam it is used as an absolute address, otherwise it is treated as an offset from the base.

8. Sending. canSend() first checks that the queue has a free object (TXQNIF), otherwise it counts a “queue full”. It writes the ID, the DLC and the data (byte 0 in the lowest bits of the first data word), then sets UINC and TXREQ together: “this object is ready, send it”.

o[0] = id & 0x7FF;                         /* T0: SID */
o[1] = (uint32_t)(len & 0x0F);             /* T1: DLC, IDE=0, RTR=0, BRS=0, FDF=0 */
o[2] = d0; o[3] = d1;
C1TXQCONL |= 0x0100 | 0x0200;              /* UINC + TXREQ */

9. Status. status() prints the mode name from OPMOD, the counters, TEC (high byte of C1TRECL) and REC (low byte), and the state from the flags in C1TRECH: bus-off, error-passive, warning or error-active.

10. loop(). Every 500 ms sendNow() builds [counter, A0 high, A0 low, button, 0xCA, 0xFE, 0, 0] and sends it as ID 0x123. Then the ring buffer is emptied and printed. ID 0x120 with byte 0 ≠ 0 switches the LED on; our own ID 0x123 (in loopback, or from another board) sets the LED from bit 0 of byte 0. Finally the commands n l s e ? are handled; a mode change always goes through configuration mode first.

Try it yourself

  1. Easy Give each board its own ID. Two boards that both send 0x123 break the CAN rule “one ID, one sender”: if they start in the same bit, arbitration cannot separate them. Change MY_ID at the top of the sketch to 0x124 on the second board (still inside the filter range).
  2. Easy Send faster: change 500 in if (millis() - last >= 500) in loop() to 10 ms and watch tx= and queue full in the ? output, with and without a second node.
  3. Medium Change the bit rate to 250 kbit/s by setting BRP to 1 (2 × 50 ns per tq) in C1NBTCFGH in canBegin(). All nodes on the bus must be changed, including a USB-CAN adapter.
  4. Medium Accept only ID 0x120 exactly: set C1MASK0L = 0x7FF and C1FLTOBJ0L = 0x120. What happens to the loopback frames 0x123 now, and why?
  5. Challenge Move the sample point to 87.5 % (CiA recommendation for long buses) while keeping 40 tq per bit: choose TSEG1 and TSEG2 so that (1 + TSEG1) / 40 = 0.875, and keep SJW ≤ TSEG2.

Troubleshooting

SymptomLikely causeFix
Compile error Lab26 needs Tools > Clock = 100 MIPSClock menu set to 4 MIPSTools > Clock > 100 MIPS, upload again

Check your understanding

Nodes A (ID 0x100) and B (ID 0x0F0) start a frame at the same moment. Who wins, and is A’s frame lost?

B wins, because the lower ID has the higher priority (its first differing bit is a dominant 0). A notices it lost arbitration, becomes a receiver, and tries again when the bus is free. Nothing is destroyed.

Why does a single board in normal mode show TEC rising?

No other node drives the ACK bit, so every frame ends with an acknowledge error. The sender adds 8 to TEC each time and retries. Loopback mode avoids this, because the controller acknowledges its own frames internally.

With a 20 MHz CAN clock, BRP = 0, TSEG1 = 31 tq, TSEG2 = 8 tq: what is the bit rate and the sample point?

1 + 31 + 8 = 40 tq of 50 ns = 2 µs per bit = 500 kbit/s. The sample point is after 1 + 31 = 32 tq, 32 / 40 = 80 %.

Filter 0x100, mask 0x700. Is ID 0x1A5 accepted? And 0x0A5?

0x1A5 & 0x700 = 0x100, equal to the filter: accepted. 0x0A5 & 0x700 = 0x000: rejected by the hardware before the CPU sees it.

Not verified on hardware: the MPLAB simulator does not run the CAN module (the mode request stays pending), so this lab is compile-verified only. One detail is open: whether CxFIFOUA holds an absolute address or an offset. objPtr() accepts both. If ? still says “configuration”, the mode change did not complete; check CANCLKCON and, for normal mode, the transceiver’s RXD.

2710BASE-T1S single-pair Ethernet (LAN8651 MAC-PHY over SPI)

Put the board on automotive/industrial single-pair Ethernet: 10 Mbit/s over one twisted pair, many nodes on the same wire, collision-free with PLCA, all through an SPI chip.

applicationIEEE 802.3cg10BASE-T1SPLCAOPEN Alliance TC6SPIEthernet framesMAC-PHYparity

Objectives

  • After this lab you can explain what 10BASE-T1S is and how it differs from the Ethernet in your PC (one pair, multidrop, 10 Mbit/s).
  • After this lab you can explain how PLCA gives every node a turn, so that there are no collisions on a shared wire.
  • After this lab you can build OPEN Alliance TC6 control headers (register read/write) and data chunks, including the odd-parity bit.
  • After this lab you can lay out an Ethernet frame (destination MAC, source MAC, EtherType, payload) and send and receive it through a LAN8651.
  • After this lab you can use the footer fields RCA and TXC to know when data is waiting and how much buffer space is free.

Background

Ethernet in one paragraph. Ethernet sends data in frames. Each frame starts with a 6-byte destination MAC address (ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff = “broadcast”, everyone), a 6-byte source MAC address, and a 2-byte EtherType that says what is inside (0x0800 would be IPv4). Then come at least 46 bytes of payload, so a frame is at least 60 bytes, plus a 4-byte check value (FCS) that the MAC hardware adds. The MAC (media access controller) builds and checks frames; the PHY (physical layer) turns bits into signals on the wire.

Ethernet frame as this lab sends it (64 bytes + FCS added by the MAC): 0 6 12 14 64 | dst MAC | src MAC |type| payload: "dsPIC33CK Nano node N count C"\0 ... zeros | FCS | ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff 02:00:00:00:00:N 0x88B5

10BASE-T1S. Office Ethernet uses one cable per device, running to a switch. 10BASE-T1S (IEEE 802.3cg) is Ethernet for cars and machines: 10 Mbit/s on one twisted pair, and multidrop: 8 or more nodes hang on the same pair, like on a CAN bus, with a 100 Ω termination at each end. Sensors and actuators become normal Ethernet devices without a switch.

PLCA. If two nodes on one wire start sending at the same time, their signals collide. Old shared Ethernet detected collisions and retried after a random wait, so the delay was unpredictable. PLCA (Physical Layer Collision Avoidance) solves it with turns. Every node has an ID from 0 to N−1. Node 0, the coordinator, sends a short BEACON. After it, node 0 gets a transmit opportunity, then node 1, node 2 … If a node has nothing to send, its opportunity is skipped after a very short timeout. Then a new beacon starts the next cycle. Only one node may send at a time, so there are no collisions, and the longest wait is known in advance (“deterministic latency”).

10BASE-T1S multidrop: node0 ──┬── node1 ──┬── node2 ... (one twisted pair, 100 ohm at both ends) PLCA cycle: BEACON | TO 0 | TO 1 | TO 2 | ... | TO 7 | BEACON | TO 0 | ... (node 0) ^ node 0 may send here ^ node 1 here TO = transmit opportunity an empty TO is skipped quickly; a node with a frame sends it in its own TO

MAC-PHY and OPEN Alliance TC6. The dsPIC33CK has no Ethernet MAC. The Microchip LAN8650/LAN8651 is a “MAC-PHY”: MAC and PHY in one chip, connected to the microcontroller over plain SPI. The SPI protocol is a standard, OPEN Alliance TC6 (“10BASE-T1x MAC-PHY Serial Interface”). Every SPI transfer begins with a 32-bit header, sent most significant bit first. Bit 31, DNC (data-not-control), says what kind of transfer it is:

  • Control transaction (DNC = 0): read or write registers. The header holds WNR (1 = write), MMS (memory map selector: which register block), the 16-bit address and the length. The MAC-PHY echoes the header one 32-bit word later, so every transfer is one word longer than you would expect.
  • Data transaction (DNC = 1): Ethernet frames move in 64-byte chunks. The host sends a 4-byte header and 64 bytes; at the same time it receives 64 bytes and a 4-byte footer. A frame is cut into chunks: SV (start valid) marks the first, EV (end valid) plus EBO (end byte offset, index of the last valid byte) the last. In the footer, RCA (receive chunks available) says how many RX chunks wait in the chip, and TXC (transmit credits) how many free TX chunk buffers there are.
CONTROL host -> [hdr: DNC=0 HDRB WNR AID MMS(4) ADDR(16) LEN(7) P] [data] [0 ] chip -> [ ... ] [echo] [value ] DATA host -> [hdr: DNC=1 ... DV SV SWO EV EBO ... P] [64 bytes TX ...........] chip -> [64 bytes RX ...........] [footer: EXST HDRB SYNC RCA DV SV SWO EV EBO TXC P]

Parity. The last bit (P) of every header and footer makes the number of 1 bits in the 32-bit word odd. If one bit is damaged on the wire, the count becomes even and the receiver knows the word is bad. The MAC-PHY reports a bad header with the HDRB bit in its footer.

You need

PartQtyNotes
dsPIC33CK Nano board2 (or 1 + USB adapter)Tools > Clock: 100 MIPS recommended
USB-C power supply / cable1 per boardUSB-C is power only
3.3 V USB-serial adapter1 per boardon J5, Serial Monitor at 115200
LAN8651 MAC-PHY board1 per Nano boarde.g. MikroE Two-Wire ETH Click (LAN8651, 3.3 V)
Twisted pair1between the two clicks; 100 Ω termination at both ends (click jumpers)
10BASE-T1S USB adapter (optional)1e.g. Microchip EVB-LAN8670-USB, with Wireshark on a PC
Jumper wires8 per board–

Wiring

LAN8651 clickBoardNotes
SCKRC4 J3-6SPI1 clock
SDI (MOSI)RC5 J3-5data to the MAC-PHY
SDO (MISO)RC8 J3-14data from the MAC-PHY
CSRC9 = D30 J3-13chip select, driven by the sketch
IRQ (active low)RB7 = D12 J3-9LOW when data is waiting or on an error
RSTRD8 = D36 J3-12hardware reset, LOW = reset
3V3 / GNDJ3-1 / J3-23.3 V supply
SerialJ5-2 TX, J5-3 RX, J5-4 GNDadapter RX, adapter TX, GND (leave J5-1 open)
T1S pair: N–N, P–P between the clicks; 100 Ω termination at both ends of the pair.

Step by step

  1. Wire one click to board A and upload Lab27_10BaseT1S with the USER button released. You read the banner and OA_ID / OA_PHYID. A PHY ID that is not 0 and not 0xFFFFFFFF means SPI and the MAC-PHY are working. If you read no MAC-PHY answering, the LED blinks fast and the sketch stops there.
  2. Next you read STATUS0. If it adds (RESETC set: reset complete), the chip finished its reset; the sketch then writes the value back to clear the status bits.
  3. The last start-up line is # PLCA node 0 of 8 (coordinator). Board A is the coordinator and sends the PLCA beacons.
  4. From now on board A prints a line # tx … rx … credits … chunk errors … once a second: it sends one broadcast frame per second. chunk errors 0 means the MAC-PHY accepted every header (parity correct).
  5. Wire board B the same way and connect the two clicks with the twisted pair (N–N, P–P, terminations on). Hold USER on board B while pressing RESET, release it after the banner. Board B prints # PLCA node 1 of 8 and its MAC address ends in 01.
  6. Now each board prints the other’s frames: rx 64 B from 02:00:00:00:00:01 type 0x88B5 "dsPIC33CK Nano node 1 count 7". The counter in the text goes up by one each second. The USER LED switches on when a frame arrives and off when the board sends.
  7. Watch rx grow on both boards. If board B is reset without USER held, both are node 0: two coordinators on one wire break the PLCA schedule, and frames may be lost.
  8. Optional: connect a 10BASE-T1S USB adapter to the pair and start Wireshark on its network interface. You see the same frames as real Ethernet, with EtherType 0x88B5 and the text in the payload.

Expected output

Lab 27 - 10BASE-T1S via LAN8651 (OPEN Alliance TC6 over SPI)
# OA_ID=0x..  OA_PHYID=0x........   (non-zero = MAC-PHY answering; exact values per LAN8651 datasheet)
# STATUS0=0x..  (RESETC set: reset complete)
# PLCA node 0 of 8 (coordinator)
rx 64 B from 02:00:00:00:00:01 type 0x88B5  "dsPIC33CK Nano node 1 count 7"
# tx 8  rx 7  credits 31  chunk errors 0

The register values depend on the chip and the counters on how long it runs (example values). Nothing here was captured from real hardware.

How the code works

1. Pins and register addresses. CS, IRQ and RST are plain digital pins; SCK, MOSI and MISO belong to the SPI library. Each register is named by its memory map (MMS) and address.

const uint8_t PIN_CS  = 30;   /* RC9 = SS */
const uint8_t PIN_IRQ = 12;   /* RB7 */
const uint8_t PIN_RST = 36;   /* RD8 */
...
#define MMS_OA   0
#define MMS_MAC  1
#define MMS_VS   4
...
#define VS_PLCA_CTRL0  0xCA01   /* EN bit 15 */
#define VS_PLCA_CTRL1  0xCA02   /* NCNT[15:8] | ID[7:0] */

2. Odd parity. withParity() folds the 32 bits onto each other with XOR until bit 0 holds the parity of the whole word, then sets bit 0 so that the total number of 1s is odd.

h &= ~1UL;
uint32_t x = h; x ^= x >> 16; x ^= x >> 8; x ^= x >> 4; x ^= x >> 2; x ^= x >> 1;
return h | ((~x) & 1UL);

3. Control header and register access. ctrlHeader() puts WNR in bit 29, MMS in bits 27–24, the address in bits 23–8 and the length (minus 1) in bits 7–1. A read sends the header, then two empty words: during the first the echo of the header comes back, during the second the register value. A write sends the header, the value, and one more word to clock out the echo.

uint32_t regRead(uint8_t mms, uint16_t addr)
{
    ...
    digitalWrite(PIN_CS, LOW);
    xfer32(ctrlHeader(false, mms, addr, 0));
    xfer32(0);                                       /* echoed header comes back here */
    uint32_t v = xfer32(0);                          /* register value */
    digitalWrite(PIN_CS, HIGH);
    ...
}

4. One data chunk. dataChunk() sends a data header (DNC = 1; DV, SV, EV and EBO only when there is TX data), 64 bytes out and 64 bytes in, and then reads the footer. If HDRB is set, the chip rejected our header and the chunk is counted as an error. Otherwise RCA and TXC are saved. If the footer says the chunk carries RX data (DV), the valid bytes are collected into rxFrame from the start word offset (SWO × 4) to the end byte offset; on EV the complete frame goes to handleFrame().

uint32_t h = 1UL << 31;                          /* DNC = 1: data */
if (tx) {
    h |= 1UL << 21;                              /* DV: this chunk carries TX data */
    if (sv) h |= 1UL << 20;                      /* SV: start of frame, SWO = 0 */
    if (ev) { h |= 1UL << 14; h |= (uint32_t)(ebo & 0x3F) << 8; }   /* EV + EBO */
}
...
if (f & (1UL << 30)) { chunkErrors++; return; }  /* header bad (parity) */
rxAvail   = (uint8_t)((f >> 24) & 0x1F);
txCredits = (uint8_t)((f >> 1) & 0x1F);

SPI is full duplex, so sending and receiving happen in the same transfer: a TX chunk can bring back an RX chunk at the same time.

5. Sending a frame. sendFrame() pads the frame to the Ethernet minimum of 60 bytes and cuts it into 64-byte chunks. The first gets SV, the last gets EV with EBO = number of bytes in it − 1. The 64-byte frame of this lab fits into one chunk, which carries both SV and EV.

6. macPhyInit(). The order of the start-up:

  1. pulse RST low for 5 ms, wait 10 ms, start SPI at 10 MHz, mode 0, MSB first;
  2. read OA_ID and OA_PHYID, give up if the PHY ID is 0 or 0xFFFFFFFF;
  3. read OA_STATUS0, report RESETC (bit 6), write the value back to clear it;
  4. write the MAC address 02:00:00:00:00:<node> into MAC_SAB1/MAC_SAT1 (“02” marks a locally administered address);
  5. write node count 8 and the node ID into PLCA_CTRL1, then enable PLCA in PLCA_CTRL0;
  6. set SYNC (bit 15) in OA_CONFIG0: “the host has finished configuring”;
  7. enable the MAC transmitter and receiver in MAC_NCR.
regWrite(MMS_VS, VS_PLCA_CTRL1, ((uint32_t)NODE_COUNT << 8) | nodeId);
regWrite(MMS_VS, VS_PLCA_CTRL0, 1UL << 15);      /* PLCA enable */
uint32_t c0 = regRead(MMS_OA, OA_CONFIG0);
regWrite(MMS_OA, OA_CONFIG0, c0 | (1UL << 15));
regWrite(MMS_MAC, MAC_NCR, (1UL << 3) | (1UL << 2));

7. setup() reads the USER button once: held = node 1, released = node 0. loop() first checks IRQ: when it is LOW, or the last footer reported waiting chunks (RCA > 0), it runs an empty data chunk to fetch them. Once a second it builds the broadcast frame with the text, sends it, switches the LED off and prints the counters.

if (digitalRead(PIN_IRQ) == LOW || rxAvail > 0) dataChunk(NULL, false, false, 0);
...
f[12] = 0x88; f[13] = 0xB5;                  /* local experimental EtherType */
snprintf(msg, sizeof(msg), "dsPIC33CK Nano node %u count %lu", nodeId, count++);
memcpy(f + 14, msg, strlen(msg) + 1);
sendFrame(f, 64);

8. handleFrame() prints the length, the source MAC (bytes 6–11) and the EtherType (bytes 12–13). For EtherType 0x88B5 it also prints the text from byte 14 up to the first zero byte and switches the LED on.

Key registers

These are registers of the LAN8651, reached over SPI with TC6 control transactions, not dsPIC registers.

Register / bitValue usedMeaning
OA_ID (MMS 0, 0x0000)readOPEN Alliance version of the TC6 interface
OA_PHYID (MMS 0, 0x0001)readPHY identifier; 0 or 0xFFFFFFFF = nobody answering
OA_STATUS0 (MMS 0, 0x0008) bit 6read, written backRESETC: reset complete; the status bits are write-1-to-clear
OA_CONFIG0 (MMS 0, 0x0004) bit 151SYNC: host configuration done, the MAC-PHY may start data transfers
OA_STDCAP, OA_RESET, OA_BUFSTS (0x0002, 0x0003, 0x000B)–defined in the sketch, not used
MAC_NCR (MMS 1, 0x0000)0x0000000Cnetwork control: TXEN (bit 3) and RXEN (bit 2)
MAC_SAB1 (MMS 1, 0x0022)0x00000002MAC address bytes 0–3 (02:00:00:00)
MAC_SAT1 (MMS 1, 0x0023)node << 8MAC address bytes 4–5 (00:<node>)
PLCA_CTRL1 (MMS 4, 0xCA02)0x0800 | nodeNCNT = 8 nodes (bits 15–8), this node’s ID (bits 7–0)
PLCA_CTRL0 (MMS 4, 0xCA01) bit 151PLCA enable
TC6 header and footer fields used
header bit 31 DNC0 / 1control / data transaction
control: bit 29 WNR, bits 27–24 MMS, 23–8 ADDR, 7–1 LEN–write-not-read, memory map, address, number of registers − 1
data header: bit 21 DV, 20 SV, 14 EV, 13–8 EBO–TX data valid, start of frame, end of frame, last valid byte in this chunk
footer: bit 30 HDRBreadthe chip received a bad header (counted as chunk error)
footer: bits 28–24 RCA, 5–1 TXCreadRX chunks waiting / free TX chunk buffers
footer: bit 21 DV, 20 SV, 19–16 SWO, 14 EV, 13–8 EBOreadRX data in this chunk, frame start and its word offset, frame end and its byte offset
bit 0 Pcomputedodd parity over the 32-bit word

Try it yourself

  1. Easy Change the text: edit the snprintf(msg, ...) line in loop(). Keep it under 40 characters (size of msg), and remember the frame is 64 bytes, with the text starting at byte 14.
  2. Easy Send twice a second: change 1000 in if (millis() - last >= 1000). Watch credits: does it ever drop?
  3. Medium Add a third node: in setup() choose node 2 another way (for example a jumper from a free pin to GND), and check that all three see each other. NODE_COUNT is already 8.
  4. Medium Unicast: send to the other node’s MAC (02:00:00:00:00:01) instead of ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff by changing the first 6 bytes of f[] in loop().
  5. Challenge Send a frame longer than 64 bytes (for example 200 bytes, so 4 chunks) with sendFrame(), and check on the other node that rx reports the full length.

Troubleshooting

SymptomLikely causeFix
no MAC-PHY answering, LED blinks fastSPI wiring, CS, RST or powerCheck SCK J3-6, MOSI J3-5, MISO J3-14, CS J3-13, RST J3-12, 3V3 J3-1; MOSI goes to the click’s SDI
chunk errors risingBad SPI signal (long wires) or wrong header bitsShorter wires; lower the SPI clock in macPhyInit() (SPISettings(10000000UL, ...))
tx rises, the other node shows no rxPair not connected, N/P swapped, terminations missing, both nodes ID 0N–N, P–P; terminations on; reset board B with USER held
Start-up runs but nothing ever arrivesRegister addresses or init writes differ from this LAN8651Compare with Microchip’s lan865x driver / application note (see the note below)
Wireshark shows nothingAdapter not on the same pair or not in PLCA mode with a free node IDGive the adapter a node ID that the boards do not use

Check your understanding

Why can PLCA promise a maximum delay, while old shared Ethernet could not?

With PLCA each node sends only in its own transmit opportunity, in a fixed order after the coordinator’s beacon. There are no collisions and no random back-off, so the longest wait is one full cycle.

Why does regRead() clock out three 32-bit words instead of two?

The MAC-PHY answers one word late: during the second word it echoes the header, and only during the third word the register value comes out.

A 64-byte frame is sent in one chunk. Which flags and which EBO does its header carry?

DV (data valid), SV (start of frame) and EV (end of frame), all in the same chunk, with EBO = 63, the index of the last valid byte.

What does a footer with RCA = 3 tell the host?

Three received chunks are waiting in the MAC-PHY. The host should run more data transactions (here empty ones from loop()) to read them.

Not verified on hardware: written from the OPEN Alliance TC6 specification and the LAN865x register map as I know it. Check the register addresses (OA_PHYID, PLCA_CTRL0/1 in MMS 4, MAC NCR) and Microchip’s recommended LAN8651 initialisation writes (their lan865x driver / application note) before relying on it. The sketch prints each step so you can see where it stops.

29Line follower robot: servo drive + Bluetooth (HC-05) remote

Build a small robot: two continuous-rotation servos as wheels, five IR sensors that find a black line, a PD controller that steers, and a phone that drives and tunes it over Bluetooth.

applicationNanoServoSCCP dual-edge compare50 Hz servo pulsesIR reflectance arraycalibrationPD controlHC-05Serial2command parser

Objectives

  • After this lab you can drive continuous-rotation servos with hardware-made pulses (NanoServo), find their stop point and set a trim.
  • After this lab you can calibrate five IR reflectance sensors and turn them into one smooth “where is the line” number.
  • After this lab you can explain a PD controller and tune its two gains on a real track, step by step.
  • After this lab you can use an HC-05 Bluetooth module as a wireless serial cable on Serial2, and set its name and baud rate with AT commands.
  • After this lab you can write a command parser that takes single letters from an RC app and text commands from a terminal.

Background

Servo pulses. A hobby servo reads one pulse every 20 ms (50 Hz). In a normal (positional) servo the pulse width sets the angle: 1.0 ms = one end, 2.0 ms = the other end, 1.5 ms = the middle. A continuous-rotation servo has no end stops; the same pulse is read as a speed: about 1.5 ms = stop, 1.0 ms = full speed one way, 2.0 ms = full speed the other way. Each servo stops at a slightly different width, so each one gets a trim, its own stop point. When the pulses stop completely, a continuous servo stands still whatever its trim; that is how the sketch stops the wheels.

servo pulse, every 20 ms: ___|¯¯¯|_______________________|¯¯¯|____ 1.0 ms .. 1.5 ms (stop) .. 2.0 ms SCCP timer 0 ............ RB ...................... PRL (20 ms) output HIGH at 0, LOW at RB wheels: left = trimL + dirL * speed% * 5 us right = trimR + dirR * speed% * 5 us speed 100 % = trim +- 500 us; dirL = +1, dirR = -1 (the wheels face opposite ways)

The two wheels are mirror images: to roll forward, one servo turns clockwise and the other anticlockwise. So “forward” is a longer pulse on one side and a shorter one on the other.

Making the pulses on the dsPIC33CK. The NanoServo library gives each servo its own SCCP module (a timer with compare outputs) in dual-edge compare mode. The timer counts a 20 ms frame; the output goes HIGH at 0 and LOW when the timer reaches the RB value. The hardware makes every pulse by itself: no interrupts, no jitter. A new width is buffered until the next frame starts. The prescaler is chosen so that 20 ms fits the 16-bit timer: 1:64 at 100 MIPS (0.64 µs steps), 1:4 at 4 MIPS (1 µs). The library hands out SCCP3, then 2, then 1, then 4, so tone() (SCCP4) keeps working with up to 3 servos. The output reaches the pin through PPS, so any remappable pin works (RA0–RA4 have no PPS).

Line sensors. A TCRT5000 is an infrared LED and a phototransistor side by side, looking down. A light floor reflects much IR, black tape very little, so the analog output changes over the line. Each sensor is a bit different and the light changes with height, so the sketch calibrates: it records each sensor’s lowest and highest reading while the robot sweeps over the line, and scales each sensor to 0…1000 (1000 = on the line). Then the weighted average gives the line position:

sensors (seen from above) S1 S2 S3 S4 S5 value 0..1000 after calibration (1000 = line) weights 0 1000 2000 3000 4000 position = sum(v*w) / sum(v) = 2000 when centred example: S3 = 1000, S4 = 500, others 0 -> (2000*1000 + 3000*500) / 1500 = 2333 (between S3 and S4)

With two sensors partly on the line the result lands in between, so the position is smooth, not just 5 steps. When no sensor sees the line, the robot keeps turning to the side where it was last seen; after 1.5 s it gives up and stops.

PD control. The error e is how far the line is from the middle, scaled to −100 (far left) … +100 (far right). The P (proportional) part turns harder the bigger the error. With P alone the robot overshoots and swings from side to side. The D (derivative) part looks at how fast the error changes (e − e_last) and brakes the turn when the robot is already swinging back, which damps the wobble. Every 10 ms:

error e = (position - 2000) / 20 -> turn = kp*e + kd*(e - e_last) left wheel = base + turn right wheel = base - turn every 10 ms

Tuning rule: start with kd = 0, raise kp until the robot follows but wobbles, then add kd until the wobble goes away, then raise the speed. The sketch keeps the gains as integers × 100 (kp 1.25 is stored as 125), so there is no floating point in the 100 Hz loop.

HC-05 Bluetooth. The HC-05 is a transparent serial link: once a phone is paired and connected, what the app sends comes out of the module’s TXD pin, and what the board writes to its RXD goes to the phone. To the program it is just Serial2 (UART2, via the NanoSerial2 library) at 9600 baud. Its optional STATE pin is HIGH while a phone is connected. Name, PIN and baud rate are set with AT commands in its AT mode, which runs at 38400 baud.

You need

PartQtyNotes
dsPIC33CK Nano board1Tools > Clock: 100 MIPS or 4 MIPS (both work)
2-wheel robot chassis with a caster1–
Continuous-rotation servo2FS90R, SG90-360, MG90-360 …
5-channel IR line sensor, analog outputs1TCRT5000 array, powered from 3.3 V
HC-05 Bluetooth module1with STATE pin (optional use)
4 × AA battery holder14.8–6 V, for the servos and the board
Passive piezo1 (optional)beeps and the V horn
3.3 V USB-serial adapter1on J5, Serial Monitor at 115200, “Newline” or “Both NL & CR”
USB-C cable1may stay plugged in (power only)
Phone with a Bluetooth app1e.g. “Serial Bluetooth Terminal” or “Bluetooth RC Controller”
Black electrical tape1 rollabout 19 mm wide, on a light floor for the track

Wiring

PartPinBoard
HC-05TXDRB10 = D15 J2-4 (Serial2 RX)
RXDRB11 = D16 J2-5 (Serial2 TX, 3.3 V logic, no divider needed)
STATE (optional)RB12 = D17 J2-6: HIGH while a phone is connected
VCC / GND5V J2-1 / GND J2-2 (the module has its own 3.3 V regulator)
IR arrayOUT1 … OUT5A0…A4 = RA0…RA4 J2-15…J2-19, OUT1 = leftmost (robot seen from above, driving away from you)
VCC / GND3V3 J3-1 / GND. Not 5 V: RA0–RA4 are not 5 V tolerant.
Left servosignal (orange / yellow)RB0 = D5 J3-21

Power: the board’s MCP1703 regulator takes up to 16 V on the 5V pin, and the Schottky diode on USB-C keeps the battery out of the USB cable. So the battery can feed the board through J2-1 while USB-C stays plugged in for the Serial Monitor. Do not run the servos from USB: one stalled servo draws about 0.7 A. Connect all grounds together.
3.3 V on the sensor inputs: power the IR array from 3V3 (J3-1), never from 5 V. RA0–RA4 are not 5 V tolerant, and a 5 V-powered array can put 5 V on them.

Step by step

  1. Bench test first, wheels in the air. Upload Lab29_LineFollower and open the Serial Monitor (115200, “Newline”). It prints Robot ready and beeps once (if a piezo is fitted). The LED blinks slowly (IDLE) and the servos are silent: no pulses at all. Send ? to see the gains, trims and directions.
  2. Find each servo’s stop point. Type pulse l 1500. If the left wheel still creeps, try pulse l 1490, pulse l 1510 … until it stands still. Then type trim l 1490 (your value, allowed 1300–1700). Do the same for the right wheel, then send S. The LED is on steadily while in MANUAL mode.
  3. Check the directions. F should turn both wheels forward. If one turns backwards, type dir l or dir r. Try B, L, R, and 3 … 9 to change the speed (0–90 %, q = 100 %). S stops.
  4. Sensors. Hold the robot over the tape and type sensors: the sensor over the line reads clearly different from the others. Mount the array 3–8 mm above the floor. Move the tape under the array and watch pos go from about 0 (left) through 2000 (centre) to 4000 (right).
  5. Bluetooth. Pair the phone with HC-05 (PIN 1234 or 0000), open the app, connect. The same letters now work from the phone, and the replies appear on both the phone and the Serial Monitor. With an RC app the arrow buttons send F/B/L/R/G/I/H/J and the slider sends 0…9 / q.
  6. Calibrate. Put the robot on the track with the middle sensor over the line, then send C. For 4 s it turns right, left and right again over the line, recording each sensor’s darkest and brightest value. It also works out whether the line reads HIGH or LOW. A sensor marked weak sees too little difference (less than 100): check its height and wiring.
  7. Follow. Send X (or press USER). The LED blinks fast. Start slow, with base 35, and tune: kd 0, raise kp until it follows the line but wobbles, then add kd (1…6) until the wobble is gone. Then raise base. Type tel to watch position, error and wheel speeds on the Serial Monitor (5 lines per second).
  8. Stop following with x, D or the USER button. (S only stops manual driving; RC apps send it all the time.)
  9. Safety: lift the robot off the line: after 1.5 s it gives up (line lost) and stops. Disconnect the phone: if STATE is wired, it stops at once. dead 500 stops manual driving when the app sends nothing for 0.5 s.
  10. Optional, HC-05 set-up: hold USER while pressing RESET. The LED blinks fast and the board bridges the Serial Monitor to the HC-05 at 38400. Power the HC-05 up with its button held, set “Both NL & CR”, type AT (answer OK), then AT+NAME=dsPIC-Robot, AT+PSWD="1234" (older firmware: AT+PSWD=1234), AT+UART=9600,0,0. Press RESET to leave.

Expected output

Lab 29 - line follower robot (servos + HC-05)
Robot ready. C = calibrate, X = follow, F/B/L/R/S = drive, help = all commands
mode CALIBRATE - line reads HIGH
  S1 min 61 max 903
  S2 min 58 max 911
  S3 min 64 max 897
  S4 min 60 max 905
  S5 min 59 max 899

The sensor and telemetry numbers depend on your sensors, track and gains (example values). And the reply to ? with the default settings, before any servo was driven:

IDLE kp 0.90 kd 3.00 base 45% man 60%
trim L 1500 R 1500  dir L 1 R -1  line HIGH  dead 0
BT no STATE  servo SCCP L0 R0

While a servo runs, SCCP L3 R2 shows which SCCP module drives it (0 = detached).

How the code works

1. Pins and tuning values. All settings that commands can change are plain globals at the top. Gains are × 100.

const uint8_t PIN_SERVO_L  = 5;     /* RB0, J3-21 */
const uint8_t PIN_SERVO_R  = 6;     /* RB1, J3-20 */
const uint8_t PIN_BT_RX    = 15;    /* RB10, J2-4  <- HC-05 TXD */
const uint8_t PIN_BT_TX    = 16;    /* RB11, J2-5  -> HC-05 RXD */
...
int16_t kp100   = 90;       /* kp = 0.90 */
int16_t kd100   = 300;      /* kd = 3.00 */
int16_t baseSpd = 45;       /* % while following */
...
const int16_t SPAN_US = 500;            /* 100 % = trim +- 500 us */

2. setup(). STATE gets a pull-down, so an unwired STATE pin reads LOW. If USER is held at start, atBridge() runs and never returns: it copies bytes both ways between Serial and Serial2 at 38400. Otherwise Serial2 starts at 9600 on RB10/RB11, the motors are switched off, and the board says “Robot ready” on both ports.

CNPDBbits.CNPDB12 = 1;           /* pull-down: STATE not wired reads LOW */
...
if (digitalRead(BUTTON_BUILTIN) == LOW) atBridge();     /* never returns */
Serial2.begin(BT_BAUD, PIN_BT_RX, PIN_BT_TX);

3. Wheels. drive() takes two speeds in % (−100…100), attaches the servos the first time (allowed range 900–2100 µs) and writes trim ± up to 500 µs. motorsOff() detaches both: no pulses, the wheels stand still.

if (!servoL.attached()) servoL.attach(PIN_SERVO_L, 1000 - 100, 2000 + 100);
...
servoL.writeMicroseconds(trimL + dirL * (int16_t)((long)outL * SPAN_US / 100));
servoR.writeMicroseconds(trimR + dirR * (int16_t)((long)outR * SPAN_US / 100));

Example: F at 60 % with trim L 1490 gives 1490 + 300 = 1790 µs on the left and 1500 − 300 = 1200 µs on the right.

4. Sensors. readSensors() scales each reading between its calibrated min and max to 0…1000, inverts it if the line reads LOW, and builds the weighted average. Values up to 50 are ignored as floor noise; at least one sensor above 300 means “on the line”. If the line is lost, the position is set fully to the side where it was last seen, so the controller keeps turning that way.

long v = (long)(raw[i] - calMin[i]) * 1000L / span;
...
if (!lineHigh) v = 1000 - v;
...
if (v > 300) onLine = true;
if (v > 50) { sum += v; wsum += v * i * 1000L; }   /* ignore floor noise */
...
position = position > 2000 ? (NSENS - 1) * 1000 : 0;

5. Calibration. calibrateStart() compares the middle sensor (on the line) with the two outer ones (on the floor) to decide whether the line reads HIGH or LOW, and resets min/max. calibrateStep() runs every 10 ms for 4 s: it updates min/max of each sensor and spins right 1 s, left 2 s, right 1 s, so the robot ends facing where it started. Then it prints each sensor’s range and flags any span under 100 as weak.

lineHigh = raw[NSENS / 2] > (raw[0] + raw[NSENS - 1]) / 2;
...
if      (t < 1000) drive( 35, -35);
else if (t < 3000) drive(-35,  35);
else if (t < 4000) drive( 35, -35);

6. PD step. followStep() runs every 10 ms in FOLLOW mode. It stops after 1.5 s without a line, computes the error and the turn with integer maths, limits the turn to ±200, and drives the wheels. drive() then clamps each wheel to ±100 %.

int16_t e = (int16_t)((position - (NSENS - 1) * 500) / 20);   /* -100..100 */
long turn = ((long)kp100 * e + (long)kd100 * (e - lastErr)) / 100L;
lastErr = e;
...
drive(baseSpd + (int16_t)turn, baseSpd - (int16_t)turn);

7. Command parser. Characters from both ports go through feed(), one line buffer per port. An upper-case letter, a digit or ? as the first character acts at once, because RC apps send them without Enter. A lower-case letter starts a word command such as kp 1.2, which waits for Enter and goes to lineCmd(). RC apps also send q x v w u alone without Enter, so if one of those is followed by nothing for 150 ms, it acts by itself.

if (in.len == 1 && now - in.t > 150 && strchr("qxvwu", in.buf[0])) {
    singleChar(in.buf[0]);
...
if (in.len == 0 && !(c >= 'a' && c <= 'z')) {     /* immediate */
    if (c != ' ') singleChar((char)c);

singleChar() maps the letters to wheel speeds (spins at 2/3 of the manual speed, curves with one wheel at 1/3). parse100() turns "1.25" into 125 without floating point, and fix100() prints 125 as "1.25". say() sends every reply to both the Serial Monitor and the phone.

8. loop(). In order: feed one character from each port to the parser; stop if STATE goes from HIGH to LOW (a phone disconnected; an unwired pin never makes that edge); toggle following on a USER press (30 ms debounce); every 10 ms run the PD step, the calibration step, or the deadman check; every 200 ms print telemetry to USB only (Bluetooth writing at 9600 baud is blocking, about 1 ms per character); and set the LED pattern: IDLE slow blink, MANUAL on, FOLLOW fast blink, CALIBRATE very fast.

bool st = digitalRead(PIN_BT_STATE);
if (lastState && !st && mode != IDLE) setMode(IDLE, "Bluetooth disconnected");
...
if (now - tick >= 10) {
    tick = now;
    if (mode == FOLLOW) followStep(now);
    else if (mode == CALIB) calibrateStep(now);
    ...

Check your understanding

Why does the sketch stop the wheels with detach() instead of writing the trim value?

With no pulses at all, a continuous-rotation servo stands still whatever its stop point is. Writing the trim only stops it if the trim is exactly right.

Calibrated values: S2 = 600, S3 = 600, the others 0. What is the position, and the error e?

(1000 × 600 + 2000 × 600) / 1200 = 1500. e = (1500 − 2000) / 20 = −25: the line is a bit to the left.

With kd = 0 the robot wobbles. What does adding kd do?

The D part reacts to how fast the error changes. When the robot swings back towards the line, e − e_last has the opposite sign of e, so the turn is reduced before it overshoots. That damps the wobble.

Why are upper-case letters acted on at once, but kp 1.2 waits for Enter?

RC apps send single letters without a line ending, so they must act immediately. Word commands start with a lower-case letter and need several characters, so the parser collects them until Enter.

Verified in the MPLAB simulator: command parsing (kp, kd, trim, base clamped to 100 %), the servo pulses (F at 60 % with trim 1490 gives exactly 1790 µs on the left and 1200 µs on the right, a 20 ms frame, PPS RB0 = OCM3 and RB1 = OCM2), and the “line lost” stop after 1.5 s. Not tested on hardware: the real servo, sensor and HC-05 behaviour, and the gains. The defaults (kp 0.90, kd 3.00, base 45) are a starting point, so tune them on your track.

30PID temperature control

Hold a heater at a set temperature with a PID controller. See what P, I and D each do, tune it by hand, let the relay autotune find the gains, and watch it all as curves in the Serial Plotter. No parts? The sketch has a built-in simulated heater.

applicationPIDclosed loopanti-windupderivative on measurementrelay autotuneZiegler-NicholsPWM heaterMOSFETMCP9700ASerial Plotter

Objectives

  • After this lab you can explain the difference between open-loop and closed-loop (feedback) control.
  • After this lab you can say what the P, I and D parts of a PID controller each do, and what goes wrong without each of them.
  • After this lab you can tune a PID by hand and with the relay autotune method, and read the result in the Serial Plotter.
  • After this lab you can explain integral windup and derivative kick, and how this code avoids them.
  • After this lab you can switch a power load (a heater) with a logic-level MOSFET and PWM, and add a safety cut-off.

Background

Open loop vs closed loop. If you switch the heater on at a fixed 30 % (open loop), the temperature rises and levels off somewhere. Where it ends depends on the room temperature, a draught, the supply voltage. A closed-loop controller measures the temperature all the time and adjusts the power so that the measurement stays at the setpoint (the temperature you want). The difference between the two is the error: e = setpoint − temperature.

+--------------------------- controller ---------------------------+ setpoint -->(+)-- e --> P + I + D --> power 0..100 % --> PWM D5 --> MOSFET --> 10 ohm heater ^ - | | heat flows into the sensor +---- temperature <---- ADC A0 <---- MCP9700A <-----------------+

P – proportional, "now". P = kp × e. Far below the setpoint, a big error gives a lot of power; close to it, little power. P alone always leaves a small error, because some power is needed just to hold the temperature against the losses, and P gives power only while there is an error. This is the steady-state error. A very large kp makes the temperature swing up and down: the heat needs time to reach the sensor, so by the time the sensor sees the change it is already too late.

I – integral, "the past". I = I + ki × e × dt adds up the error over time. As long as the temperature is a little too low, I keeps growing until the power is exactly right; then e = 0 and I stays where it is. That removes the steady-state error. Too much ki makes it slow to settle and causes overshoot.

D – derivative, "the future". D looks at how fast the temperature changes. When it is rising fast towards the setpoint, D takes power away before the setpoint is reached, so it does not overshoot. Here it is D = −kd × d(temperature)/dt.

Two traps, and how the code avoids them.

  • Integral windup: during the warm-up the output is stuck at 100 % for minutes, and a plain I would keep growing all that time. When the temperature finally arrives, the huge I takes a long time to shrink, and the temperature overshoots badly. The fix is anti-windup: while the output is at a limit, I does not grow further in that direction.
  • Derivative kick: if D used the error, then changing the setpoint from 50 to 60 °C would make the error jump, and D would give one huge spike. Taking D from the measurement (which never jumps) avoids that. The measurement is also noisy, so D is low-pass filtered: it follows changes with a time constant of 2 s.

Autotune (relay method, Åström–Hägglund). Instead of guessing the gains, the controller can measure the system. It switches the power to 100 % below the setpoint and to 0 % above it, like a thermostat. The temperature then swings up and down around the setpoint with a regular period. From the size of the swing a (°C) and its period Pu (s), the ultimate gain is Ku = 4d / (π a), where d = 50 % is half the power step. Ku is the gain at which a P controller alone would oscillate. Tuning rules turn Ku and Pu into gains; this sketch uses the gentle Ziegler–Nichols "some overshoot" rule: kp = 0.33 Ku, ki = kp / (Pu/2), kd = kp × Pu/3.

Units in this lab. The error is in °C and the output in %, so kp is "% power per °C", ki is "% per °C per second", and kd is "% per (°C per second)". With the default kp = 8, an error of 5 °C gives 40 % from the P part.

On the dsPIC33CK. The heater is driven with analogWrite() on D5 = RB0, about 490 Hz PWM from SCCP1 (Lab 05). A thermal system is slow (time constants of a minute), so 490 Hz PWM looks like smooth power to it. The MCP9700A gives 0.5 V + 10 mV/°C, read with the 10-bit ADC: one step is 3.2 mV = 0.32 °C. Averaging 64 readings gives a smoother, finer value. The PID uses floating point; at 10 steps per second that costs the CPU almost nothing.

Hot! At 100 % the resistor takes 0.5 A = 2.5 W and gets hotter than 80 °C. Don’t touch it, and keep it off the breadboard plastic (stand it on its legs or on a piece of wood). The sketch switches the heater off above 90 °C, and also when the sensor reads nonsense: outside −20…125 °C, for example 0 V on A0 = −50 °C (a shorted or reversed sensor).
Why the 10 kΩ: while the dsPIC is in reset its pins float, and a floating MOSFET gate can switch the heater on. The pull-down keeps it off. The 100 Ω limits the current that charges the gate at each PWM edge.

Step by step

  1. Upload Lab30_PIDTemperature and open the Serial Monitor (115200, “Newline”). It prints the mode, the room temperature (about 20–30 °C) and the gains. If it prints SAFETY ... sensor is not connected, check the sensor wiring. No parts? Send x for the simulated heater, and do the same steps.
  2. Open loop first: send m30 (fixed 30 % power). Close the Serial Monitor and open Tools → Serial Plotter at 115200. You see three curves: set, temp and power. The temperature rises fast at first, then slower, and levels off after a few minutes. That curve is the “plant”, the thing the PID has to control. Note how long it takes to get halfway: that is roughly its time constant.
  3. Send o (heater off) and let it cool down to near room temperature.
  4. PID: send a. The power jumps to 100 % (the error is large), the temperature climbs towards the 50 °C setpoint, the power comes down by itself before it gets there, and it settles where the heating balances the losses. The power you see then is the “holding power”.
  5. P only: send o, wait until it is cool, then i0 and a. Without I it settles below the setpoint: the steady-state error. Put it back with i0.08.
  6. Too much P: p30 → the temperature swings up and down around the setpoint. Back to normal with p8.
  7. Without D: d0 → more overshoot after the warm-up. Back with d40. Send v to add the P, I and D parts to the plot: you can see I slowly taking over from P as the error goes to zero, and D braking during the climb.
  8. Setpoint steps and disturbances: while in AUTO, send s60, then later s40. Blow on the resistor or fan it: the temperature dips and the power goes up to bring it back.
  9. Autotune: send s50 and t. The power now jumps between 100 % and 0 % each time the temperature crosses the setpoint, and the temperature swings around 50 °C. After a few swings it prints autotune done: Ku=... Pu=... and the new gains, and switches to AUTO with them. Compare the result with your own hand tuning.
  10. Safety: pull the sensor’s VOUT wire out of J2-15 and connect J2-15 to GND instead: A0 reads 0 V = −50 °C, the mode becomes FAULT - heater off and the USER LED blinks fast. (A wire that is just left open floats and can read anything.) Put the sensor back and send o, then a.

How the code works

The control loop runs every 100 ms. It measures, checks safety, and lets the current mode decide the power:

void controlStep()
{
    temperature = readTemperature();
    if (!heaterSafe(temperature)) {
        if (mode != FAULT) { setMode(FAULT); ... }
        return;
    }
    switch (mode) {
    case AUTO:   heaterSet(PIDcompute(setpoint, temperature)); break;
    case MANUAL: heaterSet(manualPower); break;
    case TUNE:   heaterSet(PIDtuneStep(temperature)); ...
    default:     heaterSet(0); break;          /* OFF, FAULT */
    }
}

In loop() it is called on a fixed 100 ms grid (tLoop += LOOP_MS). If the loop ever falls behind (for example during a long print), the timing jumps to “now” instead of running many steps in a burst.

PIDcompute() (in PID.h) measures its own time step and builds the three parts:

    float e = setpoint - measured;
    if (dt > 0.0f) {
        float rate = (measured - pidLastPv) / dt;
        pidDfilt += dt / (dt + PID_D_FILTER) * (rate - pidDfilt);
    }
    pidP = pidKp * e;
    float iStep = pidKi * e * dt;
    pidI += iStep;
    ...
    pidD = -pidKd * pidDfilt;
    float out = pidP + pidI + pidD;
    /* anti-windup: at a limit, take back an I step that pushes further out */
    if (out > pidMax) { if (iStep > 0) pidI -= iStep; out = pidMax; }
    else if (out < pidMin) { if (iStep < 0) pidI -= iStep; out = pidMin; }

The D part uses the rate of change of the measurement, filtered with a 2 s time constant. The last two lines are the anti-windup: if the output is already at 100 % and the error would push I up further, that step of I is taken back.

PIDreset(heaterPower) is called when you switch to AUTO. It sets I to the present power, so switching from MANUAL 30 % to AUTO continues smoothly from 30 % (“bumpless transfer”) instead of jumping.

The autotune switches between max and min with a 0.3 °C hysteresis, so sensor noise does not make it chatter. It records the highest and lowest temperature of each swing and the time between switch-ups. The first two swings are skipped (the warm-up is not typical), then three swings are averaged:

            float a  = (tuneHiSum - tuneLoSum) / tuneCount / 2.0f;
            float d  = (pidMax - pidMin) / 2.0f;
            tunePu = tunePerSum / 1000.0f / tuneCount;
            tuneKu = a > 0.01f ? 4.0f * d / (3.14159265f * a) : 0;
            ...
                float kp = 0.33f * tuneKu;
                PIDset(kp, kp / (tunePu / 2.0f), kp * tunePu / 3.0f);

Heater.h converts the ADC reading: volts = average × 3.3 / 1023, °C = (volts − 0.5) / 0.010. heaterSafe() forces the heater off above 90 °C or when the reading is outside −20…125 °C. The simulated heater is two lags in a row: the resistor heats with a 60 s time constant towards 25 + 60 × power/100 °C, and the sensor follows the resistor with 8 s. Some noise and the 0.32 °C ADC steps make it look like the real thing.

The plotter line set:50.00,temp:48.12,power:35.2 uses the “label:value” format that the Arduino IDE 2 Serial Plotter understands. Lines starting with # are messages.

Check your understanding

Why does a P-only controller settle below the setpoint?

Holding the temperature needs some power. P gives power only when there is an error, so a small error must remain to produce that holding power.

What is integral windup, and what happens without anti-windup?

While the output is stuck at 100 % (warm-up), I keeps adding up the large error and becomes huge. When the setpoint is reached it takes a long time to shrink again, so the temperature overshoots a lot.

Why is D taken from the measurement and not from the error?

The setpoint can jump (s50 → s60), and so can the error. Its derivative would be a huge spike ("derivative kick"). The measured temperature changes smoothly.

The autotune measures a swing of ±0.5 °C with the power switching 0/100 %. What is Ku?

d = 50 %, a = 0.5 °C, so Ku = 4 × 50 / (π × 0.5) ≈ 127 % per °C.

Simulator-tested with the simulated heater (MPLAB simulator; the heater model and the PID clock both run 20× faster, so the run takes minutes). Default gains, cold start 25 → 50 °C: no overshoot (highest 50.03 °C), within ±0.5 °C after 255 s, then 49.7…50.0 °C at about 41 % power. Step to 60 °C: no overshoot, within ±0.5 °C after 100 s. Autotune at 60 °C: Ku = 127.55, Pu = 18.6 s, giving kp = 42.1, ki = 4.53, kd = 261; with these, 0.6 °C overshoot at 60 °C, and the step down to 50 °C settles within ±0.5 °C after 55 s. The simulator has no working ADC, so the real sensor path was compile-checked only.
Not tested on hardware yet: the real heater, sensor and MOSFET, and gains for them. The default gains are a starting point; use the autotune on your own setup.

LED works backwardsUse LED_ON/LED_OFF, not HIGH/LOW — the LED is active low.
analogRead always 0 or 1023Wire on the right header pin (A0 = J2-15, not J3-15)? Pot ends on 3V3 and GND?
PWM / tone stops unexpectedlytone() and D8 PWM share SCCP4; Lab 13 uses SCCP3 (D7); Labs 14, 16 and 19 use SCCP2 (D6).
I2C scanner finds nothingPull-ups present? SDA/SCL swapped? Module is 3.3 V?
Lab 21 “no GPS data”GPS TX → J2-4, 9600 baud, GPS powered (its own LED blinks once it has a fix).
Lab 22 flickers / wrong coloursClock = 100 MIPS, common GND, 330 Ω in series, big capacitor; check colour order with effect 3.
Lab 24 timeoutsA/B swapped? DE+/RE on J2-6? Both boards 9600? Slave started without USER held?
Lab 14 “trigger path: NONE”The DMA/ADC setup needs register-level debugging — report the line printed and check DMACNT0 in the debugger.
Lab 17 settings lostExpected after any upload (the upload erases the app area). They only survive RESET / power-off.
Lab 16 measured frequency is not 20 kHzThe PWM clock is not FCY on your silicon: scale PCLK_HZ (e.g. FCY/2). “no edges on RB14” = PWM not running: check Clock = 100 MIPS.
Lab 12 says “POLLED fallback”The UART3 TX interrupt did not fire. Data still flows; report it so the UTXISEL setting can be corrected.
Lab 19 freezes / resetsA task stack overflowed (SPLIM trap): raise STACK_WORDS; check the “stack” column.
Lab 23 “no OLED at 0x3C”Run Lab 08; try OLED_ADDR 0x3D; SDA/SCL swapped? Blank but found: wrong OLED_H (32 vs 64).
Lab 18 never wakes from SleepPress USER (RC12). Sleep stops the UART too, so the PC sees nothing until wake-up. RESET always works.
Lab 15 J2-18 reads 0 VJumper to J2-17 for the read-back. If the pin stays at 0 V, DACOUT1 may need an output-enable this lab doesn’t set; the comparator (k) still works.
Lab 26 stays in “configuration” / bus-offClock = 100 MIPS? Normal mode needs a second node to ACK, a transceiver on RC6/RC7, 120 Ω at both ends. Use l (loopback) to test alone.
Lab 25 bitErrors risingJumper/transceiver on J2-5/J2-4? Same checksum type (c/e) on both nodes? 12 V on the transceivers’ VBAT?
Lab 27 OA_PHYID = 0 or FFFFFFFFSPI wiring (MISO on RC8), CS on RC9, RST on RD8 high, 3V3 to the click. Then check the register map against Microchip’s LAN865x driver.
